articles.title: College football refs ruin another game, Paige Spiranac whips up some eggs & Tony Romo's next move
articles.excerpt:
A'ja Wilson's mom reacts to question about what her "love beats hate" sign means after Las Vegas Aces defeated the Indiana Fever in the playoffs.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on ...
articles.body_text:
A'ja Wilson's mom reacts to question about what her "love beats hate" sign means after Las Vegas Aces defeated the Indiana Fever in the playoffs.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

First Friday of October? Come on! Might be right up there with the best weekend of the year. Fall is in the air. The leaves are turning. The sun is setting just a tad earlier every night. The weather is crisping up nicely.

Unless, of course, you're down here in Florida. It's rained every single day this week. It's raining right now. It'll be raining later. It's horrible.

We actually lost power, briefly, during the Braves game earlier this week. My wife is a huge Braves fan. It was chaos. I thought we were all done for.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Luckily, it came back on a few minutes later. The Braves went on to win. And then they won again last night. That means it's gonna be a much better first October weekend in this house.

Officials review Tulsa's two-point conversion attempt to verify the call at the end of the North Texas vs. Tulsa football game at H.A. Chapman Stadium in Tulsa, Okla., on Oct. 1, 2026. (Ron Lane/Cal Sport Media/Sipa USA via Reuters Connect)

Welcome to a Friday Nightcaps — the one where the college football refs ruined yet another game last night. Amazing.

What else? I've got Paige Spiranac whipping up some breakfast to get our weekend started with a bang, Lexie Hull getting tossed around like a ragdoll while the equally insufferable WNBA refs turned a blind eye and the Tony Romo era at CBS is officially donezo.

But have we heard that last from Tony? I doubt it. You'll see.

OK, grab you whatever you need to get you through the final few hours of this work day, and settle in for a first-Friday-of-October 'Cap!

This is gonna be a quick class, because it's a Friday and we have college football to bet on tonight.

How about Virginia Tech, by the way? The Hokies are 4-0 and now we're getting a meaningful night game in Blacksburg for the first time in what feels like a decade?

Goodness, how lucky are we? Pitt-Va. Tech. at 7 p.m., and we also get Northwestern christening their new stadium against Penn State at 8 p.m. over on Fox. Like I said yesterday — this is the best time of year.

Soak it all in, boys and girls. Don't waste a single second.

OK, now we're gonna start class with last night's debacle in Oklahoma, where Tulsa was screwed out of a game-winning two-point conversion ...

But they also shouldn't have been there in the first place:

In no world is that first "touchdown" a touchdown. It's just simply the incorrect call. I couldn't believe my eyes as I was watching it live. You can't step out and then touch the ball before reestablishing yourself. That's Football 101. It was clear as day, they reviewed it for 20 seconds, and then upheld the call.

Ridiculous. What are we doing here? There has to be some accountability. It's nonsense.

BREAKING UP TROY AIKMAN AND JOE BUCK WOULD BE A BIG MISTAKE FOR ESPN | BOBBY BURACK

As for the non-call in overtime ... that one is a little tougher for me. It's certainly not as clear as the first play.

This angle makes me think it was a conversion:

I don't see a knee on the ground. I don't see a shin on the ground. I don't see a cheek on the ground. I see the ball break the plane.

Again, that one's a tougher call because it's close. The call on the field worked against Tulsa, so I can see them upholding it. Don't agree with it, but I understand the logic behind it.

The first one, though? That's nasty work by the refs. Both teams deserved better last night.

And you know who else deserved better? Lexie Hull, who's spending her first day of the WNBA offseason in an ice bath:

Goodness gracious. Just a violent takedown. And, somehow, the foul is called on the player who is currently getting arm-barred into next week.

The entire sequence is just so perfect for the WNBA. It's everything right — and wrong — with that league.

The officiating is just horrible. That's No. 1. We forget about just how truly awful the officials are most of the year because there's so much other nonsense going on, but at the end of the day, they are undoubtedly the worst officials in all of sports.

And that includes the nonsense we saw in Tulsa last night!

Indiana Fever guard Lexie Hull reacts to a call Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026, during the first half of Game 3 of the first round of the WNBA Playoffs at Michelob ULTRA Arena in Las Vegas. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Remember earlier this summer when Sophie Cunningham got her teeth cracked by an elbow and no foul was called? Amazing. Same thing here with Lexie Hull.

Good riddance, WNBA. No, the season isn't over. But nobody will watch or care anymore. Caitlin Clark is out. Sophie Cunningham is out. It's over.

Can't wait to see the girls lace 'em back up next May! All eyes on the draft.

OK, let's rapid-fire this Friday class into a big Friday night. First up? We've ripped college football and WNBA officials so far today ...

Might as well end it with the fellas in the NFL!

This isn't a great look for the "there's no Patrick Mahomes bias in the NFL!" crowd ...

Lordy. I knew it was bad when I watched it live last Sunday. I said as much in Monday's class. But I didn't realize it was that bad.

Next? On the way out, let's all say goodbye to Tony Romo ... for now:

I'll be the first to admit, I didn't think CBS would do it. When Romo got arrested last summer, I figured he'd be back in the booth in no time.

I believe I even said he'd be back before Game 1. I was wrong.

Things were very clearly bad behind the scenes. So bad, CBS basically bought him out and decided to eat the contract. I'm not a huge Romo fan. I think he's been pretty awful the past few years.

Jim Nantz and Tony Romo, CBS Sports, speak on stage during the New York Upfront Partnership Event 2026 at Storied NYC on April 23, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images)

That being said ... I'd be shocked if he doesn't land a pretty big gig next season. I have no clue where it'll be, but I wouldn't bet against him.

Maybe Netflix? They appear to be getting pretty serious about the NFL.

There's also something ... fishy ... going on with Troy Aikman and ESPN at the moment. Joe Buck just signed a massive contract extension with ESPN, but it's been all quiet on the Aikman front. Him and Buck have historically been a package deal.

Maybe it's nothing. But, maybe it's something worth watching.

OK, that's it for today — and this week. Happy first weekend of October, everyone. Let's go have a big one.

Thoughts on the Tulsa game? Zach.Dean@OutKick.com.

ROSIE O'DONNELL CLAIMS TRUMP HAS 'PTSD RESPONSE' TO HER AS BACKLASH ERUPTS

"I don’t know where it came [from]. It’s complete assumption," she said. "I heard it and I went, ‘What the …?’ I don’t ever remember talking to her about this, so she’s just assuming.’"

"I’m not angry," she said, describing herself as confused by O’Donnell’s comments.

But Judd said there was never a political conversation for O’Donnell to draw that conclusion from.

Rosie O'Donnell and Wynonna Judd have maintained a friendship for decades. (Sylvain Gaboury / FilmMagic)

And she isn't interested in turning the misunderstanding into a celebrity political battle.

"I just don’t want drama," Judd said. "So, if there’s going to be drama [about it], I’m like, ‘Oh for crap’s sake, there’s so much going on right now in the world. Can we just love each other?’"

Fox News Digital has reached out to O’Donnell for comment.

Judd's comments come after O’Donnell discussed their friendship during an August appearance on "The Tangle with Kyle Ridley" podcast.

Wynonna Judd said Rosie O'Donnell made a "complete assumption" about her political beliefs. (Jason Kempin)

O’Donnell said Judd was the one Trump supporter in her life she still maintained a friendship with, explaining that their bond had allowed them to put politics aside.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I am friends with Wynonna Judd, who I love very much, and I’ve known her for many, many years. And she is a supporter of Trump. And somehow, we never bring it up," O’Donnell said.

O’Donnell went on to describe why she believed she could separate Judd’s alleged political views from their personal relationship.

Rosie O'Donnell said she believed longtime friend Wynonna Judd supported President Donald Trump. (Mike Marsland/Getty Images for Sky & NOW; Charly Triballeau/AFP via Getty Images)

"I kind of give her a grace in a way. She’s had so much in her life, with her mom taking her own life, and just the complicated nature of her upbringing. And I really love her and I care about her and for some reason I’m able to put that aside when we interact."

Her relationship with O’Donnell stretches back decades. Judd was a recurring guest on O’Donnell’s daytime talk show in the 1990s, and the pair have remained friends long after the program ended.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Meanwhile, O'Donnell has been an outspoken critic of Trump for years, with the comedian and president repeatedly trading public barbs.

After Trump won the 2024 presidential election, O’Donnell moved to Ireland with her child and has continued speaking publicly about American politics.

Stephanie Giang-Paunon is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Republicans pull funding of Trump-backed Senate candidate in critical North Carolina race
articles.excerpt:
Senate Leadership Fund is redirecting ad spending from Michael Whatley’s campaign to support other candidates

A major Republican political action committee pulled the plug on financial support for it...
articles.body_text:
Senate Leadership Fund is redirecting ad spending from Michael Whatley’s campaign to support other candidates

A major Republican political action committee pulled the plug on financial support for its Senate candidate in North Carolina, Michael Whatley, according to multiple reports, as the party begins to triage resources amid increasingly dire midterm polling.

The Senate Leadership Fund (SLF), the campaign arm of the Senate majority leader, John Thune, has withdrawn its ad spending in North Carolina to redirect support to other candidates, Semafor reported on Friday. The New York Times, CNN and other publications have confirmed the report with sources close to the fund.

The retirement of Thom Tillis from the US Senate opened the door for Democrats to flip the seat. Former governor Roy Cooper, a venerable presence in the state’s politics, easily won the Democratic nomination. Whatley, a former chair of the Republican National Committee, was handpicked by Donald Trump and viewed as a more mainstream candidate than other Republican contenders in the closely contested state.

The SLF had pledged $71m to hold North Carolina’s US Senate seat, and started targeting Cooper before he even won the nomination. The fund ran ads last year trying to link Cooper with the murder of Iryna Zarutska, a 23-year-old Ukrainian refugee, in an unprovoked attack onboard a light-rail train in Charlotte. Cooper was not in office at the time of the attack.

The Pac’s advertising in North Carolina has consistently focused on crime and public safety, featuring a series of interviews with crime victims. Ronald Hayes, whose son Shemar was murdered in 2024, appeared in one such ad. Hayes later said he had been “swindled” by the SLF, believing he was going to appear in an advertisement against gun violence and not a political campaign ad.

The SLF had planned to spend $30m more supporting Whatley. But polling data presents an increasingly difficult political map for Republicans trying to hold control of the Senate. Republicans have a 53-47 majority today. With the vice-president, JD Vance, as a tiebreaker, Republicans can afford to lose no more than three seats to keep control.

The Cook Political Report rates the North Carolina Senate race as “leans Democratic”. Seven other races are toss-ups; five are currently held by Republicans, including seats in Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio and Texas. Roger Marshall, the senator from Kansas, is facing a stiff challenge from Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor. Cook rates the race as “leans Republican”.

The SLF reportedly will redirect its North Carolina spending to support Marshall.

Cooper has persistently maintained a polling lead over Whatley despite the deluge of political ads. An AARP poll released on Monday gave Cooper an 11-point lead, consistent with other recent polls. Cooper has never had less than a four-point lead on Whatley in any poll this year.

In-person early voting starts on 15 October in North Carolina.

articles.title: Kennedy Center Honors awards moved to new venue amid Trump’s onslaught
articles.excerpt:
Ceremony will not be hosted at its traditional home for the first time since awards began in 1978

The Kennedy Center Honors will take place away from its traditional home this year for the first time...
articles.body_text:
Ceremony will not be hosted at its traditional home for the first time since awards began in 1978

The Kennedy Center Honors will take place away from its traditional home this year for the first time in its history as the John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts remains in jeopardy amid Donald Trump’s ongoing battle to have it named after himself.

The Capital One Arena in Washington DC is now set to host the ceremony on 7 December, a Kennedy Center spokespersonsaid. The list of honorees this year has not yet been announced.

The ceremony has been staged in the Kennedy Center’s Opera House each year since the awards began in 1978.

The change came as the Trump administration faces challenges in Congress and the courts over its plans for Washington landmark, including the possibility of demolishing it. The Kennedy Center Honors are widely regarded as one of the leading US distinctions recognizing achievement in the performing arts.

Last month, Christopher Cooper, a US district judge, directed the Trump administration to give at least 30 days notice before taking any action toward tearing down the building. Earlier this week, the Republican senator Mike Lee blocked a bipartisan bill that would have prevented Trump from demolishing the Kennedy Center without the approval of Congress.

Trump addressed the future of the center while speaking with reporters last month, threatening to tear the whole facility down. The center had abruptly closed for renovations, following cratering ticket sales amid his influence over programing there since he retook the White House, followed by a limbo.

“I think that the Trump administration should certainly have recognition. Because frankly, if we don’t do that, it’s going to close. It’ll end up being ripped down,” Trump said.

The dispute has involved efforts to put Trump’s name on the facility. The center’s board, whose members were largely appointed by the Republican president, had voted in December to add his name to the institution. Congress established the facility, which opened in 1971, as a memorial to President John F Kennedy, who was assassinated in November 1963.

In May, Cooper ordered the Kennedy Center to remove Trump’s name. In his ruling, he said the venue “must be named for, and is meant to honor, President Kennedy alone”.

Last month, Trump ordered that the Kennedy Center be closed “immediately” and warned that he would cancel the planned renovation of the institution unless federal courts permitted his name to appear on the front of the building.

That move followed another vote by Trump’s handpicked board to shut down the institution’s performing arts building. The board cited financial and safety concerns in support of the decision.

Trump’s plans for the Kennedy Center have also led to protests.

articles.title: UCLA law school accused by justice department of illegally using race in admissions
articles.excerpt:
University denies allegations, saying it is committed to making admissions decisions in compliance with all laws

The Department of Justice said on Thursday that the law school at the University of Ca...
articles.body_text:
University denies allegations, saying it is committed to making admissions decisions in compliance with all laws

The Department of Justice said on Thursday that the law school at the University of California, Los Angeles illegally considered race in admissions.

The announcement follows a similar accusation against the university’s medical school and comes as the Trump administration ramps up scrutiny of colleges’ processes for selecting students.

The Trump administration has also accused the UC Berkeley School of Law and the medical school at the University of California, San Diego of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants.

The UCLA School of Law denied the accusations and said in a statement that it was committed to making admissions decisions in compliance with all applicable laws.

“Students are admitted through a comprehensive, merit-based review process that considers each applicant’s achievements and experiences,” the statement said. “We are confident in our process.”

Affirmative action in college admissions has been illegal since a 2023 supreme court ruling forbade it. The same ruling said colleges could continue to assess how applicants’ backgrounds might speak to broader characteristics, but the president has accused colleges of using applicants’ personal statements and other proxies to consider race in admissions – which conservatives view as illegal discrimination.

The justice department said UCLA’s law school discriminated against white and Asian American students by favoring Black and Hispanic applicants in its 2023, 2024 and 2025 incoming classes. The department said its analysis found the mean LSAT score was lower for admitted Black applicants than for admitted white applicants.

The department also said admissions staff at the law school instructed applicants during recruitment efforts, including one called the “Diversity Admissions Open House”, how to reveal their race in essays.

“Like many of its peer institutions, UCLA Law School runs a two-tiered admissions system whose academic bar for acceptance shifts up or down depending on the color of your skin,” said Harmeet Dhillon, head of the justice department’s civil rights division, in a news release.

The Trump administration earlier this year tried to compel higher education institutions to release data including the race and sex of colleges’ applicants, admitted students and enrolled students to enable it to investigate whether the schools were considering race in admissions.

A federal judge in August halted that effort, granting a preliminary injunction after 17 Democratic state attorneys general filed suit.

The federal judge said the federal government probably had the authority to collect the data, but the demand was rolled out to universities in a “rushed and chaotic” manner.

The states argued the data collection risked invading student privacy and leading to baseless investigations of colleges and universities. They also argued that universities had not been given enough time to collect the data.

articles.title: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage
articles.excerpt:
Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police

The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in co...
articles.body_text:
Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, charged with one count of preparation of terrorist acts, say police

The man accused of murdering Ann Widdecombe has been charged with engaging in conduct in preparation of acts of terrorism including against Nigel Farage, police have said.

Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was charged by the Crown Prosecution Service on Friday with one count of preparation of terrorist acts. The charge relates to activity alleged to have taken place between 31 May 2024 and 8 July this year, counter-terrorism police said.

The senior national coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP), Deputy Assistant Commissioner Vicki Evans, said: “We have been running a hugely intensive and complex investigation for some time. The charge announced today is a result of the tireless work of investigators across the Counter Terrorism Policing network.

“This investigation has been led by a dedicated team of detectives, analysts, and forensic experts, working on multiple lines of enquiry, which has resulted in this very serious charge.”

Kerry was due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Wednesday, police said.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said the charge raised “serious questions” about the security of MPs.

She wrote on X: “I know the new charges made today will be extremely concerning. My profound sympathies are with Nigel Farage and his family.

“Let no one make any mistake: an attack on anyone in politics is an attack on us all.

“This case raises serious questions about the security of those in public life. We must use this as an opportunity to reset. Once parliament returns, I will update on our work to strengthen protections for those who choose to serve.”

Widdecombe, 78, a spokesperson for Farage’s Reform UK party and a former Conservative minister, died in July after being hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, a court previously heard.

She was found lying face down on her kitchen floor by her gardener on the morning of 9 July and declared dead by emergency services shortly afterwards.

Kerry is accused of her murder. The suspect spoke only to confirm his name, date of birth and address during a hearing at Westminster magistrates court in July. He was not asked to indicate a plea.

Olivia Field, the chief executive of the Jo Cox Foundation, which was set up in honour of the Labour MP who was murdered in 2016 in West Yorkshire, said: “No one in public life should have to fear for their safety.

“Violence, abuse and intimidation not only endanger individuals and their families, but threaten our democracy and have no place in public life.

“We must do more to prevent the rising levels of abuse and intimidation in politics. That means looking across society – from education and political literacy to the safety of online environments – alongside ensuring that appropriate security and support are in place for politicians, their staff and families.”

In August, CTP reopened a year-long investigation into an alleged firebomb attack at Farage’s home in south London.

The Metropolitan police and CTP London said they investigated the incident as an “attempted burglary” but made no arrests before the case was closed pending any new lines of inquiry.

Following its reopening, CTP London identified a line of inquiry that it said “may have been relevant” but had not been “identified and pursued by them at the time”.

articles.title: NFL suspends and fines 49ers owner Jed York for violation of conduct policy tied to prostitution arrest
articles.excerpt:
San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York is seen stunned after being arrested by police in East Palestine, Ohio. (Credit: East Palestine Police Department)

Going hunting for a prostitute in a trailer park ...
articles.body_text:
San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York is seen stunned after being arrested by police in East Palestine, Ohio. (Credit: East Palestine Police Department)

Going hunting for a prostitute in a trailer park wasn't the smartest thing San Francisco 49ers owner Jed York ever did and the NFL on Friday fined and suspended him for it.

The NFL announced York has been suspended six games and fined $500,000 for violating the league's Personal Conduct Policy. Three games of the suspension have already been served by York.

York released a statement in which he apologized for his "inexcusable mistake."

NFL RESTARTS SOCIAL JUSTICE MESSAGING WHILE BATTLING DOMESTIC ABUSE, DRUNK DRIVING AND PROSTITUTION ARRESTS

Kyle Shanahan and Jed York arrive on the red carpet for the NFL Honors show at Cyrus Northrop Memorial Auditorium at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis, Minn., on Feb. 3, 2018. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

"Today, the NFL concluded its review, and I accept its decision in fully," York said in a statement. "To my family, to the players, coaches, and employees of the San Francisco 49ers, to our fans and partners, I am deeply sorry.

"This was an inexcusable mistake and I take full responsibility. What I did does not reflect my values or the man I strive to be for my family. While I fell short of the model I want to set for my sons, I now hope to show them the importance of owning up to one's failures, and that even our worst moments teach us to be better.

"Leading the 49ers is a privilege, and one I don't take lightly. Your trust will have to be earned back over time, and I look forward to that work ahead."

The San Francisco 49ers pray in the locker room before their game against the Miami Dolphins at Levi's Stadium on Sept. 20, 2026, in Santa Clara, Calif. The 49ers defeated the Dolphins 35-13. (Getty Images)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

York had $160 on his person when he was taken into custody by the East Palestine police department in conjunction with the Mahoning Valley Human Trafficking Task Force on Aug. 23.

The arrest happened when York allegedly responded to an online prostitution advertisement and upon his arrival at a meeting site that was actually a residential trailer park.

So the NFL's fine and suspension, court costs and other fees, makes this a pretty expensive, not to mention embarrassing, attempt to hire an imaginary sex worker.

York has stayed away from the 49ers since he pleaded no contest to two misdemeanor charges of disorderly conduct and possessing criminal tools, meaning his cell phone, which he used to seek out the meeting.

Fans cheer during an NFL match between the Los Angeles Rams and San Francisco 49ers at Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) in Melbourne on Sept. 11, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)

A BRUTAL SUMMER JUST GOT WORSE FOR THE 49ERS AND THEY DON'T HAVE AN ANSWER FOR IT

York was sentenced to two days in the Columbiana County Jail with credit for one day already served, ordered to complete an online anti-prostitution course, and fined $1,150.

Adding the court fine, the NFL fine, and the $160 seized during the sting and forfeited to the task force, York's total cost will be $501,310.

Kyle Juszczyk No. 44 of the San Francisco 49ers celebrates after a receiving touchdown against the Miami Dolphins in the third quarter of a game at Levi's Stadium on Sept. 20, 2026, in Santa Clara, Calif. (Getty Images)

"During the time the league's investigation has been proceeding, York has stayed away from the 49ers first three regular-season games, as well as from NFL league meetings," the NFL said in a statement.

"Those three missed games are counted toward his suspension, and he may return on Oct. 20."

Despite his statement, York has not answered questions in person about this incident. But the NFL has a fall meeting scheduled for Oct. 20-22, and reporters will surely be present.

FOLLOW ARMANDO SALGUERO ON X: @ARMANDOSALGUERO

Armando Salguero is OutKick's Senior NFL Writer.

articles.title: Trump campaign insider reveals strategy behind midterm blitz that White House hopes pays off big
articles.excerpt:
A strategist and communications consultant told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's midterm campaign stops in deep red states are being misconstrued by much of the media.

A veteran campaig...
articles.body_text:
A strategist and communications consultant told Fox News Digital that President Donald Trump's midterm campaign stops in deep red states are being misconstrued by much of the media.

A veteran campaign strategist who worked for Donald Trump's 2024 reelection bid told Fox News Digital that pundits are misreading the strategy behind the president's 32-state pre-midterms rally tour, which includes stops in deep red states.

Thursday, the president spoke in Denton, Texas, a suburb of Dallas before traveling to Oklahoma, a longtime bastion of conservatism that hasn't been carried by a Democrat in a presidential election since Lyndon B. Johnson in 1964. Trump on Friday will rally in Mobile, Alabama, another traditionally Republican-dominated state.

While political analysts speculate Trump's blitz signals doom for the GOP in November, Luke Ball, who knows intimately the inner-workings of how the 47th president operates on the campaign trail, has a different view.

CAN THE 'BEST SHOWMAN IN POLITICS' DELIVER AGAIN? GOP BETS ON TRUMP AT HISTORIC MIDTERM CONVENTION

President Donald Trump speaks during a campaign event in Durant, Oklahoma, on Thursday, Oct. 1, 2026. President Trump and Vice President Vance are expected to be on the campaign trail almost every day in October, as surveys show Republicans rapidly losing ground amid voter anger over the economy and the war in Iran. (Dylan Hollingsworth/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"So, for people who are maybe commenting and doing it from a perspective of 'the president's in trouble,' I think that it's kind of a lazy analysis for you to just take it at surface value that he's in red states," Ball said.

He added that Texas and Oklahoma go "hand in hand," and that the appearing in both places can boost Republican midterm turnout in November across swing district or more competitive districts found in some deep red states.

Though he admits the strategy is a "risk" for Trump, he says the month-long tour isn't a fly-by-night operation.

GOP FACES BRUTAL MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS REPUBLICANS PAINT ELECTION AS ‘COMPETITION WITH COMMUNISM’

"They keep saying — and it's a risk politically for the president — but they keep saying that he is on the ballot and on the top of the ballot, but the reason they're doing it is because the RNC the MAGA Incs, and the James Blair's of the world have the data that show who's going to turn out for the president and nobody else," said Ball.

MAGA Inc. is a Super PAC that poured more than $375 million into electing Trump in 2024, and is now backing Republican congressional candidates nationwide. James Blair was Trump's 2024 campaign political director, and is now the White House Deputy Chief of Staff.

President Donald Trump arrives to speak about the economy at a rally Tuesday, Jan. 27, 2026, in Clive, Iowa. (Charlie Neibergall/AP Photo)

BLACK CONSERVATIVE REVEALS HOW GOP CAN LOCK DOWN MINORITY VOTERS WITHOUT TRUMP ON BALLOT

"The next stop is in Mobile, Alabama, another media market that I worked in, which is going to encompass Pensacola, Florida — which always brings out the vote for the rest of the state," Ball said. "So if you want to solidify your standing in Florida and show that you still are the kingmaker in that state that used to be purple a few years ago, and now Democrats don't even bother spending in it, you've got to make sure that you lock that down."

"So, great optics in Alabama, great optics in Oklahoma, but in addition to that, you're getting a red area of Texas motivated to turn out and a very, very red area of Florida to turn out for those elections."

Nationwide media coverage of the rallies is in itself part of the strategy, too.

"Other traditional candidates would strategically target and fine-tune the principal's time in various states, but people were saying Trump wasn't going to go out on the campaign trail at all, and now it's the total opposite," Ball explained. "It's, 'why is he doing so much? Why is he hitting all of these deep red states?' It's also from a perspective too, when you have these major rallies in Mobile, Alabama, or Oklahoma or deep red states across the nation, that still gets major national coverage."

U.S. President Donald Trump during an event in Rocky Mount, North Carolina on Friday, Dec. 19, 2025. (Cornell Watson/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

LARGEST-EVER US STEEL PLANT IS COMING TO A KEY RED STATE AS TRUMP UNVEILS $15B INVESTMENT

In Denton, Trump toured a Peterbilt truck manufacturing plant, where he met with employees of the company and made brief remarks. Stops like that are part of a broader campaign strategy, according to Ball.

"When we were on the campaign trail, I remember [former co-campaign manager] Susie Wiles saying that at every stop he goes to, she wants him at an off the record event, whether that's going into the Bluebird Diner in Iowa or eating a hoagie in Buc-ee's or whatever it might be, and I almost see a little bit of parallel here with the macro strategy behind the tour," he said.

Wiles is now Trump's closely trusted White House Chief of Staff.

"Instead of popping into a mom and pop show or store, he's touring manufacturing or he's going to a specific industry in one state and then holding a rally that captures the media market in another. So you're not just showing up and leaving," Ball continued. "You always think about what's the additional thing you can do to draw out voters in that state."

Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Florida Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov exits Sharks game with apparent leg injury as fans hold breath
articles.excerpt: NHL players and Olympic gold medalists Brady and Matthew Tkachuk discuss the pride of representing the USA in sports. They reflect on their Olympic hockey wins and offer advice to the current US socce...
articles.body_text:
NHL players and Olympic gold medalists Brady and Matthew Tkachuk discuss the pride of representing the USA in sports. They reflect on their Olympic hockey wins and offer advice to the current US soccer team in the World Cup.

The Florida Panthers were able to mount a valiant comeback in San Jose, rallying from three goals down in the second period and scoring two in the third before ultimately falling in overtime.

But while the Cats were able to salvage a point in the Bay Area, they potentially came away with far worse news.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Following an awkward fall in the second period, Panthers captain Aleksander Barkov left the ice with an apparent knee injury, looking visibly frustrated as he made his way down the tunnel and into the locker room.

NHL DEFENSEMAN BROCK FABER OUT INDEFINITELY AFTER SUFFERING SKULL FRACTURE FROM SHOT TO HEAD

Aleksander Barkov #16 of the Florida Panthers lies on the ice during a game against the San Jose Sharks on Oct. 1, 2026, at SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Barkov was able to skate and walk on his own, however, there are fears that this could be more severe than initially expected, with one South Florida doctor who is familiar with hockey-related injuries saying on social media an ACL tear could still be possible.

While coach Paul Maurice was unable to confirm the severity of the injury in his postgame press conference, Florida fans are especially anxious, considering an ACL tear kept Barkov out for the entire season last year.

MAPLE LEAFS STAR MAX DOMI REPORTEDLY FACING SCARY COMPLICATIONS, MOBILITY ISSUES AFTER SURGERY

This injury is thought to be unrelated to last year's, but you can hardly blame anyone for fearing the worst.

A little over a year ago, the Panthers were thought to be the favorites to make it back to the Stanley Cup Finals and even potentially become the first NHL team to three-peat since the New York Islanders teams of the early 1980s.

Florida Panthers center Aleksander Barkov (C) and NHL Deputy Commissioner Bill Daly, right, pose with the Prince of Wales trophy at the end of Game 5 of the NHL hockey Stanley Cup Eastern Conference finals Wednesday, May 28, 2025, in Raleigh, N.C. They advance to the Stanley Cup finals. (AP Photo/Chris Seward)

Then, during a routine practice towards the end of training camp, Barkov's leg bent awkwardly as he went down on the ice.

Florida would never recover after that, as a rash of injuries to other star players in addition to their captain saw the Panthers go from Cup favorites to missing the playoffs for the first time since 2019.

NHL STAR REVEALS HE HAD A BRUTAL BACTERIAL LUNG INFECTION DURING SEASON: 'I THOUGHT I WAS DYING'

Should Barkov miss an extended period of time, it will be interesting to see how the Cats shift their lineup accordingly.

Players like Sam Bennett or Anton Lundell could slide into his spot as the top line center, while the rumors will swirl whether Florida could play around with their cap space and sign Dylan Larkin from Detroit.

That would likely only be possible if the Panthers were able to put Barkov on long-term injured reserve (LTIR) as a form of salary cap relief.

Red Wings captain Dylan Larkin got a bit of an awkward happy birthday from his team after he requested a trade earlier this offseason. ((Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images))

Larkin has been fairly vocal about his frustrations in the Motor City, and Barkov's $10 million coming off the books could free up the space to make a move for the American center.

Regardless, losing the heart and soul of their Stanley Cup-winning squads is a blow the Panthers can ill afford, so here's hoping the road to recovery is quick for Barkov.

articles.title: Cornell rape allegations prompt NY Attorney General Letitia James to open ‘active criminal investigation’
articles.excerpt:
New York Attorney General Letitia James opens active criminal investigation in alleged Cornell rape

New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Friday morning she has opened an "active criminal...
articles.body_text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James opens active criminal investigation in alleged Cornell rape

New York Attorney General Letitia James announced Friday morning she has opened an "active criminal investigation" into an alleged gang rape at Cornell University in 2024.

"This is now an active criminal investigation led by the office of the attorney general," James said after New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed her as an independent special prosecutor in the case.

"Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, it will be investigated fully and fairly, that they will be seen and heard. That is the promise of our justice system," she said.

'CAME OUT OF NOWHERE': CORNELL STUDENT SAYS PRESIDENT'S CONFRONTATION IS UNLIKE ANYTHING SEEN ON CAMPUS

"I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law. In the coming months, my office will dutifully carry out the responsibilities the governor has conferred upon us in this executive order. We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses, and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions. I know that you want answers. I do too," she added.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James attend a press conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University, in New York City, US, October 2, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon)

Hochul signed an executive order appointing James as the special prosecutor on Thursday, citing "serious questions about the investigation conducted by the Cornell Police Department and the decision by the Tompkins County District Attorney not to prosecute an alleged sexual assault on Cornell University's campus in October 2024."

FRAT HOUSE TURNS INTO CRIME SCENE AFTER MEMBER ALLEGEDLY SEXUALLY ASSAULTS WOMAN, POLICE SAY

A woman identified only as Jane Doe filed a civil complaint in September accusing seven members of Cornell's Chi Phi fraternity of sexual assault and rape.

In the complaint, Doe alleges she "was plied with alcohol and drugs to the point of intoxication by members of Xi chapter's fraternal organization," which resulted in her "being sexually assaulted and raped by members of Xi chapter's regional fraternal organization at Cornell University."

HARVEY WEINSTEIN SENTENCED TO 15 YEARS IN PRISON FOR 2006 SEX CRIME IN NEW YORK

The Tompkins County District Attorney reviewed the case at the time and chose not to pursue criminal charges.

"Jane Doe’s sworn statement in November of 2024 did not allege that she was drugged against her will or gang raped. On the contrary, Jane Doe’s statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual. My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later," the District Attorney's office wrote in a Sept. 28, 2026 statement.

THE FRAT OMERTÀ: WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS OF ‘CODE OF SILENCE’ AFTER OLE MISS DEATHS, ALLEGED PENN STATE COKE RING

In a statement to Fox News following Friday's press conference, Cornell University said, "We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State’s rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case."

The offices of New York's attorney general and the Tompkins County district attorney did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital’s requests for comment.

"According to new reports, [Jane Doe] could not have been clearer that she was 100% confident that she had been raped. Yet, shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors," Hochul explained, citing a New York Times article. The report claimed Doe did tell Cornell police officers that she was raped but that information did not make its way into the voluntary statement the department sent to the district attorney's office.

CONVICTED RAPIST WHO PREYED ON WOMEN AT AMERICA'S TOP PARTY SCHOOL FACES RECKONING AFTER COURTHOUSE DASH

"The attorney general then declined to pursue charges after reviewing that incomplete account and never interviewing her. Think about that. In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney? In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved, or even request the full transcript?" Hochul asked.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James attend a press conference regarding an investigation into alleged sexual assault at Cornell University, in New York City, US, October 2, 2026. (REUTERS/Jeenah Moon)

Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, claimed he had never been informed the statement he received was inaccurate or incomplete.

"I have never been contacted by Jane Doe’s attorneys. Not to inform me the original statement was inaccurate and not to ask me to reconsider our decision. Rather, I reached out to Jane Doe’s attorneys after the lawsuit was filed to understand the discrepancy between the original statement and the lawsuit’s allegations and the proper path forward in light of the lawsuit’s allegations," he wrote in his statement.

Students on Libe Slope at the Cornell University campus in Ithaca, US, on Tuesday, April 11, 2023. (Bing Guan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Hochul told the public during her press conference that, in addition to James' criminal investigation, Cornell University has also reopened an investigation.

articles.title: US Coast Guard says it has intercepted ship carrying fuel to Cuba
articles.excerpt:
US says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continues

The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fue...
articles.body_text:
US says ship thought to be using common ‘dark fleet’ tactics was boarded and taken to Mexico as embargo continues

The US Coast ⁠Guard has announced that it intercepted a large cargo ship carrying fuel bound for Cuba, as the ⁠Trump administration’s crippling ⁠oil embargo against ​the island nation continued.

The vessel named Grace was stopped on 5 September in the Caribbean Sea between Cuba ⁠and Mexico while using tactics to evade authorities, the Coast Guard said. The New York Times reported that the ship ⁠was 91 metres (300ft) long.

“Grace was transiting to Cuba, carrying fuel, ​and was believed to be employing ‌tactics common amongst the ‌dark fleet,” the Coast Guard said in a statement.

A Coast Guard team ‌boarded the ship and escorted it to Mexico, where a Mexican navy inspection team “confirmed the presence of large quantities of fuel in the vessel’s ballast tanks”. The vessel was also carrying several containers believed to contain illicit fuel, the statement said.

The Trump administration has openly stated ‌that its goal is to change Cuba’s government. A US-imposed oil blockade implemented earlier this year has put the country ​under severe strain as it contends with fuel shortages and blackouts exacerbated by failing infrastructure.

Oil shipments from Cuba’s traditional suppliers, Venezuela and Mexico, ended abruptly after the US ousted the Venezuelan president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. US Coast Guard ⁠cutters patrol the waters off Cuba, while sanctions and threats have dissuaded ​tankers from even ​setting sail.

“The high seas ​are not a sanctuary for lawlessness,” Adm Kevin Lunday, the commandant ​of the Coast ‌Guard, said. “Dark fleet ​actors who employ ​deceptive tactics to engage in illicit activities will not evade justice.”

The statement did not say how authorities knew the fuel was headed to Cuba or how much fuel Grace was carrying.

articles.title: Top Democrats slam ‘Trump’s failing economic agenda’ after weaker-than-expected jobs growth – US politics live
articles.excerpt:
Elizabeth Warren and Chuck Schumer criticize president after US added 29,000 new jobs in September, sharply less than the 84,000 economists had predicted

Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Sen...
articles.body_text:
Elizabeth Warren and Chuck Schumer criticize president after US added 29,000 new jobs in September, sharply less than the 84,000 economists had predicted

Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, has blasted Donald Trump’s “failing economic agenda” following the latest jobs report – which many experts have described as “mediocre” and “weak”.

“Since January 2025, Trump’s economy has only added 33,000 jobs a month on average, far below the 120,000-a-month average in 2024,” Warren said. “Since the start of Trump’s war, real wages have fallen 0.7% as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up.”

Ahead of the November midterms, Democrats are hammering home that many of the Trump administration’s policies have resulted in a cost of living crisis, and urging voters to eschew Republicans vying for seats in Congress at the ballot box.

Meanwhile, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, noted that “American families are being squeezed on all sides by Trump’s disastrous economy”, in response to Friday’s figures.

Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, announced today that there will be a “one-day stand-down” this month, for service members to vote in the upcoming midterm elections. He added that many members of the military “face unnecessary, difficult ways of obtaining, completing, and returning absentee ballots while serving far from home” and said the directive would take place this year and every election year to come.

“We’re not telling you who to vote for, but we will give you every opportunity to do so,” Hegseth said in a straight-to-camera video. “Take that day to fill out your absentee ballot. Help your family members do the same, or go to the polling place yourself and exercise your right to vote.”

My colleagues are covering the move from G7 leaders to release up to 100m barrels of diesel reserves within four months, to mitigate the ongoing energy crisis as a result of the US-Israel war on Iran.

Earlier, as I reported, Trump welcomed the news after urging European countries this week to tap into reserves while he weighed an export ban. However, the president offered few details about which countries had signed on to the deal.

On today’s episode of Politics Weekly America, Jonathan Freedland is digging into the Texas Senate race.

The Democratic Senate nominee, James Talarico, is surprising everyone, as polls have him leading his Republican opponent, Ken Paxton.

Jonathan speaks to James Henson, founder and executive director of the Texas Politics Project, about why a blue wave in the Lone Star state – which hasn’t seen a Democrat win a Senate seat in almost 40 years – would be seismic.

On Truth Social, Donald Trump has claimed that Europe has “just agreed to release a massive amount of their heavily stocked Diesel Oil”. This comes after the administration urged European allies to release their diesel reserves as fuel prices continue to rise due to the ongoing Iran war and the president continues to weigh an export ban. The president added that “the process will begin immediately”.

In the US the average price for a gallon of diesel sits at $6.3, up from $3.7 a year ago – a 70% hike.

Trump said on Wednesday that he was still “thinking about” a ban on diesel exports to curb the soaring cost of energy domestically. However, he noted that an embargo “might raise the price of other things.” Europe has warned of a further economic tailspin in the event of a ban.

A reminder that major sectors of US agriculture, manufacturing and commercial fishing depend heavily on diesel.

Europe has also becoming increasingly reliant on US diesel exports after Ukrainian strikes destroyed Russian oil refineries and Moscow implemented its own export ban earlier this year to preserve its supply.

And as we bring you the latest on how the jobs report stands to impact voter sentiment ahead of the November midterms, my colleagues have done all the hard work in mapping out the battle for Congress and the key states, candidates and districts that will ultimately decide the balance of power on Capitol Hill.

Many indicators of voter sentiment suggest the Democrats are favored to take back control of the House of Representatives, and potentially the Senate. Winning either would be a significant victory for the party and give it the power to block Trump’s legislative agenda and more aggressively investigate his administration.

A reminder that my colleagues are covering the latest market reactions to today’s job report, including allayed fears about future interest rate hikes in light of the weaker-than-expected numbers reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate banking committee, has blasted Donald Trump’s “failing economic agenda” following the latest jobs report – which many experts have described as “mediocre” and “weak”.

“Since January 2025, Trump’s economy has only added 33,000 jobs a month on average, far below the 120,000-a-month average in 2024,” Warren said. “Since the start of Trump’s war, real wages have fallen 0.7% as his failed agenda keeps pushing prices up.”

Ahead of the November midterms, Democrats are hammering home that many of the Trump administration’s policies have resulted in a cost of living crisis, and urging voters to eschew Republicans vying for seats in Congress at the ballot box.

Meanwhile, Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader, noted that “American families are being squeezed on all sides by Trump’s disastrous economy”, in response to Friday’s figures.

Of note, the wage growth according to the latest jobs report, sits at 3% – which is still lower than the current 3.4% inflation rate. The gap here is crucial as voters prepare to vote in the upcoming midterms, and affordability is consistently polled as the key election issue ahead of November.

New figures, released by the Bureau of Labor Statistics, shows that the number of new jobs added in the US was weaker than expected, while unemployment saw an uptick.

The US added 29,000 new jobs in September, significantly fewer than the roughly 90,000 economists forecasted. Unemployment increased slightly to 4.2% – up by 0.1 point compared to last month’s data.

The latest report shows a drop in the overall number of jobs in September, compared to August, where the revised numbers show that the US added 133,000 new jobs.

Donald Trump will begin his day in Washington after spending Thursday campaigning in Durant, Oklahoma. He’ll travel to Mobile, Alabama, at 12.30pm ET today for a campaign rally. It’s part of the president’s 32-day blitz to juice support for Republicans ahead of the November midterm elections. He won Mobile county by almost 17 points in the 2024 presidential election.

Despite the president initially saying that he would focus his attention on competitive districts, in recent days he’s made speeches in Republican strongholds as his approval rating is still under water.

On Monday, following public outcry, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, said his office would reopen the investigation into the Cornell case, nearly two years after the student victim of the alleged gang-rape gave a statement to police.

My colleagues Richard Luscombe and Maya Yang covered the story earlier this week. They wrote:

double quotation markAccording to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.

None of the seven were arrested, they said, and the others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions.

On Monday, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.

Later on Monday, Van Houten released a fuller statement defending his office’s past decision to not seek charges.

“While I generally refrain from commenting publicly on criminal investigations, the community outrage stemming from the incomplete news and social media coverage requires that I provide an answer to why the investigation resulted in a lack of criminal charges,” he said.

Top lawyers, doctors and members of the faith community are calling for a moratorium on the US death penalty after Tennessee’s failed attempt to execute Christa Pike left the prisoner alive but in critical condition and receiving life-saving medical care.

The recent spate of harrowingly botched executions across US death penalty states reached a new low late on Wednesday when Tennessee’s governor Bill Lee called off the procedure after Pike had been injected with two full syringes of pentobarbital. She is the only person to have survived being administered 5mg of the sedative – a massive dose that under normal circumstances is considered fatal.

An hour after the first injection was given, she was overheard by eyewitnesses to be still breathing, choking and struggling, and was found to have a heartbeat. Her lawyers said that her current condition, and the degree to which she may have been brain damaged through oxygen deprivation, were as yet unknown.

Sandra Babcock, a death penalty scholar at Cornell law school who advises Pike’s legal team, told the Guardian that the events that unfolded were “unimaginably barbaric. They demand accountability.”

Letitia James is no stranger to high profile investigations involving powerful individuals and institutions.

Her most prominent case in recent years was the civil fraud action against Donald Trump and the Trump Organization. In February 2024, a New York judge ruled in her favour and ordered Trump to pay a $450m penalty after finding he fraudulently overstated his net worth to dupe lenders. A five-judge panel tossed the financial penalty last year, but James’s office has appealed to reinstate it.

In this profile of James in February 2024, Guardian US reporter Lauren Aratani wrote:

double quotation markRaised in Brooklyn with her seven siblings, James attended public schools before getting her law degree at Howard University in Washington DC. She rose through the ranks as a public defender before entering New York politics as a councilmember and then as public advocate, the first Black woman to hold the watchdog role and one where she filed a record number of suits on behalf of people with disabilities, seniors and tenants.

When she won the attorney general’s office, another first for a Black woman, James vowed to “take that power back” from corporations and corrupt politicians.

“The law is the great equalizer and the biggest pillar of our democracy,” she said in her inaugural speech in 2019. “I will shine a light into the murkiest of swamps and act as a steward of justice.”

The profile is more than two years old but still worth a read for useful background on James’s career and her involvement in several of the big cases that have defined her tenure as attorney general.

The governor of New York, Kathy Hochul, has named New York attorney general Letitia James as special prosecutor to investigate an alleged gang-rape at Cornell University in 2024, saying she had lost faith in the local district attorney’s ability to handle the case.

Both Hochul and James are due to speak today to provide an update on the investigation following the attorney general’s appointment.

Hochul said newly released information raised questions about the investigation conducted by Cornell police and the decision by Tompkins County prosecutors not to file charges.

“This has, in turn, undercut my faith, and the public’s faith, in the district attorney’s ability to effectively investigate and prosecute the case at this time,” she said in a statement.

James will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury, Hochul added.

Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins County district attorney, declined at the time of the alleged assault to file charges, saying his office chose not to prosecute because the victim’s testimony did not establish a lack of consent.

But with renewed attention on the case and mounting public pressure, Van Houten said on Monday that his office would reopen the investigation.

A woman, known as Jane Doe in court documents, filed a civil lawsuit last month alleging she had been drugged with ketamine and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house near Cornell University’s campus in October 2024. She reported the incident to the Cornell University police department several weeks later, but no criminal charges were filed.

James said her office would “fully and fairly” investigate the allegations.

You can read our latest report on this story here:

Donald Trump is heading to Alabama today as part of his near month-long midterm campaign blitz. He began the 32-day tour yesterday in safe Republican territory, starting with Texas and Oklahoma and continuing to Ohio this weekend and Nebraska on Monday. The US president is expected to campaign almost daily ahead of November’s midterm elections, as the Republicans wrestle to retain its slim majorities in both the House and Senate.

The Labor Department’s ⁠Bureau of Labor Statistics will publish its employment report today, with Reuters reporting that US job growth likely slowed in September while the unemployment ⁠rate held steady at 4.1% for a third month in a row.

articles.title: Woman in alleged Cornell gang-rape case was ‘failed’ by system, New York governor says
articles.excerpt:
Kathy Hochul briefs journalists with state attorney general Letitia James, who will be taking over the entire case

Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell

Kathy Ho...
articles.body_text:
Kathy Hochul briefs journalists with state attorney general Letitia James, who will be taking over the entire case

Letitia James appointed special prosecutor in alleged gang-rape at Cornell

Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, said on Friday that she would “ensure” that all the facts of the alleged gang-rape in a fraternity house at Cornell University “are brought into light” while harshly criticizing the institution for how they handled the 2024 case.

Hochul, a Democrat, said the woman in the case, was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including the police and the county prosecutor.

“I’m deeply disturbed at Cornell University’s police and how they handled this,” Hochul said of the Ivy League university in Ithaca in upstate New York.

In a rare legal development, Hochul late on Thursday announced that the state attorney general, Letitia James, was taking over the entire case as a special prosecutor.

“I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” Hochul said in a press conference on Friday morning alongside James.

“Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, they will be investigated fully and fairly. That they will be seen and heard. I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law,” James said. James will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury in a process that could lead to the pressing of criminal charges.

Hochul sharply criticized the investigation that began in 2024 after the woman in the case went to the police.

“In what world would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang-raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney,” Hochul said, of the alleged assaults.

The governor also criticized what she called “a gap in state law” relating to claiming a sexual crime was committed when the alleged victim was voluntarily intoxicated.

She said: “If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang-rape. Period.”

Hochul said on Thursday she was appointing James after she “lost faith” in the ability of the local Tompkins county district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, to oversee the case after he decided not to prosecute the case in 2024, among other reasons.

A former Cornell University student, who identifies by the pseudonym Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in September alleging she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024, when she was 20. She said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. The case has sparked national outrage, roiled the campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.

Thomas Giuffra, a lawyer for Jane Doe, said his client was “not doing well” amid the uproar.

Two members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell were expelled, but none of the seven were arrested nor faced any legal consequences, according to lawyers for the student. Some were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions. Now, Doe is suing the seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, and also the university itself, the fraternity and others.

Lawyers for two of the men she is suing have denied they perpetrated a sexual assault. One said his client had not touched the woman or engaged in any drug use.

On Monday, Van Houten said the allegations presented in the lawsuit were “dramatically different” from the statement the alleged victim gave the police two years ago. According to his account, the woman’s first testimony did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. However, he later told CBS News he had never seen her detailed account, but relied on a statement written by a campus police officer.

Hochul further said on Friday that Van Houten had said that Doe’s statement “did not establish that a crime had occurred” – but that new reporting raises serious questions about the information his office relied upon when it made that decision.

Now, she demanded that James conduct a “fresh and thorough review of all the facts” and “go wherever it leads”.

Hochul said: “Every parent who sends their child off to college expects them to be safe, and if something terrible happens, the student deserves to know that the people they turn to will listen to them, protect them, and fight for them. That is the bare minimum.”

James said her first priority was the criminal investigation into the alleged rape. “At this time we will not be focusing on the actions of the district attorney,” she said.

Cornell, which is a private sector elite university, has suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely. A fraternity is a selective, traditionally all-male club at a university in which some male undergraduate members may live together in residential fraternity houses on or near campus.

Cornell agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

articles.title: Welsh first minister calls on Burnham to deliever ‘new deal’ on devolution
articles.excerpt:
Plaid Cymru’s Rhun ap Iorwerth says he has asked PM to ‘put Wales on equal footing with Scotland as bare minimum’

The Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, has formally called on the prime minister...
articles.body_text:
Plaid Cymru’s Rhun ap Iorwerth says he has asked PM to ‘put Wales on equal footing with Scotland as bare minimum’

The Welsh first minister, Rhun ap Iorwerth, has formally called on the prime minister, Andy Burnham, to deliver a “new deal” in his first address to a Plaid Cymru annual conference since taking office.

Ap Iorwerth told party members during a keynote speech in Llandudno on Friday that his government had a “clear mandate” for devolving more powers from Westminster.

The first minister, who beat Labour to lead his nationalist party to victory in May’s Senedd elections for the first time, said he had written to Burnham on Thursday to ask him for “a new deal to redress the historic unfairness of our fiscal and constitutional settlement and to put Wales on an equal footing with Scotland as a bare minimum”.

After a standing ovation, ap Iorwerth added: “A new deal – the first of its kind – whereby a Welsh first minister invites the UK government to genuinely treat Wales not as a region of England but as a nation in its own right. A new deal to secure powers … not as an end in themselves but as a means of growing our economy and improving outcomes for everyone.”

The 2,000-word letter to Burnham made the case for transferring powers over policing and justice, rail infrastructure and the crown estate.

Ap Iorwerth recently told the Guardian he had been encouraged by warm initial discussions with Burnham – a stark contrast to his interactions with Keir Starmer. However, the Welsh wing of the Labour party in Westminster is generally sceptical of devolving more powers to Cardiff, especially now Labour no longer controls the Senedd.

The first minister said on Friday: “I do believe the new prime minister and I both want to have a constructive and positive relationship. I’ve looked him in the eyes and said do not undermine Wales as a nation … do not bypass our Senedd, and he looked me in the eyes and promised he would not. I will hold him to that.”

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has made much of his support for regional devolution of power and resources in England, but his approach to the existing devolved administrations in Belfast, Cardiff and Edinburgh is still forming.

Plaid Cymru’s Welsh election win ended 100 years of Labour dominance in Wales and blocked the momentum of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK. Welsh Labour had governed in Wales since devolution began in 1999 but won just nine of the 96 seats in the new Senedd. Support for the party had been ebbing for some years, driven by frustration over the management of public services, which have fallen behind the other UK nations on many metrics.

Ap Iorwerth’s win also put separatist parties in government in all three of the UK’s Celtic nations for the first time, although Plaid Cymru has ruled out an independence referendum during its first term.

The party’s last autumn conference in Swansea had been full of excitement as members sensed the tide turning in Welsh politics. Its first as a party of government remained more relaxed and homely than those of rivals with deeper pockets and more seats in Westminster.

The first minister’s demands for a “new deal” came a few weeks after a landmark summit of Plaid Cymru, Sinn Féin and Scottish National party leaders during which they affirmed their respective nations’ right to seek independence from the UK.

Support for independence in Scotland has hovered between 45% and 50% since the 2014 referendum. Data suggests it is rising in Wales and Northern Ireland, and stands at 32% and 36% respectively.

Burnham is expected to meet the three first ministers at the end of October.

A UK government spokesperson said: “This government is committed to building a stronger and fairer Wales in a stronger and fairer United Kingdom.

“That’s why our focus is now on working with the Welsh government to empower local leaders and communities to deliver good growth and jobs in every postcode.”

articles.title: Ben Affleck rejects 'propaganda' opposing AI, insists emerging technology will help filmmakers
articles.excerpt:
Actor Ben Affleck defended AI usage in Hollywood during a conversation with Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw on Thursday.

LOS ANGELES — Ben Affleck is fed up with what he calls "propaganda" against artificial ...
articles.body_text:
Actor Ben Affleck defended AI usage in Hollywood during a conversation with Bloomberg's Lucas Shaw on Thursday.

LOS ANGELES — Ben Affleck is fed up with what he calls "propaganda" against artificial intelligence as he has become one of Hollywood's most vocal proponents of the emerging technology.

Affleck made headlines in July when it was announced that Netflix paid him a whopping $587 million for his AI startup InterPositive, a venture virtually no one in the industry knew he had been working on.

Appearing Wednesday at the Bloomberg Screentime summit, Affleck was asked about the "cynical take" critics had over the deal, which claimed Netflix bought his company so it can do "despicable things" with AI with a reputable filmmaker attached to "provide cover."

"Well, that's a very cynical view indeed," Affleck reacted to the question.

NETFLIX CHIEF ADMITS TRUMP IS HELPING SHOWBIZ INDUSTRY AS FEDERAL TAX CREDIT BILL AIMS TO FUEL HOLLYWOOD JOBS

Oscar-winning filmmaker and actor Ben Affleck speaks at Bloomberg Screentime 2026 in Los Angeles, California, on Wednesday, Sept. 30, 2026. (Joseph A. Wulfsohn/Fox News Digital)

The Oscar-winning writer and producer insisted Netflix isn't in a position to do "despicable things" and alienate artists because "they need to be in business with people," describing the streamer as being "super judicious" when it comes to his various projects.

"I'm sitting down with directors going, 'Look, man, you can just, you can change the background here, you can do this, you can do that.' And what I find is that filmmakers and people — once they sit with it and have a sense of control and a sense of understanding what's happening, and it moves from this nebulous abstract terrifying alien, you know, 'It's gonna to kill us all like we're paper clips…' all this propaganda," Affleck said.

"And they actually see what it is — it's another form of computing that does tools and is a technological advancement that's really in keeping with a long-standing series of technological improvements we've made in the film and television business."

CONAN O'BRIEN COMPARES DECLINING LATE-NIGHT TV LANDSCAPE TO DETROIT

Netflix bought Affleck's AI start-up InterPositive for a whopping $587 million. (Mike Blake/Reuters)

"It's like the switch. They go, 'Oh great, wonderful.' And it's being used on films now where they're the same number of people. In fact, more people, technically, are being employed. And I think it's — they have been absolutely, in my view, true to their word of we want to make what we're doing better. We're not trying to just, you know, slash cost or do heinous things," he continued.

The "Argo" director revealed he used AI for "lots of things" in his forthcoming Netflix film "Animals," but refrained from pointing to specific examples of it, comparing it to a magician spoiling their tricks.

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

Affleck, who directed and stars in the new Netflix thriller "Animals" with Kerry Washington, said he used AI "for lots of things" when making the film. (Warrick Page/Netflix © 2026.)

When asked what parts of the industry he thought would be most affected by AI, Affleck dismissed concerns about an industry takeover by the technology.

"When I worry about AI, I worry about like my kids in school. I worry about 30% rise in, you know, the number of A's given out at colleges over the last three years. I worry about learned helplessness. I worry about responsible use. I don't worry about Skynet and I don't think that it's going to take over this business in any meaningful way. I think it's going to be additive," Affleck said, referencing the fictional AI system in the "Terminator" movies.

"But I think someone has to actually step in and do it in a way where it is that you can't just bury your head in the sand. It needs to be incorporated. Like a lot of technologies, it requires getting comfortable and getting familiar with. And then immediately it's knowable. You see all the ways in which it doesn't work, all the failures. The sort of dumb nature of it in a lot of ways, and it becomes a knowable thing," he added.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: Spain’s parliament rejects gov’t housing decrees amid mass protests
articles.excerpt: Spain’s government has lost key votes to ratify emergency measures aimed at tackling the nation’s housing affordability crisis, after protests intensified last month following the eviction of an 87-ye...
articles.body_text:
Spain’s government has lost key votes to ratify emergency measures aimed at tackling the nation’s housing affordability crisis, after protests intensified last month following the eviction of an 87-year-old woman.

The proposed measures, which comprised two separate decrees, were both shot down by the majority of ⁠the 350-seat lower house of parliament on Friday.

The move is a heavy blow to Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, whose government faces public pressure, including from the hundreds of protesters who had gathered outside parliament demanding help for renters.

The first decree was meant to stop evictions of vulnerable people, make real estate speculation harder, impose tighter restrictions on short-term leases and provide tax incentives to encourage renting and the construction of housing.

The second decree proposed making leases automatically renew when they are set to expire, essentially making them indefinite. A property owner would have to pay a tenant 12 months of rent to break the contract.

The right-wing ⁠Catalan separatist ⁠party Junts refused to back the housing decrees, saying they would ultimately tighten the housing market. The centre-right Popular Party and far-right Vox also voted against the measures.

Sanchez, who leads a coalition government composed of his Socialist Party and the far-left Sumar, ⁠appealed to lawmakers in the run-up to the vote to put aside political calculations and pressure.

“Think about ordinary people, about those who most need the protection of public institutions. Think about the millions of young people who ⁠cannot afford to ⁠move out of their parents’ homes. Think about the families living with the constant ⁠anxiety of ever-rising rents,” he said.

“Do the right ⁠thing, because I ⁠believe that if you do not, history will judge you sooner than you ‌think, and far more harshly than you can imagine.”

Miriam Nogueras of Junts argued the decrees would only lead to owners removing their properties from the rental market, and thus driving up prices even further.

“These decrees still allow speculators to buy property and to evict people,” Nogueras said.

As the vote was under way, protesters marched on the parliament demanding help for renters.

The government decrees were intended to quell a public uproar following the televised eviction on September 23 of Maria del Carmen Abascal, known across Spain as Maricarmen, that set off protests and a camp-in that occupied Madrid’s Puerta del Sol square ever since.

Abascal was living in the property in Madrid’s central Retiro neighbourhood under a rent-capped lease contract signed by her father in the 1950s. The property was then bought by the real estate and investment firm Urbagestion in 2018.

Urbagestion sought to terminate Abascal’s contract and evict her after raising her rent from 500 euros ($572) to 2,650 euros ($3,010) – nearly double her pension of 1,350 euros ($1,533) a month – according to Spanish newspaper El Pais.

When the police carried out her eviction on their fourth attempt, hundreds of activists who had been protesting against her losing a home she had lived in her entire life were waiting outside. Abascal has since been offered a preliminary agreement that would allow her return to her home.

Protesters rallying at the chamber in downtown Madrid on Friday held up homemade signs with images of vultures on them, denouncing the real estate speculators they blame for driving up prices.

Some people gathered outside the assembly chanted “your profits, our misery” as lawmakers voted down the government’s decree.

The average rent in Spain has almost doubled in the past 10 years. The average price per square metre has risen from 8.20 euros (about $9.08 at the time) in 2016 to 15.1 euros ($17.15) this year, according to the real estate website Idealista.

articles.title: OpenAI’s Medicare attack has exposed Australia’s ‘tech debt’. Fixing it could bring a big bill for taxpayers
articles.excerpt:
Home affairs department orders all federal government agencies to conduct review of ‘legacy technology’ amid fallout from AI agent hacks

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

T...
articles.body_text:
Home affairs department orders all federal government agencies to conduct review of ‘legacy technology’ amid fallout from AI agent hacks

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The Australian government faces significant “tech debt” that could bring a big bill for taxpayers after the OpenAI Medicare breach, as government agencies will need to fortify their defences against future attacks by AI agents.
