articles.title: Wong thanks ‘heroes’ who thwarted flydubai pilot’s alleged attack on co-pilot as Australians confirmed safe
articles.excerpt:
Israeli embassy says the Sydney couple were on board flight that was dramatically diverted after one pilot allegedly stabbed the other

Two Australian citizens were onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that w...
articles.body_text:
Israeli embassy says the Sydney couple were on board flight that was dramatically diverted after one pilot allegedly stabbed the other

Two Australian citizens were onboard a flight to Tel Aviv that was diverted after one of the pilots allegedly stabbed the other in an attack, according to the Israeli embassy.

The passengers are a Jewish couple from Sydney, the embassy in Australia confirmed to the Guardian on Thursday. No further details were provided.

The flydubai aircraft was travelling from the United Arab Emirates to Israel when it was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

One of the pilots, whom Israeli officials said was an Omani citizen, is accused of stabbing his co-pilot. During the alleged attack, the plane plunged about 17,000 feet in just two minutes.

Passenger Yaniv Hayoun later recounted how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt pressure as the plane dived before forcing their way into the cockpit and finding the attacker at the instrument panel.

“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during a meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel. “He was trying to destroy the instruments to disable the plane.”

Israel’s ambassador to Australia, Hillel Newman, said the incident reminded him of the 11 September attacks.

“You have here a very special incident, and due to the real heroism of some people on board, they were saved.”

Newman said heightened security alerts had been issued following the attack.

“It just shows that … those that hate Israel also hate the peace.

“It’s an attempt to hit at the peace itself, at the Abraham Accords, and the relationships which Israel does have with Arab and Muslim countries.”

The Abraham Accords normalised relations between the UAE and Israel in 2020.

Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the the incident.

There are about 12,000 Australian citizens living in Israel and 25,000 in the UAE.

articles.title: Billions of dollars, none of it taxed: ATO reveals the tech giants paying zero income tax
articles.excerpt:
Database names big companies – including Microsoft subsidiary and Netflix – that pay little corporate tax but notes there could be legitimate reasons

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest up...
articles.body_text:
Database names big companies – including Microsoft subsidiary and Netflix – that pay little corporate tax but notes there could be legitimate reasons

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Microsoft’s datacentre business, Optus parent Singtel and major coal and gas companies are among a group of large corporations generating billions of dollars in revenue in Australia while paying zero income tax.

Well-known multinationals including Netflix also only pay tax on a small fraction of their turnover, according to the Australian Taxation Office.

The ATO’s transparency database for 2024-25 shows more than one-quarter of big companies, often based overseas, regularly pay no or little corporate tax in Australia.

This includes the Brazilian-owned JBS Global Meat Holdings, which generated more than $4.8bn in revenue but paid zero tax, in a recurring pattern for the global food company.

Adani Mining, the operator of the Carmichael thermal coalmine in Queensland, has never paid tax after opening in 2021, despite earning significant sums.

The sprawling Inpex-led Ichthys LNG project near Darwin also continued a years-long run of not paying tax, despite generating $9.7bn in income in 2024-25, as did energy retailer AGL, which paid no tax despite earning $13.1bn.

The New Zealand dairy giant Fonterra – with more than $2.4bn in total income – was another major earner that didn’t pay tax, as was Sony Australia ($1.6bn in revenue) and the online retailer Kogan ($642m).

While the ATO does not typically publish tax information of individuals or companies, it is required by parliament to do so for all entities that generate at least $100m in Australian income.

The report did not provide detail as to why individual companies paid zero tax but noted there could be legitimate reasons for it – including making a loss, or using deductions and offsets to lower the taxable income.

Overseas companies often reduce their taxable income by making payments to related entities located in lower-taxing jurisdictions. The practice is known as profit shifting and can attract the scrutiny of regulators.

Jason Ward, the principal analyst at the Centre for International Corporate Tax Accountability and Research, said many resource projects reduce their tax bills by shifting profits to lower taxing jurisdictions.

“Singapore is the key place to shift profits to, and has been for some time,” said Ward.

While Singapore has an official 17% corporate tax rate – almost half that of Australia’s – it also boasts a system of negotiated tax breaks and discretionary incentives.

“Companies use it as a marketing hub, and you can sell your coal or LNG to your subsidiary in Singapore, and the profit of the actual raw material is booked there, not Australia,” Ward said.

The ATO’s acting deputy commissioner, Michelle Sams, said the agency was increasingly focused on making sure digital businesses and supply chains paid their share of tax.

“We look very closely if there’s no tax being paid in significant industries, including things like datacentres, to make sure that the level of tax being paid reflects the economic activity that’s happening in Australia,” Sams said.

Microsoft’s datacentre business generated $2.3bn in revenue from Australia during the financial year but reported no taxable income. The company’s computer and software business paid $160.6m in tax after generating more than $9.2bn in revenue in Australia.

A spokesperson for Microsoft said the company pays all tax required under Australian laws.

Netflix’s local operation, which regularly pays little tax in Australia, paid the ATO $8.4m after generating more than $1.4bn in local revenue. TikTok Australia paid $17.3m in tax after recording $686.6m in revenue.

An ATO ruling designed to clamp down on profit shifting is expected to raise significant sums from technology companies. But it is expected to face legal challenges.

Parliament also passed revamped media bargaining laws in August, clearing the way for levies on global tech platforms that fail to strike deals with Australian news outlets over the use of their journalism.

Ward said many technology companies reduce their tax bills by using offshore tax havens.

“Sadly, it’s pretty easy to do. You just put your intellectual property in a tax haven jurisdiction, and rather than book the value of the sale in Australia, it’s essentially shifted to somewhere else where it gets a much lower, lighter tax treatment,” he said.

Singtel went from a regular taxpayer in Australia before 2020 to a company that now regularly reports zero taxable income.

In 2024-25, it generated more than $8.3bn in total income but didn’t pay tax.

Optus was contacted for comment on Thursday.

An Optus spokesperson has previously said the company’s negative tax position was due to infrastructure investments and operating expenses.

articles.title: Daredevil Jaan Roose completes slackline walk high above central Seoul
articles.excerpt:
Estonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on Thursday

The lunchtime crowds drifted slowly ba...
articles.body_text:
Estonian completed first of two attempts to navigate narrow ribbon, 160 metres long and 120 metres high, near the city’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace on Thursday

The lunchtime crowds drifted slowly back to their offices along central Seoul’s main boulevard, heads up and phones raised to the sky.

High above, a narrow ribbon ran between the Koreana hotel and the Dong-A Media Center, a few hundred metres from the capital’s famous Gyeongbokgung palace and Gwanghwamun square.

A countdown ticked down on a big screen, and at 1pm, a figure stepped off the roof of the Koreana and out over the drop.

Jaan Roose, an Estonian aerial athlete and three-time slackline world champion, was in Seoul to cross a 160-metre long highline suspended 120 metres above the city, in what organisers called South Korea’s first high-altitude slackline performance.

The 34-year-old has made a name for himself slacklining dramatic urban environments, such as his 185-metre high feat between Qatar’s Katara towers.

In 2024, he became the first person to slackline the strait of Messina between mainland Italy and Sicily, completing the 3.6km traverse despite a fall near the end, caught by his safety harness. Last month, he covered 14.7km over 12 hours on a line above the Danube in Bratislava, Slovakia.

Below Roose, the Seoul traffic kept moving and the crowd held its breath each time he wobbled.

“Just looking at him makes my legs go weak,” said Kim Young-sook, an office worker. “I can’t imagine how he can do that without being scared. It’s incredible.”

Midway across, Roose sat cross-legged on the line, then lay flat on his back, drawing gasps from below, before the daredevil rose and continued.

“I’m worried he might fall”, said Choi Eun-jung, who came out to see Roose. “I know he’s a professional, but it’s still a little frightening to watch.”

On reaching Dong-A Media Center, he turned around, and started his return to the hotel rooftop.

At the halfway point, he again dropped down and waved at the crowd. But this time he hung from the line with one arm and then dangled by his feet.

When he finished his performance, the crowds clapped, some clearly relieved.

At nearby Cheonggye plaza, people tried out their skills on slacklines, but these were set a mere 30cm and 50cm off the ground. Roose was scheduled for a second performance at 4pm.

Roose said a visit in 2022 to South Korea inspired his Gwanghwamun walk.

On that trip, Roose encountered jultagi, Korea’s traditional tightrope walking, which Unesco added to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2011.

Unlike tightrope walking elsewhere, jultagi is as much comedy as acrobatics. The walker sings, jokes and dances on the rope, trading banter with a clown on the ground as musicians play.

articles.title: Charity threatens legal action over two-year NHS wait for ADHD and autism assessments
articles.excerpt:
Exclusive: ADHD UK may seek judicial review of West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board’s ‘unlawful’ policy

ADHD UK has threatened legal action against an NHS organisation over its decision to impose...
articles.body_text:
Exclusive: ADHD UK may seek judicial review of West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board’s ‘unlawful’ policy

ADHD UK has threatened legal action against an NHS organisation over its decision to impose a minimum two-year wait for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder and autism assessments.

In a legal letter to West Yorkshire NHS integrated care board (ICB), seen by the Guardian, the charity alleges that the decision to force patients to wait at least two years for such assessments was unlawful and says it will seek a judicial review if the board fails to reverse the policy.

West Yorkshire ICB introduced the two-year minimum wait this year, affecting thousands of people with possible ADHD or autism in Leeds, Bradford, Kirklees, Calderdale and Wakefield.

West Yorkshire is not the only ICB to ration access to assessment for neurodiversity. The Guardian revealed last week that it was one of four – alongside Devon, Somerset, and North East and North Cumbria – to have imposed minimum waits amid spiralling costs due to the volume of assessments being sought. A further 11 have introduced other mechanisms to ration the number of assessments.

ADHD UK claims West Yorkshire failed to follow correct procedures, alleging the ICB breached equalities legislation, denied patients their legal right to choose non-NHS care, failed to involve patients, carers or the public in the decision, and that the decision ran counter to NHS contract regulations.

Henry Shelford, the chief executive of ADHD UK, said: “We have sent formal notice warning West Yorkshire that we are prepared to go to court unless it scraps that rule. We believe locking patients out of NHS choice is illegal because it breaches patients’ legal right to choose where they receive NHS care.

“We believe the processes they’ve strung together to push this through have been used incorrectly and, in some cases, improperly.”

The charity’s legal “letter before claim” to West Yorkshire ICB states: “There is no published decision record, equality impact assessment, public involvement, demand and capacity analysis, clinical safety assessment or statement of reasons specific to the two-year minimum.”

It says that unless West Yorkshire withdraws or suspends the two-year minimum, to retake any decision lawfully and to provide the information and documents that will allow the issues to be narrowed or resolved without proceedings, ADHD UK will seek a judicial review.

The disclosure comes ahead of a government-commissioned review of mental health, ADHD and autism prevalence led by Prof Peter Fonagy. The review is expected to recommend a “needs-based” system whereby patients with ADHD symptoms should not automatically be formally diagnosed but should be “triaged” and offered support without requiring a formal diagnosis. It is also expected to propose greater regulation of private psychiatry clinics.

Corinne Hunter, the chief executive of Stripes, a charity supporting children and adults with ADHD in West Yorkshire, said the ICB’s decision was devastating for patients and that the board had not let the charity know it planned to impose a minimum wait.

She said: “We weren’t consulted or told in advance about the decision – we initially heard about it through word of mouth from our own service users. There are ‘right to choose’ providers that are able to offer assessments much sooner, so for people in West Yorkshire to now face a minimum two-year wait is devastating.

“People often put off seeking an ADHD assessment for years, until they reach the point where they are really struggling to cope. Getting referred can finally feel like there is some light at the end of the tunnel, only to then be told that light could be another two years away.”

A spokesperson for NHS West Yorkshire ICB said: “We have received correspondence from ADHD UK. As this matter may be subject to legal proceedings, it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage.”

articles.title: Modi’s India takes on Trump more openly, from ‘terrorism’ to tariffs
articles.excerpt: New Delhi, India — Speaking at an event in New York this week, India’s Foreign Affairs Minister S Jaishankar offered a blunt assessment of Washington: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s con...
articles.body_text:
New Delhi, India — Speaking at an event in New York this week, India’s Foreign Affairs Minister S Jaishankar offered a blunt assessment of Washington: It has been an insensitive partner to India’s concerns over “terrorism”; has warmed to its arch-rival Pakistan; and has pursued “self-centered” trade policies that have disproportionately hurt the Global South.

That tone marks a new edge in how New Delhi is dealing with US President Donald Trump’s administration in Washington, analysts say, on the back of rising bilateral tensions between the capitals.

For decades, India has dealt with divisive issues with otherwise friendly nations quietly behind the scenes, away from spectacle. That has especially been New Delhi’s approach with Washington, where the relationship has broadly enjoyed wide bipartisan support.

However, after months of tensions, New Delhi is adopting a more openly critical tone towards Washington to address the volatility and uncertainty that Trump brings to the White House.

The changing tune in New Delhi also comes at a critical time for Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who faces mounting domestic pressure and criticism from the opposition for allegedly bowing down to US pressure, time and again. On Wednesday, Modi held a telephone call with Trump, which the Indian PM called “productive” — a cold and formal depiction far removed from his description of the US president as a “good friend” in previous years.

Chietigj Bajpaee, a senior research fellow for South Asia at the Chatham House think tank, said that Jaishankar’s remarks “offer a frank assessment” on the current state of the India-US relationship. “Clearly, the shine has come off the bilateral relationship after India was initially among the most optimistic about a second Trump term,” he said.

Jaishankar addressed frictions between India and the US while speaking at an Asia Society event after the UN General Assembly in New York ended on Monday.

“If I stand back and look at the [India-US] relationship, I note that much of the world has had a more difficult relationship with the US,” he said. “I mean that may not be a consolation, but that’s a reality.”

Trade has been one of the flashpoints. Washington is India’s largest trading partner, with bilateral goods trade reaching $149.1 billion in 2025; but the relationship remains tilted towards India with a $58.4 billion goods surplus.

Jaishankar started by noting: “Countries should not be so self-centred that you’re in your own world and take your decision and say, ‘Well, it was not my intention to make your life difficult’.”

The minister was partly referring to the economic spillover of the wars in Iran and Ukraine, urging that “sound common sense” should ensure that the basic needs of countries were not neglected.

But then, he referred to the trade negotiations between India and the US, that have so far yielded a roadmap to a deal — but not a deal itself. “Apart from the per capita gap between India and the United States, the nature of production and the nature of society is very different,” he noted.

The agricultural sector has been among the most contested points between the two, where India has kept its market largely closed for decades to safeguard its farmers. “The expectation that it could rapidly move forward was tested against the ground reality, which was much more complex,” he said, adding that “there is more or less an understanding on the trade agreement.”

At one point, India was among the countries facing the worst tariff rates imposed by Trump. After the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s sweeping tariffs in February, his administration swiftly turned to other tools, including a new 10 percent global tariff. Earlier this month, Trump signed a law under which the US can impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries like India that purchase Russian oil.

Jaishankar pointed to these changes, noting that the negotiations created “bumps last year for the relationship,” and added that once the deal is closed, it “would contribute to a better relationship.”

Ajay Bisaria, a retired diplomat who served as high commissioner to Canada and Pakistan, and as ambassador to Poland, told Al Jazeera that with Washington, in particular, “India has decided to be more public because there has been a lot of public criticism and a sentiment that the US is bullying India and India has been silent.”

The new 100 percent tariff on India, due to come into effect in less than a month, “is sort of a deal breaker in the relationship right now,” said Bisaria. “If that becomes reality, then all Indian efforts [to reach out to the US] would come under scrutiny.”

But trade isn’t the only challenge in the relationship. A major rupture emerged in May last year, when New Delhi engaged in a four-day war with its bitter neighbour, Pakistan, after an attack by armed fighters in Indian-administered Kashmir killed 26 civilians.

New Delhi was upstaged as President Trump announced a ceasefire, claiming that he threatened both countries with economic damage if they didn’t stop fighting. For India, any question on Kashmir is strictly bilateral with Pakistan, with no room for so-called third-party intervention.

Nevertheless, Trump has gone on to claim dozens of times that he brokered the crucial ceasefire — as recently as at the UNGA in New York — that halted the war between two nuclear-armed neighbours. India took offence to these claims.

On the other hand, Pakistan’s leaders cozied up to Trump, showered high praise, and nominated him for a Nobel Peace Prize. Since then, the relationship between Islamabad and Washington has bloomed, to New Delhi’s obvious irk.

For India, Jaishankar said, “particularly important is the issue of terrorism.”

“As a country, perhaps there are very few countries which have been subjected to the kind of terrorism that we have from a neighbour as part of a deliberate, conscious policy over many, many decades,” Jaishankar said, referring to Pakistan.

“Now, if something which matters so deeply to us, there isn’t enough understanding or appreciation or empathy of that, I think that creates a problem too,” he said, adding that India’s primary concerns are “not fully appreciated” by its partner, the US.

New Delhi’s changing tone while addressing Washington “is a lesson learnt from its experiences,” said Bisaria, the former diplomat. “After the ceasefire issue, the moods changed — and it all became worse.”

Harsh Pant, vice president of the Observer Research Foundation, a New Delhi-based think tank, said that “the obsession with Pakistan in the Trump administration without taking India’s sensitivities into account contributed to the sense that, look, we need to start articulating it.”

“When at the top level, you don’t see reciprocity, then calculations change and decisions are taken to bring differences out in the open,” Pant told Al Jazeera, referring to Jaishankar’s comments.

Indians have been the biggest beneficiaries of the US’s H1B programme which allows hiring of foreign workers with training in specialty fields. But that has come under fire from Trump, under whose watch Washington has raised barriers and fees for applicants, amid growing criticism of the scheme from supporters of his MAGA movement.

“For many years, mobility was seen as an economic gain. Today the economics of mobility and the politics of mobility are at odds with each other, at least in some quarters,” Jaishankar said, referring to Trump’s anti-immigration politics.

“That certainly in public perception is an issue,” the minister said.

Domestic pressure appears to be finally catching up in New Delhi. “Modi is feeling domestic pressure, with key state elections coming up next year, especially amid some anti-incumbency,” said Bisaria. “It dictates that the government’s posture should not be one of taking bullying from the US.”

Pant said issues like migration impact the general public in India, with the world’s largest population. For years, such connections made the US “an attractive partner for a large mass of Indians.” But today, he said, ”the same issues are becoming a negative drag on the relationship.”

“The public mood in India is also changing perceptibly towards the US. And I think the government is articulating that negative sentiment now publicly,” Pant said.

When Trump returned to the White House for his second presidential run, many in New Delhi’s strategic community were optimistic about bilateral relations, because of the US president’s warm personal relations with PM Modi during his first term.

But things unravelled in the coming months.

Still, Chatham House’s Bajpaee said that despite widening divisions between the US and India, “both have not given up on reviving their relationship”.

He pointed to Jaishankar’s remarks that India isn’t singled out in having a difficult relationship with the US. “Rather, the downturn in India-US relations is a reflection of the Trump administration’s transactional and often unpredictable or erratic foreign policy,” he told Al Jazeera.

“This offers a potential off-ramp for an eventual reset in relations. The conclusion of a bilateral trade agreement is a key watchpoint for this,” Bajpaee added.

For New Delhi, Pant said, “it is now just the question of waiting Mr. Trump out.” Though he added, with a laugh, that India is not alone in that queue.

“Everyone is waiting him out. President Trump has little respect for conventions and norms of inter-state behaviour. How do you just deal with that individual?” Pant said.

articles.title: Mourners bury DR Congo official killed after defending Ebola response
articles.excerpt: Mourners have gathered in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to bury a local politician who his party said was beaten to death after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radi...
articles.body_text:
Mourners have gathered in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) to bury a local politician who his party said was beaten to death after he defended the government’s Ebola response on the radio.

The funeral for Marie-Celestin Karondwa was held in the city of Butembo on Wednesday.

Karondwa was attacked on Sunday at his home in Butembo, an Ebola hotspot in North Kivu province, according to his political party, the Union for Democracy and Social Progress (UDSP), which leads the DRC government. He died of his injuries at a local hospital.

“They beat him up and then set the house on fire,” his granddaughter, Sagesse Kavira, told The Associated Press news agency at the funeral.

The party said Karondwa was “an innocent victim for having defended the party’s position on the existence of the Ebola virus disease … and the threat it poses to the population”.

It was not immediately clear who carried out the attack, how many were involved or what motivated it.

The killing follows a series of attacks on health workers and other responders as the Central African nation battles its 17th and deadliest Ebola outbreak, which has so far recorded more than 8,000 cases, including nearly 4,000 deaths.

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, for which there is no vaccine or specific treatment, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). Researchers are testing potential candidates, the agency said.

The WHO said Ebola was present in provinces including Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Sud Ubangi and Tshopo. It said Ituri remained the most affected.

Officials have tried to fight the outbreak through a village-based approach, but some residents have resisted, dismissing Ebola as a hoax amid deep distrust of the government.

Many believe the disease is a ruse for officials to siphon off money. Some refuse to report their symptoms due to disbelief or shame surrounding being an Ebola patient.

Responders say the scepticism has complicated their work, including in remote communities and newly emerging hotspots that are short of medical supplies and health workers.

The mistrust has been especially hard to overcome in rebel-held areas of eastern DRC, where decades of conflict and human rights abuses have left many residents wary of outsiders and state authorities.

Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO’s director general, has said the country’s east faces “a catastrophic collision of disease and conflict” hampering the response.

articles.title: Healey urged to offer energy support in budget as bills rise 4%
articles.excerpt:
Millions of people in Great Britain face increase from Thursday to an average of £1,723 a year for a typical home

John Healey is under growing pressure to offer fresh energy support for households in...
articles.body_text:
Millions of people in Great Britain face increase from Thursday to an average of £1,723 a year for a typical home

John Healey is under growing pressure to offer fresh energy support for households in next month’s budget as millions face a 4% rise in charges from Thursday to an average of £1,723 a year for a typical home.

In his speech at Labour’s conference in Liverpool this week, the chancellor warned that the government had limited resources to cushion the worldwide economic shocks hitting Britain, while arguing his budget would have fiscal discipline at its core.

The quarterly energy price cap, set by the regulator for Great Britain, Ofgem, will rise to its highest level in three years despite Andy Burnham’s decision to cut VAT from electricity bills to save the average household £45 a year from 1 October.

Households also face rising road fuel costs after diesel prices reached a record high of almost £2 a litre this week, which is expected to accelerate the rising cost of goods across the economy.

Treasury sources insist the 28 October budget will be tightly focused amid the challenging global backdrop, as bond market jitters add to the pressure on the public finances.

Insiders said tax devolution was likely to be centre stage to meet Andy Burnham’s promise to shake up Whitehall, while several big decisions could be pushed back to a spending review next year.

Some MPs are privately concerned that Healey and his team have failed to grasp the severity of the energy crunch ahead. “Without it [fresh energy support], the vibes will end,” said one Labour MP. “The problem is the Treasury are just not understanding where the country are.”

Healey warned in his speech that the money New Labour had in the 1990s was “simply not there now”, although he also vowed to offer “a bit of breathing space” for households and businesses.

As energy bills rise for millions of households from Thursday, a group of leading campaigners, charities, trade unions and thinktanks warned that failure to take action would risk deepening the cost of living crisis.

Writing in an open letter to the chancellor and the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, the group – including the New Economics Foundation, the Joseph Rowntree Foundation and Generation Rent – called for a package of universal energy support as well as targeted measures to help those most in need.

Coordinated by the Cost of Living Action campaign group, other signatories included Neal Lawson of Compass and Mathew Lawrence of Common Wealth – both of whose ideas have fed into Burnham’s policymaking.

With the war in the Middle East pushing up global oil and gas prices, the leading energy forecaster Cornwall Insight predicts the cap will increase by a further 16% from January to £1,999 for the average annual dual-fuel bill.

Paul Nowak, the general secretary of the TUC, said this “energy bill emergency” meant the government should “go further and faster” at the budget to protect households.

On Wednesday, Burnham said Labour “will do our best” but warned that the government faced tough financial constraints, telling the BBC there was not “huge room for manoeuvre” to take further action.

In his first weeks in office, the prime minister announced the six-month VAT holiday on electricity bills and a £2 cap on bus fares in England.

The Treasury is under pressure to extend the six-month VAT holiday, and shift the levies used to support new clean energy projects and grid upgrades from energy bills into general taxation.

The changes are understood to already be under consideration by Fahnbulleh, who is reportedly hoping to save customers an average of £120 a year on their energy bills – but this could involve putting up taxes by as much as £3bn.

However, the campaigners warned that further cost of living support was needed. “It is clear that this does not go far enough and that what is coming down the track this winter requires a much more substantial response,” they wrote.

Highlighting the risks from soaring energy bills, new polling carried out by More in Common on behalf of the Joseph Rowntree Foundation shows 28% of households are extremely worried about the prospect of the Iran war pushing up bills this winter, while 43% are quite concerned.

It found 66% of British adults think the government needs to do more to tackle the cost of energy.

Calling for bolder action, NEF urged the government to introduce a new “national energy guarantee” giving all households a basic amount of energy at a fixed low cost, with higher levels of consumption charged at market prices.

Responding to the letter, Fahnbulleh said:“I know energy price rises weigh heavily on homes across the UK this winter.

“From today, our VAT cut will give households some much-needed breathing space, making the energy price cap £45 a year less than it would have been. This follows the £150 of costs we removed from bills earlier this year.

“Alongside this, we continue to look at what more we can do to protect families from unaffordable bills, as we drive down bills for good through clean power.”

Burnham said: “For many families, the energy bill is the one they dread the most. I don’t accept that it has to be this way, and I am determined to bring down costs for good.”

articles.title: Prisoners freed early in England and Wales risk living on the streets, say probation officers
articles.excerpt:
Warning of a lack of hostel places for 2,000 criminals due to be released over the next month to ease overcrowding

Hundreds of prisoners are due to be released early from jail on Thursday amid warnin...
articles.body_text:
Warning of a lack of hostel places for 2,000 criminals due to be released over the next month to ease overcrowding

Hundreds of prisoners are due to be released early from jail on Thursday amid warnings that many will have nowhere to live and the probation system will struggle to monitor them.

About 2,000 criminals including domestic abusers and violent offenders are to be freed over the next month, with another 3,000 in stages over the next year to ease overcrowding. The number was reduced from 6,000 after an intervention by the prime minister, Andy Burnham.

Prisoners are supposed to be found appropriate accommodation before their release, significantly reducing reoffending rates.

But a probation source told the Guardian that their colleagues in some towns and cities were struggling to find hostel places.

“We have a handful of places for ex-offenders and they are full. We are now looking at releasing some people straight on to the street,” the source said.

Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “We know that leaving prison homeless can put people on a path back into custody. It is vital that the whole system from prisons and probation to councils and community providers work together to give people a roof over their heads.”

Napo, the probation officers’ union, has raised the issue of the accommodation shortage with prison bosses. The task of finding beds for prisoners is expected to reach critical levels from 13 October, when a second tranche of prisoners is due for release.

Ben Cockburn, the union’s national chair, said HM Prison Service seemed to be in “absolute denial” about the state of the Probation Service.

“We have massive staff shortages, unsustainable and dangerously high workloads and electronic monitoring is failing to deliver,” he said.

Ministers say the expanded early release scheme is needed to prevent the collapse of the criminal justice system. They say the Conservatives in their time in power added too few prison places while increasing the length of sentences.

Criminals will be excluded from the scheme if they have been jailed in child grooming gang cases or convicted of indecent assault. Those guilty of manslaughter will also be excluded, meaning the killers of Andrew Harper, a police officer who died in the line of duty in 2019, will not be eligible.

The releases will take place across dozens of prisons across England and Wales from Thursday.

The expansion of the scheme is happening as a result of the 2026 Sentencing Act, which allows ministers to reduce the point at which certain prisoners can be freed from 40% of a fixed-term sentence to a third.

Several hundred people are likely to be released on 1 October as part of the first phase of the expanded scheme, with more to follow in subsequent months.

The Ministry of Justice says it is launching the biggest ever expansion of electronic monitoring, with a new presumption that offenders will be electronically tagged and monitored when they leave prison.

But a report released this week by probation and police watchdogs warned that some criminals were waiting up to five months to be fitted with a tag, leading to repeated breaches of court and prison orders.

Only 55% of GPS and radio frequency tags were fitted on time, according to the report’s findings. The figure was 60% for alcohol monitoring tags.

Keir Starmer’s government launched an early release scheme in September 2024, months after the general election. Images of prisoners swigging champagne, being driven away in sports cars and thanking the then prime minister were seized upon by the government’s critics.

Figures show the number of people behind bars has jumped by more than 1,700 in the past three months. The prison population of England and Wales stood at 87,499 on Monday, according to weekly government data.

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “This government inherited prisons on the brink of collapse and a homelessness crisis, with rough sleeping more than doubling since 2010.

“We’re pulling every lever to fix this, building 14,000 new prison places and working with councils and charities to halve prison leaver homelessness by 2029, supported by a record £700m investment in probation and community services.”

articles.title: ‘Catastrophic year’ as Swiss glaciers lose 5% of ice after heatwaves
articles.excerpt:
‘Catastrophic year’ as Swiss glaciers lose 5% of ice after heatwaves

articles.body_text:

articles.title: Netanyahu says too early to tell who was behind plane incident as flydubai halts all flights to Israel
articles.excerpt:
Israeli prime minister cautions against early conclusions when asked if there were any signs of Iranian involvement

Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the ...
articles.body_text:
Israeli prime minister cautions against early conclusions when asked if there were any signs of Iranian involvement

Benjamin Netanyahu has said it was too early to tell who was ultimately behind the apparent attempt to crash a ⁠Tel Aviv-bound flydubai flight, even as Israel’s ambassador to the United Nations called the incident a “terror attack”, without apportioning blame.

Danny Danon told Fox News on Wednesday night that Israel had “no doubt that it was a terror attack from a radical individual. We still cannot link it to a terror state or terror organisation, but for sure we know there was an intention to bring that plane down.”

Flydubai said its flights to and from Israel would be suspended while the investigation takes place and urged all parties “to refrain from premature speculation while authorities gather the facts”.

The incident – which began when one pilot stabbed another on the flight deck in an apparent attempt to take control of the aircraft – is under investigation. The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv had more than 170 people on board, most of them from Israel.

In what have been hailed as acts of tremendous bravery, several passenger rushed the cockpit of the flight and wrestled the controls from the alleged attacker even as the plane descended sharply, managing to eventually taking control and stabilising the plane before making an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia.

Netanyahu, Israel’s prime minister, told Fox News host Sean Hannity: “We’ll get to the root of ⁠this attacker, whether he had accomplices” but cautioned that it was “too early to say” when asked whether there was any indication of Iranian involvement.

The pilot accused of carrying out the stabbing was being questioned by Saudi authorities, the Israeli prime minister said, adding that he expected he would soon be taken to the UAE, where the flight took off from. Netanyahu said earlier that he had spoken with the UAE’s president, who agreed that Israel would join the interrogation of the suspect.

Israeli officials, speaking on condition of anonymity to reporters, said the attacker was an Omani national, but there was no comment from Oman or the UAE.

Israel’s foreign ministry later briefed its diplomats around the world that the incident was an “attempted terrorist attack against Israelis, the United Arab Emirates, and the Abraham Accords,” referring to the deal that normalised relations between the two countries in 2020.

But on Wednesday evening Donald Trump told reporters the incident remained unclear, after he had spoken to Netanyahu. “It seems as though the co-pilot was perhaps a terrorist or perhaps a whack-job, and he stabbed the pilot,” the US president told reporters in the Oval Office.

Netanyahu was among the world leaders celebrating the bravery of the passengers and crew of the flydubai flight on Wednesday.

A video shared by the prime minister’s office showed passenger Yaniv Hayoun, a plumber, speaking to Netanyahu at length about how the events on board played out.

Hayoun told the prime minister how he and other passengers heard screaming and felt the air pressure change as the plane dived before they forced their way into the cockpit and found the attacker at the instrument panel.

“I grabbed the attacker, put him in a chokehold, and dragged him out first,” Hayoun said during the meeting with Netanyahu after the plane had landed safely and the passengers were flown to Israel.

As others wrestled with the attacker, Hayoun said he grabbed the controls and pulled them the way he had seen on television. Then other crew members took over.

The stabbed pilot was identified as Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, who was said to have made the emergency call and opened the door to the cockpit, allowing others to rush in and subdue the attacker.

In a post on X early on Thursday, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi lauded Machchhar a “hero”. “In the face of the gravest danger and despite being seriously ‌injured, he showed immense courage and an unwavering resolve to protect the lives of others. His valour helped save hundreds of lives and avert a great tragedy,” Modi ​said.

Machchhar, an Indian citizen from Mumbai, is being treated in a hospital in Saudi Arabia’s north-western city of Tabuk, where the plane landed safely.

articles.title: Pakistan says 22 fighters killed in air attacks on Afghanistan

The announcement by Pakistan’s Min...
articles.body_text:
Pakistan has launched air attacks on Afghanistan, saying it targeted “camps and hideouts” used by armed groups in two locations and killed an estimated 22 fighters.

The announcement by Pakistan’s Ministry of Information on Thursday came as Kabul accused Islamabad of killing at least nine women and children in attacks on its Kunar and Helmand provinces.

Al Jazeera could not independently verify the casualty claims.

Zabihullah Mujahid, the spokesman for Afghanistan’s government, said the strikes took place late on Wednesday and that at least nine people were killed and 11 others wounded.

In a post on X, he said the attacks on northeastern Kunar and southern Helmand destroyed three houses.

“We condemn this act and consider it an aggression and crime against all accepted principles,” he wrote.

The alleged attacks come amid an escalation in fighting between the neighbouring countries after three months of relative calm. Islamabad accuses Kabul of harbouring armed groups, including the Tehrik-i-Taliban Pakistan, who stage cross-border attacks on its territory.

The Afghan government ‌denies the charge and says the Pakistani attacks have targeted civilian homes, killing and wounding women and children.

articles.title: South Korea’s exports hit record high on AI boom
articles.excerpt:
South Korea’s exports have surged to a monthly record amid explosive demand for chips used to power artificial intelligence.

Exports jumped 83.5 percent year-on-year to $120.9bn in September, eclipsi...
articles.body_text:
South Korea’s exports have surged to a monthly record amid explosive demand for chips used to power artificial intelligence.

Exports jumped 83.5 percent year-on-year to $120.9bn in September, eclipsing the previous monthly record of $102.25bn set in June, preliminary customs figures showed on Thursday.

Chip shipments accounted for nearly half of exports, soaring more than 260 percent to $60.3bn, according to data from the Korea Customs Service.

Total exports from January through September hit $814.5bn, exceeding those for all of 2025, when exports reached a record $709.7bn.

During the first nine months of the year, the country recorded a trade surplus of $49.85bn.

“This is a valuable achievement that once again demonstrates the strength of our industries and companies, and is thanks to the sweat and efforts of our entrepreneurs who have competed fiercely in the global market,” said Kim Jeong-kwan, South Korea’s minister for trade and industry, in a statement.

“While we expect to achieve $1 trillion in annual exports, the strengthening of global protectionism and tensions in the Middle East remain major variables affecting our exports,” Kim said.

South Korea’s economy has been running red-hot this year amid a global shortage of memory chips used in AI.

Asia’s fourth-largest economy is home to one of the world’s largest semiconductor industries, led by top memory chip makers SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics.

SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics together control roughly 80 percent of the global market for high-bandwidth memory and 60 percent of the market for dynamic random-access memory, according to Counterpoint Research.

South Korea’s nominal gross domestic product (GDP) growth hit a five-decade high in the April-June quarter, skyrocketing 26.4 percent year-on-year.

South Korea’s Ministry of Finance and Economy has forecast real GDP to grow 3 percent in 2026, which would be the strongest performance since 2017, excluding the outlier years of the COVID-19 pandemic.

The AI boom has also propelled the country’s stock market into the ranks of the best-performing bourses this year, with the benchmark Kospi rising nearly 60 percent.

articles.title: ICE arrests illegal alien accused of sexually assaulting children after Fairfax County release: DHS
articles.excerpt: Fairfax County, Virginia, officials face scrutiny as illegal immigrant crime, including child sexual offenses and murders, dramatically rises. A DHS report reveals an alleged 75% of all murders in Fai...
articles.body_text:
Fairfax County, Virginia, officials face scrutiny as illegal immigrant crime, including child sexual offenses and murders, dramatically rises. A DHS report reveals an alleged 75% of all murders in Fairfax County are committed by illegal aliens, fueling intense debate over the county's controversial sanctuary city policies and their impact on public safety.

A Honduran illegal immigrant facing multiple child sex crime charges is back in federal custody after authorities in Fairfax County, Virginia, previously released him from an immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrested Oscar Evaristo Nunez on Sept. 15, during a targeted enforcement operation, DHS announced Wednesday.

Nunez was initially arrested over a year ago on Aug. 27, 2025, on charges of aggravated sexual battery involving children and offenses related to the non-consensual filming of an undressed minor, according to DHS.

ICE lodged a detainer with the Fairfax County Adult Detention Center two days later, but DHS said local authorities did not honor it and released Nunez without notifying the agency.

GUATEMALAN MAN CHARGED WITH CHILD PORN POSSESSION RELEASED BY FAIRFAX COUNTY DESPITE ICE DETAINER, DHS SAYS

Oscar Evaristo Nunez, a Honduran national facing multiple child sex crime charges in Virginia. (Department of Homeland Security)

The case has become the latest point of contention between the Trump administration and Virginia officials over cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

"Another criminal illegal alien has been taken off the streets by the brave men and women of ICE, with no help from sanctuary politicians in Fairfax County," DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a news release. "This illegal alien from Honduras had been arrested for child sex crimes in August last year, but Fairfax County refused to honor ICE’s detainer and let this creep back out onto the streets.

"Once again, ICE did the job that these heartless sanctuary politicians won’t do: enforce the law and protect American lives. DHS is calling on Governor Abigail Spanberger and her fellow sanctuary politicians to stop putting the needs of illegal aliens over the safety of the American people."‘OUT OF CONTROL’ KILLINGS IN SPANBERGER’S VIRGINIA REACH ‘INSANE’ POINT AS MIGRANT CHARGED IN STABBING SPREE

The case has become the latest point of contention between the Trump administration and Virginia officials over cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. (Jaque Silva/NurPhoto via Getty Images, File)

Spanberger, a Democrat, was not governor when Nunez was arrested and ICE lodged the detainer in August 2025. She took office in January 2026.

Spanberger has moved Virginia away from some forms of state participation in federal immigration enforcement since taking office, including directing state agencies to terminate agreements with ICE under the federal 287(g) program.

A representative for Fairfax County did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Oscar Evaristo Nunez sits in a vehicle following his arrest by ICE on Sept. 15. (Department of Homeland Security)

DHS said Nunez illegally entered the U.S. near Arizona around September 2003.

Nunez remains in ICE custody pending immigration proceedings.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: US Supreme Court allows execution of Christa Pike to go ahead
articles.excerpt:
The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for death row inmate Christa Pike to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The justices overturned a last-minute reprieve that ...
articles.body_text:
The US Supreme Court has cleared the way for death row inmate Christa Pike to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

The justices overturned a last-minute reprieve that was granted by an appeals court on Wednesday morning about an hour before Pike, 50, was due to be put to death.

Tennessee's attorney general had asked the Supreme Court to overrule the lower court. Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of Colleen Slemmer.

She was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed the 19-year-old, whom they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh, a conservative, granted Wednesday evening's application to vacate the stay of the execution. No explanation was provided in the order.

The top court's three liberal justices - Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson - dissented.

Sotomayor wrote that the decision cleared the way for Tennessee to execute Pike before her pending legal challenges to her conviction "can be properly considered".

"Tennessee's desire to expedite Pike's execution by a few days or even weeks cannot outweigh her 'fundamental interest in [her] own life," she said.

The latest Supreme Court ruling landed just before 18:00 local time. The state's execution order is due to expire at midnight.

If time runs out, the Tennessee Supreme Court would need to set a new execution date, the Associated Press news agency reports.

In a ruling earlier on Wednesday, judges from the Sixth Circuit Appeals court paused the execution saying they needed more time to consider the arguments in Pike's case.

Pike's lawyers said that for years, the state of Tennessee had argued in court that she lied about being sexually abused as a child.

But at a recent hearing about her execution method, the state said it did not dispute that she had suffered sexual abuse and rape.

Pike's legal team asked the appeals court to send her motion back to the district court, arguing that if the federal courts had based their ruling on the state's earlier claim that she was lying, then the federal review was affected.

It was the second time in as many days that the US Supreme Court gave the go-ahead for the convicted murderer's death by lethal injection. On Tuesday, the justices rejected a different appeal from Pike.

Tennessee's governor also denied a clemency request this week from the death row inmate.

articles.title: Swiss glaciers suffer 'disastrous' year of ice loss, threatening water supplies
articles.excerpt:
The front of Morteratsch Glacier in south-east Switzerland, which has been attacked by warm air and water

Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense su...
articles.body_text:
The front of Morteratsch Glacier in south-east Switzerland, which has been attacked by warm air and water

Swiss glaciers have suffered a near-record loss of ice in 2026, new data shows, as intense summer heatwaves take their toll on Alpine peaks.

More than 5% of the country's remaining glacier ice has disappeared in the last 12 months, which scientists say is "extraordinary".

They warn that such rapid melting is no longer a surprise given the pace of climate change, but it could threaten water supplies for farming, hydropower and transport in the decades ahead.

The loss of glacier ice can also destabilise mountain slopes and increase the risk of landslides in some places - which can lead to flash flooding in extreme cases, as seen in Nepal in August.

There were multiple factors involved in that event, which was triggered when a large area of bedrock and glacier ice collapsed.

But scientists say long-term glacier thinning and the thawing of frozen ground likely raised the risks.

The notable finding from this latest report is not so much that Swiss glaciers are shrinking - which is to be expected in our warming climate, driven primarily by fossil fuel emissions - but the sheer pace of melting.

Until recently, glaciologists in the Alps considered 2% of ice lost in a single year to be "extreme". This year has seen an estimated 5.5% disappear.

"It's really just disastrous," said Dr Matthias Huss, director of Glacier Monitoring Switzerland, which produced the report.

Swiss glaciers started the summer in an already difficult place, covered by less snow than usual after a mild winter.

And much of that snow disappeared quickly in the early and intense heatwaves of May and June, exposing the glacier ice below.

Bare ice is darker and less reflective than fresh snow, so absorbs more of the Sun's energy.

That left glaciers vulnerable to melting even faster in subsequent heatwaves.

"Ten years ago, I wouldn't have thought that it's possible to lose glaciers so quickly," said Dr Fabien Maussion, a glaciologist at the University of Bristol, who was not involved in the Swiss report.

"What's happened over the summer now is extremely distressing… but at the same time it was to be expected from a climate scientist's perspective," he added.

Meltwater from glaciers can be an important source of water for irrigation, hydropower and even shipping traffic during hot, dry conditions.

Scientists estimate that Swiss glaciers released 2.2 trillion litres of meltwater between July and September.

Although that helped to ease water shortages this summer, it has rapidly diminished the frozen supply.

The loss of ice could pose long-term challenges, Huss warned, with smaller glaciers unable to top up water levels to the same extent.

"Every drop of water that runs off during these heatwaves is kind of old water that's been stocked in the glacier ice centuries or decades ago," said Huss.

"It's helping us [now] but it's unsustainable, so we won't have it at [our] disposal in the next heatwave."

The River Rhine reached record lows in places this summer, affecting shipping navigation routes and increasing transport costs.

One of the most ominous findings is what researchers observed at measurement sites at the highest elevations, where temperatures are lowest and glaciers are typically snow-covered.

Even as high as 3,500 metres above sea level, scientists found no snow remaining at the end of summer.

"At some glaciers we've seen four metres of ice loss at the highest point, where they should be covered by several metres of winter snow at this time of the year," said Huss, from Glacier Monitoring Switzerland.

Snow is like glacier food - and under stable conditions some of it would eventually compact into ice.

But if no snow survives the summer, it cannot replace the ice lost to melting at lower, warmer elevations. The glacier will starve, shrink and eventually disappear.

"Glaciers are complex because they gain mass at the top and they flow downstream, so there is a lot of physics," explained Maussion.

"But in its simplest form, what we see right now is that we took an ice cube out of the fridge and it's just melting in front of our eyes."

Scientists say the climate is now too warm for many Alpine glaciers to survive.

Some, like Plattalva in eastern Switzerland, have already disappeared.

But researchers stress that sharp cuts to carbon emissions can still save much of the world's glacier ice.

This is particularly the case for the Himalayas and the polar regions, where most of the planet's ice resides.

"There we still can make a big difference with protecting the climate," said Huss.

"If these ice masses can be saved or stabilised, we can limit the rise of global sea levels… which could affect billions of people living along the coast."

Shoebridge addresses Faruqi’s decision to move outside Greens leadership

David Shoebridge has addressed comments from former deputy Mehree...
articles.body_text:

Shoebridge addresses Faruqi’s decision to move outside Greens leadership

David Shoebridge has addressed comments from former deputy Mehreen Faruqi that her work on major global challenges was more effective outside the leadership team.

The new Greens leader rejected Sally Sara’s contention that it “sounds like she doesn’t want to work with you”.

Yesterday Faruqi – who nominated for the Greens party leadership – revealed she did not run for her deputy position in the ballot.

Naming challenges including conflict, genocide, racism, climate change, and cost of living, Faruqi posted to Instagram:

double quotation markOn reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team.

Speaking to ABC Radio National this morning, Shoebridge said:

double quotation markThe Greens are unusual in that we pretty much everyone, every member of our team is a frontbencher with a huge portfolio load to get out and work in that portfolio …

I am looking forward to senator Faruqi getting out there and campaigning on matters that she’s clearly got a passion and a talent to connect with big parts of this country. And I think that’s great.

‘Like living in a wildlife documentary’: Antarctic outpost job applications now open

The Australian Antarctic Program has opened recruitment today for more than 200 roles for the 2027/28 Antarctic season, with plenty of tradies needed to deliver research station improvements, AAP reports.

“You can be walking to work at 10 o’clock in the morning and have an aurora over your head,” says Nelson Clegg, a Bureau of Meteorology technical officer who is currently posted at Davis station:

double quotation markGetting to see penguin rookeries and seal colonies. It’s like living in a wildlife documentary.

The program has contracts ranging from six months to 12-plus months available across 29 roles including electricians, carpenters, mechanics, plumbers and chefs. There are also spots for specialists in science, aviation, voyage and field leadership roles and telecommunications.

Last year, the program had to sift through 6,200 applications.

Candidates need trade qualifications and several years’ experience to be successful and must be an Australian citizen. There is also a thorough application process examining personal characteristics, as well as medical and psychological assessments.

This article includes content provided by Facebook. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

One of Australia’s big four aluminium smelters gets $200m lifeline

A government funding package has helped secure a five-year power deal at one of Australia’s big four aluminium smelters, AAP reports.

The electricity contract for northern Tasmania’s Bell Bay Aluminium, one of Australia’s big four aluminium smelters, was due to expire at the end of 2026, and it had been at loggerheads with state-owned Hydro Tasmania for months over a deal.

A $200m joint support package from the Tasmanian and federal governments has soothed some concerns surrounding the future of the smelter, even though the parties were bargaining for a 10-year deal.

It employs 550 workers, and 1,000 more workers indirectly cross northern Tasmania.

Disability groups urge Queensland to act on Thriving Kids program

Three disability advocacy groups have urged the Queensland government end “uncertainly” for families in the state awaiting the Thriving Kids program.

The state-delivered program will ultimately replace the NDIS for children with mild to moderate autism or developmental delays in January 2028.

But three groups, People with Disability Australia, Children and Young People with Disability Australia, and the Queensland Independent Disability Advocacy Network say the state government has left them in the dark.

“Queensland’s decision not to sign the bilateral agreement has consequences,” an open letter reads:

double quotation markWhile other jurisdictions move into implementation, Queensland families are being asked to live with continued uncertainty about what supports will be available here and when.

If the government is not satisfied that the current arrangements protect Queensland children and families, it now needs to set out a credible pathway to arrangements that will.

People with disability, families and the organisations that represent and advocate alongside them must be part of that work.

The premier, David Crisafulli, yesterday said he was concerned the plan could become “a cost-shifting exercise” and complained of a lack of detail from the commonwealth.

double quotation markI say to those families, we’re on your side, and we’re trying to get some common sense out of Canberra to make sure that you don’t fall through the cracks

Sydney Trains warns extra travel time needed after incident at Central

Just a quick note for Sydney commuters: Sydney Trains is urging anyone travelling this morning to allow extra time to get into work due to an incident at Central station.

Trains are expected to stop on platforms or between stations for longer than normal, or stops may change at short notice.

You can check for updates on trip planner apps.

Queensland’s state government has missed a deadline to sign up to the federal government’s Thriving Kids program before its rollout begins today.

Under the program, state governments will provide supports to children up to 8 years old with mild to moderate autism or developmental delays. They will be made ineligible for federal aid through the NDIS in 2028.

Thriving Kids will be rolled out in every state but Queensland from today. The sunshine state signed up to the deal in principle in January in return for billions for the state’s health system, but hasn’t agreed to implement it.

The premier, David Crisafulli, said on Wednesday he didn’t want the change to be a “cost-shifting exercise”.

The state government has repeatedly said it won’t sign up without additional information from the commonwealth, including about its costs. But disability services say the state has been unclear about its own position and has not given specifics about what information it is looking for.

New figures show 102,594 first home buyers have used the government’s 5% deposit scheme over the last year after the Labor government expanded the initiative.

One in two first home buyers nationally are now using the scheme to get into the market. Government figures estimate the policy has saved Australians more than $2.5bn in lenders mortgage insurance in total, with about $1.4bn of that saved in the last 12 months.

99% of buyers are ahead or on track with repayments.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said in a statement:

double quotation markThis scheme is helping Australians, particularly young Australians, get their foot in the door and achieve the dream of home ownership. When it comes to housing challenges, we’re tackling it from every angle – making it easier for first home buyers, boosting supply and helping renters get a better deal.

Link between technology and young people’s mental health ‘more complex’ than portrayed, study finds

A new report by the National Mental Health Commission has found the link between digital technology and the mental health of young Australians is “more complex than often portrayed”.

The study focused on Australians aged 5 to 25 found mental health symptoms may be prompting people to use social media in harmful ways, rather than technology causing mental health symptoms.

It calls for a greater focus on creating safe digital environments for children, rather than simply limiting screen time.

The commission’s chief executive, David McGrath, said policy needs to be “guided by evidence and not assumptions”:

double quotation markThis landmark Australian study helps move the conversation beyond screen time and towards understanding the real experiences children and young people are having online. The evidence shows those experiences are complex, it is important that policy responses reflect that complexity.

The report shows digital technology is neither simply good nor bad. What matters is how children and young people are using it, what they’re experiencing online, and whether digital environments are designed with their wellbeing in mind.

Shoebridge says people sick of ‘messaging without substance’

David Shoebridge, the new Greens leader, says Australians are “sick of the messaging without substance”.

Shoebridge spoke to RN Breakfast this morning, saying the Greens are in a “terrific position” with robust support while the other major parties have seen their support “getting decimated and ripped apart”.

He said the Greens would continue to work to “not just deliver some message and some pathetic, half-baked pretend reform”.

double quotation markPeople are sick of the messaging without substance. What they’re asking for is a political party that’s going to go and fight for them and take on the 1% and take on the corporations. They want to see us fighting for that.

Shoebridge added the rise of One Nation was a challenge to politics across the board, saying he wants the Greens to grow the party and bring members in amid a shift in the political landscape.

double quotation markWe have an incredibly united membership base. We have an incredibly united party across the country. And I expect that to be how we operate as a party room, how we operate as a leadership team and how we operate as a growing movement.

Debit and credit card surcharges will be eliminated from today as part of Reserve Bank reforms that will do away with extra checkout fees on Visa, Mastercard, and Eftpos payments.

The RBA made the changes after reviewing Australia’s card payments system, which the bank’s governor, Michele Bullock, said was no longer fit for purpose.

Businesses have already made swift rule changes as they decide how to handle fees they are no longer permitted to pass on to customers.

The ATO has joined them, saying that as a government agency, it had decided it would not be appropriate for the “cost of credit card merchant fees to be transferred to the community”.

Guardian Australia has asked the ATO what it means by saying the fees would be transferred to the community.

While most Australians do not pay tax with a credit card, the ATO says it understands the changes may require some adjustments from the small group of individuals and businesses who do make their payments this way.

Taxpayers with a direct debit arrangement linked to a credit card must update their payment method before their next instalment due after 30 November to ensure compliance with their payment plan, the ATO says.

double quotation markThe ATO is committed to helping taxpayers transition to alternative payment methods and will continue to support those experiencing financial hardship or other circumstances that make it difficult to meet their obligations.

You can read more about how businesses are responding to the end of surcharging, here:

Telstra, Optus and Vodafone will from today be able to move users over to one of their rivals’ networks in areas where coverage has dropped out due to natural disasters such as cyclones, bushfires or floods.

The capability will mean users in those areas will still be able to call, message, and get basic access to the internet if the other network is up at no additional cost.

This is beyond the existing capability for networks to hand over emergency triple zero calls to other networks when the call can’t get through.

The industry has flagged there will be some scenarios - such as power outages – when switching will not be possible.

The switch-on for temporary roaming will be managed by the three carriers, and will happen automatically for customers when activated.

The temporary disaster roaming can be activated in up to three affected areas at the same time, with up to 15 mobile sites included per area, and activated for 24 hours at a time. The disaster areas must be at least 400km apart.

Metropolitan areas are excluded from the roaming arrangement.

Good morning, Nick Visser here to pick up the blog. Let’s get into Thursday.

From today, children under nine years old with mild developmental delays and autism can access early intervention services through a program called Thriving Kids, which is administered by state and territory governments.
  The change was announced by the Albanese government in August 2025 and will slowly move children off the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It will fully replace the NDIS for these children by 2028.
  Unlike the NDIS, participation in Thriving Kids won’t require a formal diagnosis, potentially speeding up services and saving families money.
  The health minister, Mark Butler, recently told parents there would be no gap in government support for their children.
  Queensland is the sole Australian state refusing to sign on to the Thriving Kids program, leaving families in limbo as the first phase of the NDIS replacement scheme launches.
  You can read more details about the change here:

More than one-quarter of big companies operating in Australia paid no income tax in 2024-25, according to the Australian Taxation Office’s latest corporate transparency report.

The report says companies mostly cited an accounting loss – when expenses outstrip revenue.

Guardian Australia has previously reported how some multinationals, including the Singtel-owned Optus and coal miner Adani, regularly pay no tax, citing infrastructure investments and operating expenses .

About 27% of entities in the report reported zero tax, which was a similar figure to the year before.

In total, 4,299 entities earning at least $100m in total income paid a combined $87.5bn in tax in 2024–25, led by Australia’s large mining sector.

The ATO acting deputy commissioner, Michelle Sams, says the agency is “increasingly focused” on making sure digital businesses and supply chains, including data centres, paid their share of tax.

double quotation markWe look very closely if there’s no tax being paid in significant industries, including things like data centres, to make sure that the level of tax being paid reflects the economic activity that’s happening in Australia.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

articles.title: Passenger's bizarre use of drinking glass on flight leaves travelers horrified
articles.excerpt:
A business class passenger on an EVA Air flight from Taiwan shocked fellow travelers when he was caught using an upturned drinking glass to repeatedly scratch his scalp. (Viral Press)

An EVA Air busi...
articles.body_text:
A business class passenger on an EVA Air flight from Taiwan shocked fellow travelers when he was caught using an upturned drinking glass to repeatedly scratch his scalp. (Viral Press)

An EVA Air business-class passenger left fellow travelers aghast by using a drinking glass to vigorously scratch his scalp while he was seated in the middle of the flight.

The odd incident aboard a recent flight out of Taiwan on Sept. 24 was all caught on video.

The man aboard the Boeing 787 Dreamliner apparently decided that the best way to soothe an itchy head was to vigorously massage his scalp using the rim of a drinking glass.

MIDAIR SCARE FORCES PACKED PASSENGER JET INTO EMERGENCY LANDING, TRAVELERS HOSPITALIZED

The bizarre in-seat grooming routine was spotted by a horrified fellow passenger seated directly behind the amateur masseur, according to news outlet Viral Press.

Watching the traveler drag the rim of the upside-down cup through his hair repeatedly and all across his scalp made the witness feel the premium cabin experience had taken a drastic and unexpected turn.

A business class passenger on an EVA Air flight from Taiwan shocked fellow travelers when he was caught using a drinking glass to aggressively scratch his scalp.  (Viral Press)

"This is disgusting. It's a cup, not a massage comb," the appalled witness complained.

Losing all appetite for the upcoming meal service, the passenger who recorded the video said, "No one wants to eat your dandruff. I'm really going to vomit," Viral Press reported.

The EVA Air flight landed safely, NewsFlare reported.

The company, headquartered in Taiwan, was founded in 1989, according to its website.

The traveler who witnessed the bizarre head-scratching incident (not pictured) was annoyed and called the behavior "disgusting."  (iStock)

Texas-based etiquette expert Diane Gottsman told Fox News Digital that "using a glass to scratch [one's] head is completely inappropriate," particularly while in public and surrounded by other people.

"Any time you see someone scratching themselves with an object, or even scratching themselves with their fingers in a public area — it’s unappealing and somewhat alarming," she added.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

In recent years, several flyers have complained that fellow passengers are crossing the line when it comes to public-facing behavior aboard planes.

In March 2026, a passenger was slammed for putting feet up on a window.

The witness taking the video (not pictured) had a huge problem with the behavior, according to Viral Press. (iStock)

At the time, a Reddit user blasted the other traveler.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"First time experiencing the feet in my face in five years. Travel monthly. In first class, and this lady put her feet on my arm rest. I shoved them off."

The writer continued, "And five minutes later, she has them up on her window. At least she has socks on. But come on, people! It’s a 4.5 hour flight."

Said Gottsman, "When you’re in your home, you are in a private space. [But] when you are out in public, there are different standards because you are around other people and must be aware of your surroundings and the comfort level of others."

Jessica Mekles is an editor on the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Man arrested over alleged plot to attack Texas state capitol
articles.excerpt:
Suspect Benny Caldera Jr held on bond as officials say they received ‘credible’ information about Austin threat

A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the T...
articles.body_text:
Suspect Benny Caldera Jr held on bond as officials say they received ‘credible’ information about Austin threat

A 40-year-old man was arrested early Wednesday on suspicion of plotting to attack the Texas state capitol, authorities said.

The Texas department of public safety said in a statement that it received “credible information about an individual planning a violent attack” for Thursday in Austin.

The tip came in Tuesday evening, and Swat officers made the arrest at about 3am on Wednesday at a residence in Converse, Texas, near San Antonio.

Benny Caldera Jr was jailed on a $75,000 bond. He could face charges including felony terroristic threat against a public servant, officials said in a statement. Messages were left seeking comment from an attorney listed for Caldera.

Officials did not provide details about the alleged plot, citing the ongoing investigation. Public safety officials notified state lawmakers about the threat and arrest early on Wednesday. The Capitol remained open during regular operating hours.

Texas senate secretary Patsy Spaw said in a notice that there will be increased security at the Capitol during the investigation.

Governor Greg Abbott said the state DPS was assisted by the FBI in making the arrest.

“Texas will NOT tolerate threats of violence against our Capitol,” the governor said in a statement on social media.
