The Tennessee man accused of killing a Kentucky state trooper was on probation and already wanted for a violation, wit...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Tennessee man accused of killing a Kentucky state trooper was on probation and already wanted for a violation, with a criminal record that included assault, fraud and illegally possessing a gun.

Emonnie Branch, 51, was denied bond Tuesday on a charge of murder of a first responder in the death of Trooper Hayden Phillips, a husband and father of three young boys.

Tennessee Department of Correction records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Branch was serving five years of probation for a fraud-related conviction. His supervision was scheduled to end in July 2030.

Sumner County District Attorney Thomas Dean told Fox 17 Nashville that Branch was already wanted for a probation violation tied to his securities fraud conviction before Monday’s shooting.

CALIFORNIA GUNMAN REPEATEDLY RELEASED BEFORE DEADLY RAMPAGE, FIERY SHOOTOUT WITH DEPUTIES

Emonnie Branch, 51, is being held without bond in the killing of Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips. (Warren County Detention Center)

"Looks like he has a very extensive and varied criminal history," Commonwealth’s Attorney Kori Bumgarner said during Tuesday’s arraignment, the outlet reported.

CHARLOTTE REPEAT OFFENDER CHARGED WITH KILLING MAN HOURS AFTER RELEASE ON BOND

Emonnie Branch was on probation when he was accused of killing Trooper Hayden Phillips, Tennessee correction records show. (Tennessee Department of Correction)

Dean said Branch’s prior convictions included attempted domestic assault, violating a no-contact order and securities fraud. Court records reviewed by the outlet also showed a 2009 conviction for illegally possessing a firearm as a convicted felon.

Fox 17 reported that Branch was arrested twice this year for probation violations. Warren County Regional Jail records reviewed by Fox News Digital show he is being held without bond on the murder charge and a fugitive charge.

SUSPECTS AT LARGE AFTER TUCSON POLICE RECRUIT KILLED, PIMA COUNTY CORRECTIONS OFFICER WOUNDED IN SHOOTING

Kentucky State Police Trooper Hayden Phillips was killed while patrolling Interstate 65 in Warren County on Monday. (KY State Police)

Phillips was shot and killed during a traffic stop on Interstate 65 in Warren County Monday, Kentucky State Police said. Authorities identified Branch as the suspect and issued a statewide Blue Alert before Louisville Metro Police captured him that evening.

"He was senselessly murdered," U.S. Attorney Kyle Bumgarner said Monday night during a news briefing. "We have a wife that expected her husband to come home. We have three little boys who don’t have a dad."

JURY CONVICTS KEVIN SALAZAR IN EXECUTION-STYLE KILLING OF LA DEPUTY RYAN CLINKUNBROOMER

Kentucky State Police released an image of a Honda Civic they said was present during the shooting of Trooper Hayden Phillips on Interstate 65. (KY State Police)

"One of our own was gunned down and murdered on the side of the road," Kyle Bumgarner added.

He pledged that the Justice Department would give state prosecutors and investigators "every tool" and "every bit of support" it could to help them pursue the maximum sentence.

Kentucky State Police Commissioner Col. Phillip Burnett Jr. condemned the suspect’s "cowardly actions" and explained why he had mentioned his name only once.

"I want you to know I only mentioned his name one time," Burnett said.

AMERICA'S WOUNDED COPS FIND HOPE, HEALING AND SECOND CHANCE THROUGH OFFICERS WHO REFUSE TO LEAVE THEM BEHIND

"We will seek justice for Hayden," he continued. "Let me repeat that, we will seek justice for Hayden. We will not rest until this happens."

Phillips was a three-year state police veteran assigned to Post 3 in Bowling Green. Burnett promised his family the agency would stand beside them.

"You will not walk this path alone," he said.

Phillips’ wife, Jordan, shared her grief Tuesday.

DRUNK WRONG-WAY DRIVER KILLED MASS TROOPER AFTER 9 DRINKS AT BAR, DA REPORT SAYS

Flowers and stuffed animals surround a cruiser outside Kentucky State Police Post 3 in tribute to fallen Trooper Hayden Phillips. (Governor Andy Beshear)

"I’ve laid here all night waiting for him to come home… for the radio to click off, the gun belt to hang," she wrote on Facebook.

"I promise to pick up all the pieces and force myself to carry on for your boys. I know you would want me to," she added.

State police escorted Phillips’ body to Glasgow Tuesday. A candlelight vigil is scheduled for Thursday at 6:30 p.m. local time.

Gov. Andy Beshear ordered flags at all state buildings lowered to half-staff from sunrise to sunset Sunday, Oct. 4, in honor of Phillips.

"Trooper Hayden Phillips was a hero who sacrificed everything protecting our people and our commonwealth, and it is our sacred duty to honor him and his family," Beshear said.

He urged Kentuckians to pray for Jordan and their three children and encouraged donations to the Kentucky State Police Foundation, saying all proceeds would go directly to the family.

Jordan asked people to share memories of her husband with their sons.

"He was just the kind of guy who is easy to celebrate," she wrote.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our new political email, free app or daily news podcast

David Shoebridge has been named the new federal leader of the Greens, with Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy, Guardian Australia understands.

The Greens will make a formal announcement in Sydney shortly.

The party’s ten senators and lone MP met to decide the new leadership team during a pre-planned two day retreat in Sydney, and followed the shock resignation of Larissa Waters on Monday, due to ill health.

The leadership became a three-way race after Shoebridge announced his run on Wednesday morning. The South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young had declared her candidacy on Tuesday, followed by a joint ticket of NSW senator and former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi and treasury spokesperson senator Nick McKim.

Shoebridge entered federal parliament in 2022, after more than a decade in NSW state politics. He holds the Greens’ defence and foreign affairs portfolios, and is a forceful presence in parliamentary debates, on social media and in Senate estimates hearings.

Before politics, he was a corporate lawyer and then became a barrister specialising in employment law, and at one point was a Labor branch member in Sydney’s inner west. In the early 2000s he met the hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon, who went on to become his mentor.

Hodgins-May is one of the Greens’ newest members, and entered parliament in May 2024, filling a casual vacancy created by Janet Rice’s retirement.

Under Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and more recently supported Labor’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The Greens also teamed up with the Coalition and crossbench in the Senate to force Labor to drop a controversial $5000 cap for veterans to access allied health services, and compelled the government to bring forward 20,000 aged care beds.

In a statement released ahead of the leadership ballot, Shoebridge and Hodgins-May said they were “excited by what we can and must do together as Greens.”

“This is the time to build our movement as the home for every Australia who wants action on the climate crisis, a fair return from our resources, a secure home and income, and not to sell out our independence to the US or the 1%.

“We do not seek to reform Labor, but to replace them.

“The answer to the rise of One Nation and the far right is giving people hope, and making people’s lives better with real economic and environmental security. It is as simple as a meal before school, as clear as no new coal and gas, and as challenging as holding back the wave of US billionaire tech bros and their vampire AI data centres.”

Waters revealed she would quit to focus on treatment for kidney disease, after her health had declined significantly since being elected leader in May last year. She is expected to take medical leave before returning to the Senate.

The party’s new leader will come under pressure to bring a more forceful approach to the job, amid frustrations with Waters’ more moderate style, and the party’s inability to exploit growing moves by voters away from Labor and the Coalition.

The former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather on Tuesday called for the party’s membership to get a vote in the leadership race.

articles.title: Judge ends federal oversight of Oakland police department after 23 years
articles.excerpt:
Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history

After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal over...
articles.body_text:
Group of officers known as ‘riders’ in 2000s prompted longest arrangement of its kind in US history

After 23 years, a district judge has released the Oakland police department (OPD) from federal oversight, marking the end of the longest arrangement of this kind in US history.

In the early 2000s, a group of police officers known as the “riders” were exposed for offenses like planting evidence, falsifying reports and using excessive force against primarily young Black men. These actions led victims to file more than 100 civil lawsuits against the department. In 2003, as a part of the settlement of these cases, OPD was put on a federal court-ordered reform program.

OPD was given more than 50 tasks to complete including collecting and analyzing data on racial profiling, dealing with complaints against officers more quickly and updating their community policing practices. Despite this, issues remained and the department’s reforms were put under the direct control of a federal judge in 2012.

Since then, the department has still had its share of scandals including allegations that several OPD officers sex-trafficked a teenage girl; nearly a dozen officers were either fired or suspended. The investigation into the trafficking of the teenager began in 2015 and OPD issued her a nearly $1m settlement in 2017.

For organizers against police misconduct and brutality, the decision to end the federal oversight scheme does not mean that the department should be free of scrutiny.

“Police cannot police themselves. Oakland’s history has already taught us that lesson,” the Anti Police-Terror Project (APTP) said in a statement following the judge’s decision. “The end of federal oversight does not mean the end of police misconduct. It does not erase the history that brought OPD under federal supervision. And it certainly does not mean Oakland should simply trust OPD to hold itself accountable.”

articles.body_text:
A record 157,957 new EVs were sold nationally between January and June, according to the Electric Vehicle Council

Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australians are buying electric vehicles at record levels, with sales more than doubling year on year and occurring at a rate equivalent to one EV sold every 100 seconds.

A record 157,957 EV sales occurred between January and June – an 117% increase on the same period last year, according to a new report released by the Electric Vehicle Council.

Comparatively, petrol and diesel vehicle sales decreased by 14% year on year, according to the council’s chief executive, Julie Delvecchio.

EVs accounted for one in four new vehicles sold in the first half of the year, up 12.1% from the first six months of 2025, the state of EVs report said.

“EVs are being taken up as a cost-of-living measure by households across Australia,” Delvecchio said of the rise, noting that the ongoing fuel crisis was an accelerating factor but was “not the starting gun”.

“It exposed the value of the policy work that had already been done – and made the lower running costs and energy security benefits of EVs much more immediate for Australian households,” she said.

The new figures include about 104,000 battery electric vehicles and 54,000 plug-in hybrids.

As of June, there were 612,000 EVs in the national vehicle fleet. “We are well on track to hit the target of 1 million EVs on Australian roads by next year,” said Aman Gaur, the head of policy and advocacy at the EV Council.

The Australian Capital Territory, where 44% of new cars registered are electric, retained its crown as the nation’s EV capital.

Tarneit, in Melbourne’s west, was the individual postcode with the highest uptake.

A key driver of the growing uptake has been the national vehicle efficiency standard, which requires carmakers to supply new vehicles that meet an average per-kilometre emissions target.

The standard had “substantially increased the options and the price competitiveness of EVs”, with nearly 200 EV models available in 2026, Gaur said.

The council is pushing for the federal government to extend the standard beyond 2029, to align with the government’s 2035 emissions reduction target.

Charging infrastructure had largely kept pace with growing EV demand, the report found, with the number of public charging locations growing to 4,268 across the country.

While Australia was no longer a global laggard compared with other electric car markets, buses and cars were “roaring ahead” of electric trucks and vans, for which sales continued to be less than 1% of their respective markets, Gaur said.

“Every truck that is electric is an upgrade to Australia’s energy security,” Delvecchio said. “We’ve barely touched the sides on that transition.”

The report also found the federal, ACT and NSW governments’ EV policies were “top of the class, while South Australia, Queensland, Tasmania and Northern Territory have gone backwards”.

“Queensland and the Northern Territory are … moving to back to fossil fuels rather than trying to electrify their transport systems,” Gaur said.

“The most disappointing example of this was when the Queensland government recently invested in 630 diesel buses.

“The diesel buses will be on Queensland roads until the end of the next decade, and they will certainly be polluting the air in Brisbane when the Olympics are held.”

articles.title: Sylvester Stallone's advice to those who are struggling 50 years after 'Rocky' changed his life
articles.excerpt: Actor and filmmaker Sylvester Stallone discusses his unlikely rise to stardom and reflects on the experiences that shaped his career. He also shares some of his biggest filmmaking influences and looks...
articles.body_text:
Actor and filmmaker Sylvester Stallone discusses his unlikely rise to stardom and reflects on the experiences that shaped his career. He also shares some of his biggest filmmaking influences and looks back on the lessons he learned from movies on ‘Special Report.’

Fifty years after "Rocky" made Sylvester Stallone a household name, the 80-year-old says his advice to people who are struggling is "you have nothing to lose" if you try.

"Rocky," a story about a low-level boxer who got the unexpected chance to become a champion, parallels the actor’s own life from being so broke he had to sell his dog to winning the Oscar for the 1976 classic.

"What would you tell the kid who’s sleeping on the bench at Port Authority with $80 in his pocket?" Fox News’ Bret Baier asked Stallone on "Special Report" on Tuesday while discussing his new memoir "The Steps."

'I PLAY ROCKY' REVIVES THE GAMBLE THAT MADE SYLVESTER STALLONE A SUPERSTAR

Sylvester Stallone said his own motto is "I tried." (Getty Images)

"You have nothing to lose. Seriously, you have nothing to lose. With failure you don’t get shot. There’s no firing squad," Stallone said. "The only thing you have to lose is your peace of mind if you don’t try. At least try. You may quit halfway through, but at least say, ‘I tried.’"

Stallone said his own motto is "I tried."

SYLVESTER STALLONE SAYS HE'D BE IN 'BIG TROUBLE' TRYING TO MAKE HIS CAREER IN TODAY'S HOLLYWOOD

As a broke 23-year-old backpacking through the Pyrenees in Europe in 1969, Stallone wrote in the book that a fortune teller predicted he would find fortune by 1976, the same year "Rocky" came out.

"And she said also, ‘A woman will bring you into the circle of attention, and that was my manager Jane Oliver who’s the only one like who plucked me from obscurity," he said.

SYLVESTER STALLONE REVEALS SURPRISING HEALTH STRUGGLE BEHIND HIS FAMOUSLY RIPPED PHYSIQUE

Actors Sylvester Stallone and Carl Weathers perform a boxing scene in the 1976 movie "Rocky." (Getty Images)

Early in his career, Stallone went by the name Mike, but decided to go back to Sylvester.

Stallone felt pre-"Rocky" that he was drifting off into "total obscurity" and thought if Humphrey Bogart could make a career with his name, then "Sylvester’s not so bad."

SYLVESTER STALLONE'S 'TULSA KING' SEASON 4 TEASER SPARKS FAN FRENZY: 'THE KING IS BACK!'

Sylvester Stallone as boxer Rocky Balboa trains with a punchbag in the 1976 film "Rocky." (Getty Images)

"I thought, that’s memorable because I’ve never met another Sylvester. So, at least it was just another hook that maybe people would remember as opposed to Mike.

Stallone told Baier that he decided to write his book now because he wanted his children to "understand the journey" it took to get him where he is now.

MATT DAMON SAYS HOLLYWOOD'S 'RUTHLESS' NATURE HAS TAKEN HIM AWAY FROM FATHERHOOD MORE THAN HE'D LIKE

The "Tulsa King" actor called ushering at a theater his "film school," explaining that he would watch three showings a night on his shift and would take notes from films like "M*A*S*H."

"I thought, where do you learn more about a film than in a theater where you actually see a reaction?"

HOLLYWOOD PRODUCER BEHIND 'APOLLO 13' REJECTS POLITICS IN HIS MOVIES, SEEKS TO UNITE AUDIENCES

He said college is "very cloistered," whereas in a theater it’s "instant enjoyment or repulsion or they leave. So, I learned a great, great deal. It’s like with a waiter – you want to learn the restaurant business? Be a waiter."

"I learned more in a movie theater than I would imagine in college," he said.

Stallone, with fellow winner Beatrice Straight, holding his Oscar after winning in 1977. (Getty Images)

TOM CRUISE ADMITS RUMORS ABOUT HIS 'INTENSE' BEHAVIOR ON MOVIE SETS ARE TRUE

Stallone also wrote that the "go the distance" speech in "Rocky" almost didn’t happen because the producers wanted to cut it.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"They did pull the plug," he told Baier. "And I have to say I really did lose my cool at that moment. Very upset. It was the first time I really crossed the line. I said, ‘You have to film this because this is the whole movie philosophy in a nutshell."

JACK NICHOLSON SPOTTED IN RARE PHOTO AS LEGENDARY ACTOR CELEBRATES TURNING 89

Sylvester Stallone said he lost his cool when producers tried to cut the "go the distance" speech in "Rocky." (GC Images)

In the end, the producers gave Stallone one take to get it.

"If the camera shook, if the sound man… I was like ‘Everyone, please be on you A-game.’"

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Stallone didn’t believe he was going to win the Academy Award in 1977, and when Jack Nicolson called his name, he said he was shocked and almost "broke down."

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

The actor dedicated the award to all the people who, like Rocky Balboa, struggle but will always "be there" working hard.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Morocco’s pro-Palestine protests challenge Rabat’s deepening Israel ties
articles.excerpt:
Pro-Palestine protests have spread across several Moroccan cities, with demonstrators demanding an end to diplomatic normalisation with Israel as Rabat deepens ties with Tel Aviv.

The latest mobilisa...
articles.body_text:
Pro-Palestine protests have spread across several Moroccan cities, with demonstrators demanding an end to diplomatic normalisation with Israel as Rabat deepens ties with Tel Aviv.

The latest mobilisation took place on September 27, at the end of three days of action called by the Moroccan Front for Supporting Palestine and Against Normalisation.

They followed a September 16 announcement that Morocco and Israel would elevate their diplomatic missions to full embassies and appoint ambassadors.

On September 25, the Moroccan Committee for Supporting the Nation’s Causes said it had organised 76 events in 45 cities under the slogan “Friday for Al-Aqsa and against normalisation”.

Moroccan media reported gatherings in cities including Rabat, Casablanca, Marrakesh, Tangier, Fez, Agadir, Oujda, Tetouan, Kenitra and Sale. The 76-event figure was the committee’s own count, with no independent national tally of participants.

In Rabat, protesters gathered outside Parliament, while a demonstration in Marrakesh developed into a march through several main streets, according to Lakome. Moroccan media also reported restrictions and arrests in some cities.

The mobilisation faced restrictions in some cities.

In Tangier, local authorities issued a decision banning a planned demonstration on September 27. Achkayen later reported that security forces dispersed hundreds of participants and that more than 12 people were detained, citing its own sources.

Lakome reported that authorities also prevented demonstrations in M’diq, while security forces surrounded a gathering in Agadir to prevent it from becoming a march.

The Moroccan Committee for Supporting the Nation’s Causes subsequently condemned what it described as bans, restrictions and arrests.

The response underscored another dimension of the dispute: Opposition to the relationship with Israel has remained visible on the streets, even as the government has continued to develop official ties.

Morocco restored diplomatic relations with Israel in December 2020 as part of the US-brokered Abraham Accords framework, alongside Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.

On September 16, Moroccan Foreign Minister Nasser Bourita and Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar met in New York at a trilateral summit hosted by US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz.

The three countries confirmed plans to elevate the Moroccan and Israeli diplomatic missions to full embassies and exchange ambassadors.

Morocco and Israel also agreed to conclude agreements on investment protection and avoiding double taxation, expand direct flights and organise high-level reciprocal visits.

The move therefore goes beyond maintaining diplomatic relations established in 2020. It sets out a broader programme of institutional, economic and transport links between the two countries.

For opponents of the relationship, the embassy agreement represents another step in a policy they have rejected since 2020.

Morocco has maintained diplomatic relations with Israel while continuing to publicly support the Palestinian cause and the establishment of a Palestinian state.

For opponents of normalisation, however, the two positions are incompatible, particularly amid Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.

“What has changed is the political context: Normalisation is being consolidated at a time when the war in Gaza has generated unprecedented public anger and intense images of Palestinian suffering,” Kathya K Berrada, senior programmes manager at the Arab Center for Research, told Al Jazeera.

“What we are seeing in Morocco is a growing disconnect between official diplomacy and public sentiment,” Moroccan activist Mouna Rahiani said, citing the latest Arab Opinion Index, which found that 89 percent of Moroccans surveyed opposed their country recognising Israel, while six percent supported it.

“While the state is moving towards deeper and more formal relations with Israel, Moroccans are still taking to the streets to say that Palestine cannot be treated as separate from our political and moral responsibilities,” she said.

The September agreement has brought an existing tension into sharper focus: public mobilisation against normalisation continues while the state pursues closer institutional ties with Israel.

Berrada said there was an important distinction between official policy and popular opinion, arguing that there is not enough reliable public data to establish how many Moroccans support or oppose normalisation.

The timing also matters for Morocco’s Western Sahara policy. The United Nations Security Council is due to consider the mandate of the UN Mission for the Referendum in Western Sahara (MINURSO) in October. Its current mandate runs until October 31, 2026.

The September 16 trilateral statement came against the backdrop of US recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara and Israel’s support for Morocco’s position on the territory.

For Rabat, the relationship with Israel sits within a wider foreign-policy framework in which ties with Washington and international support for its position on Western Sahara remain important.

For opponents of normalisation, however, that strategic calculation does not resolve their objection to closer ties with Israel, particularly while the Palestinian issue remains highly salient.

Ahmed, a Moroccan sociologist who asked to be identified by one name, said the September 16 move was “a continuation of the trilateral agreement of December 10, 2020”, but that Morocco should make the relationship “comprehensive, not selective or partial”.

The protests came days after Morocco held parliamentary elections on September 23.

The final results gave the Authenticity and Modernity Party 97 of the 395 seats, followed by the National Rally of Independents with 66, the Istiqlal Party with 65 and the Party of Justice and Development (PJD) with 54.

The PJD had won 13 seats in 2021. Turnout was 38.08 percent, compared with 50.86 percent in 2021 and 42.27 percent in 2016, according to Morocco’s Ministry of Interior.

It was the PJD in power when Morocco restored relations with Israel in 2020. Then-Prime Minister Saadeddine el-Othmani signed the Morocco-US-Israel joint declaration that December.

The PJD has maintained that opposition to normalisation was a longstanding party position. The party subsequently reaffirmed its rejection of normalisation and relations with Israel, while el-Othmani defended the 2020 decision as a state-level decision.

On September 17, following the announcement of the planned diplomatic upgrade, the PJD’s general secretariat reiterated its opposition to normalisation and to relations and agreements with Israel.

After the election, the PJD’s national council unanimously decided to remain in parliamentary opposition and not participate in the next government.

The PJD’s position has illustrated the limits of using party politics to measure the effect of opposition to normalisation. The party opposed the policy while in government, yet its prime minister signed the 2020 declaration.

Its larger parliamentary presence in 2026 gives the issue a stronger political platform, but does not by itself alter Morocco’s foreign policy.

It has not been established that the Palestine issue or opposition to normalisation was a decisive factor in voting, and neither do the PJD’s gains demonstrate that its position on Israel directly drove its increased representation.

The September demonstrations show that organisations opposed to normalisation retain the ability to mobilise across a wide geographic area. But their effect on government policy is less clear.

“There is an important distinction between state policy and popular opinion. Normalisation is an official state decision, but there is limited reliable public data allowing us to measure the level of popular support for it,” Berrada said.

“It would therefore be difficult to claim that either a majority or a minority of Moroccans endorse the policy.”

That distinction is important when assessing the significance of the protests. Demonstrations can show the strength and persistence of organised opposition, but they do not by themselves establish the views of the wider population or show that government policy will change.

The PJD now has a larger parliamentary presence than it did after the 2021 election, but it remains in opposition. It will be able to voice its opposition to normalisation in Parliament, but will not have a place in government.

At the same time, the September 16 agreement remains part of a broader Moroccan foreign-policy framework involving the United States, Israel and Western Sahara. The Security Council’s consideration of MINURSO in October will provide another diplomatic setting in which Morocco’s position on the territory is under discussion.

For now, the protests demonstrate that opposition to normalisation remains capable of sustained mobilisation, while the government continues to deepen the relationship. Whether that public opposition translates into sustained political pressure remains less clear.

Fox News Madeleine Rivera provides details on President Donald Trumps accusation that the BBC attempted to interfere in the 2024 election with an edited version of his Jan. 6 speech, omitting his comment on peacefully protesting.

The BBC removed an article that suggested the trend of leaving fingernails unpainted could perpetuate "White supremacist" beauty standards after it drew backlash on Saturday.

The original article, titled, "How the bare nails trend became a class issue," explored the beauty trend of women preferring clear and polished "naked" nails over the more stylish nail designs over the past few years. The BBC reported that while some consider this trend part of the ever-shifting standards in fashion, critics suggested the image said "something about class" and could potentially stigmatize Black, Latino and Asian communities that popularized heavily designed nails.

"That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to [B]lack and [B]rown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo told the BBC.

JK ROWLING CONFRONTS THE BBC FOR PUSHING 'PROPAGANDA' OVER ITS TRANSGENDER SPORTS HEADLINE

The BBC deleted an article titled "How the bare nails trend became a class issue" (Screenshot/BBC)

"They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate [W]hite supremacist standards of beauty," she added.

The article quickly drew widespread criticism for linking nail design to racism or class warfare.

"Such a stupid, pointless article. And to think the salary of whoever wrote it is paid by a levy on anyone in this country who watches live TV. Indefensible," Sex Matters director of advocacy Helen Joyce wrote on X.

LEGACY MEDIA TRUST HITS NEW LOW WITH SWALWELL STORY LATEST EXAMPLE OF PROTECTING DEMS

"Did one of your Hamas reporters write this one, too?" radio host Dana Loesch remarked.

American Conservation Coalition CEO Danielle Franz joked, "Bad news for the ladies who thought they were saving $80 on a manicure but were actually dogwhistling."

The Sun editor-at-large Harry Cole wrote, "This is mental. Not painting your nails is now White supremacy coded, apparently. Are they hoofing nail polish remover over there?"

The BBC quoted critics suggesting the growing popularity of bare fingernails could stigmatize Black and Latino culture. (iStock)

In an archived update to the article, the story was removed and replaced with the statement, "This article has been removed pending editorial review."

As of Tuesday, however, that statement had also been removed, and the original BBC URL led to a 404 error page.

Fox News Digital reached out to the BBC for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

DEPARTING BBC BOSS WARNS NETWORK ON 'KNIFE EDGE' AMID TRUMP DOCUMENTARY LAWSUIT, TRUST CRISIS

The BBC previously faced a lawsuit from President Donald Trump over their edit of his Jan. 6 speech in a 2024 documentary. (Richard Baker/In Pictures via Getty Images)

This move by the BBC comes one month after President Donald Trump won permission to file an amended legal complaint against the BBC for what the president claimed was "maliciously and deceptively" edited footage of his Jan. 6 speech in a 2024 "Panorama" documentary.

"Today’s strong and thoughtful ruling is a major win for President Trump’s powerhouse lawsuit against the formerly respected and now disgraced BBC, which defamed President Trump by intentionally, maliciously and deceptively doctoring his speech in a brazen attempt to interfere in the 2024 Presidential Election. President Trump is holding the leftist BBC, along with all of its comrades in the mainstream media, accountable for their peddling of Fake News through deception and maliciously defamatory conduct," a spokesman for Trump’s legal team told Fox News Digital.

The controversy preceded the November 2025 resignations of BBC News CEO Deborah Turness and Director-General Tim Davie.

Fox News' Brian Flood contributed to this report.

Lindsay Kornick is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to lindsay.kornick@fox.com and on Twitter: @lmkornick.

articles.title: Transgender athletes have taken 2,293 championship spots from biological women, new research finds
articles.excerpt: South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham speaks at a Capitol Hill news conference, warning about the physical dangers and unfairness of allowing biological males to compete in women's sports. Graham highlig...
articles.body_text:
South Carolina Sen. Darline Graham speaks at a Capitol Hill news conference, warning about the physical dangers and unfairness of allowing biological males to compete in women's sports. Graham highlights the safety risks for female athletes, citing a severe injury in North Carolina.

That's the argument certain activists keep making when it comes to the debate about trans athletes in female sports.

It's not a great position, frankly — because if something is wrong, it doesn't matter how rare it is. It should be stopped, assuming doing so doesn't trigger undue consequences.

Riley Gaines, Sophie Cunningham, and XX-XY Athletics founder Jen Sey pose courtside after an Indiana Fever game with a sign thanking Cunningham. (Riley Gaines/XX-XY Athletics)

AMERICANS CLASH OVER TRANSGENDER ATHLETES AS DEBATE HEATS UP: ‘JUST GETTING OUTRAGEOUS'

But new data suggests that this "uncommon" occurrence isn't so uncommon after all. Recent research from the Concerned Women of America found that transgender athletes have bumped biological women out of 2,293 championship spots since the mid-1980s. This is far different than simply noting the number of transgender athletes in sports. This is pointing out how many biological females would have won a specific honor if not for the trans athlete that took it.

For the report, the think tank drew on information compiled by HeCheated.org, a volunteer-operated database that tracks reported instances of trans athletes competing in women's sports. In total, it found that they have partaken in more than 14,000 female sporting events ranging from high school to college to amateur to professional.

The HeCheated.org list is extensive. The first page alone has 200 instances ranging from March 27, 2025, to September 18, 2026. It shows examples of biological males making league All-Star teams in high school lacrosse, or winning high school state championships in track and field in Washington, California and Oregon, or earning All-conference recognition in college fencing. There were also a couple of examples of trans athletes receiving "most improved" awards.

Trans athlete AB Hernandez swept jumping events at CIF Division 3 prelims, fueling ongoing fairness debate. (OutKick/Alejandro Avila) ((OutKick/Alejandro Avila))

TRANS TRACK STAR SWEEPS THREE EVENTS, SHARES FIRST-PLACE PODIUM AND QUALIFIES FOR CA STATE MEET YET AGAIN

And as long as laws that allow this to happen exist, there is no evidence of this slowing down.

Author Abigail Shrier wrote the book "Irreversible Damage" in 2020, in which she noted a 1,000 to 5,000 percent increase in the number of trans-identifying youth over a several-year period. Other research has noted that this uptick has no end in sight.

In 2023, the CDC Youth Risk Behavior Survey found that about three percent of high-school students identified as transgender. In 2025, the Williams Institute estimated that 724,000 Americans ages 13–17 identify as transgender, which was roughly equivalent to 3.6 percent.

And the Society for Evidence Based Gender Medicine (SEGM) estimated that trans/nonbinary identification for college students is at an all-time high, ranging from 4.7 percent to 6.7 percent. That last number shouldn't affect participation in the NCAA, which requires athletes play on teams that match their sex assigned at birth. But when we're talking about, say, the WNBA, which still doesn't have a concrete rule about gender restrictions, who's to say one of these college kids doesn't try to pull a much-more-subtle Enes Kanter and work their way into the league?

US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD LAUNCHES PETITION CALLING FOR WNBA TO RESTRICT GENDER ELIGIBILITY

Women athletes and supporters stand as Kim Jones, co-founder of the Independent Council on Women's Sport, and Carly Smolak, former goalkeeper for the San Diego Spirit women's professional soccer team, testify before the Senate Judiciary Committee on Sept. 23, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The committee held a hearing titled "Standing Up for Women in Sports: Ensuring Opportunity, Fairness and Safety for Female Athletes." (Getty Images)

When I was at The Seattle Times, I interviewed a high school athlete named Ahnaleigh Wilson, who lost to a boy in a high school track meet when she was in eighth grade. She told me that she had since competed against four biological males in high school. I couldn't confirm that, but when I see research documenting biological males competing in more than 14,000 events involving females, and consider that alongside a UCLA study estimating that as many as 122,000 transgender youth may be competing in high school sports, I tend to believe her.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

There's a common pattern among the Left when it comes to issues such as these. First, they say it's not happening. Then, they say "OK, it's happening, but it's rare." Then, they say "OK, it's happening frequently, but that's a good thing!" We're getting closer and closer to that third one.

I suppose what's "rare" and what isn't is open to interpretation. But there's no denying that trans athletes are upstaging females often enough for anyone paying attention to notice.

Common sense doesn't appear as though it's going to stop this trend anytime soon. Laws, on the other hand, would.

articles.title: Reparations activists call out blue states for using slavery history to fund broader agenda
articles.excerpt:
Members of the U.S. Freedmen Project, a reparations advocacy organization, told Fox News Digital that eligibility should be based on lineage to survive constitutional challenges.

Reparations activist...
articles.body_text:
Members of the U.S. Freedmen Project, a reparations advocacy organization, told Fox News Digital that eligibility should be based on lineage to survive constitutional challenges.

Reparations activists from a grassroots organization called the U.S. Freedmen Project told Fox News Digital that recent immigrants and non-foundational Black Americans should not be included in government reparations programs.

"I also think it’s not morally correct, you know? You don't give out remedies to people who haven't experienced the harm," Annette Wilcox, a spokesperson for the group, told Fox News Digital.

"A lot of these policies — the Commission on Racial Equity in the city, the Mayor’s Office on Equity and Justice — they talk constantly about slavery, Jim Crow, redlining, convict leasing. All of those things that happened to a specific group of people," Wilcox added. "Then, when it comes time to give out resources and remedies, it's going to everybody: underserved communities, POC [people of color], immigrants, marginalized groups. You’re using one group of people's history to then give remedies to a wider group."

The U.S. Freedmen Project, composed of self-identified "Foundational Black Americans," aims to educate the public on the legal and historical distinctions between African Americans who are direct descendants of enslaved people in the U.S. and those who immigrated to the country voluntarily in recent decades.

CHAOS ERUPTS AT NY REPARATIONS HEARING AS ‘FOUNDATIONAL’ BLACK AMERICANS CLASH WITH LEFT-LEANING GROUPS

Evanston, Illinois, will issue $25,000 to 44 residents in reparations payments, the City’s Reparations Committee has announced. (Carolyn Cole/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

Wilcox reacted sharply to efforts by New Jersey Democrats pushing the state to consider direct reparations proposals that could include residents who are not direct descendants of enslaved people.

The proposed legislation — the Truth, Reconciliation, and Repair Act, spearheaded by Assemblywoman Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and state Sen. Angela McKnight — aims to address wealth disparities stemming from historical slavery and systemic discrimination. Informed by research from the New Jersey Reparations Council, the bill seeks to establish a framework for state-level reparative policies.

U.S. Freedmen Project president Devine Prince told Fox News Digital that lawmakers and certain advocates are "conflating reparations with racial justice and social justice."

Fox News Digital previously spoke with New York residents who voiced similar concerns during a public hearing for the New York State Community Commission on Reparations Remedies at Hempstead High School on Long Island. Residents warned state officials that broadening the scope of reparations to include recent immigrants and other marginalized groups risks co-opting and diluting the movement.

NEW YORK FAR-LEFT GROUP CLAIMS REPARATIONS 'OWED' AS BLACKS' MEDIAN WEALTH 'NEARLY 15 TIMES LESS' THAN WHITES

An attorney suing the City of Evanston, Illinois over its reparations program told Fox News Digital that if this case swings in their favor, other cities planning to implement reparations may have to reconsider. (Alex Wong/Getty Images)

One supporter, Aubrey Muhammad, delivered tense testimony accusing politicians of misallocating resources away from historic Black communities amidst demographic shifts.

"The Democrats, in a sick way, imported 25 million immigrants. And 70% of them came into poor Black neighborhoods," Muhammad argued in a follow-up interview with Fox News Digital. "Hempstead, since the '90s, has been flooded with immigrants. That's taking the resources, putting them towards others."

Demographic data from the U.S. Census Bureau reflect significant changes in the Village of Hempstead over the last three decades. Today, the community of roughly 59,000 is nearly evenly split between Black residents (43.2%) and Hispanic or Latino residents (45.3%). In 1990, the Hispanic population made up roughly 14% of the village.

"That’s why, frankly, I think we're in the situation today, where descendants of slavery in the United States are at the bottom of just about every socioeconomic parameter," Wilcox said.

Prince expounded on the issue, arguing that broader social challenges deserve their own dedicated solutions rather than being packaged under the umbrella of reparations.

TRUMP ADMIN VOWS TO STOP REPARATIONS PROGRAMS, ACCUSES OFFICIALS OF 'VIRTUE SIGNALING' TO GET 'VOTES'

Aubrey Muhammad told the New York State Community Commission on Reparations Remedies Saturday during a public hearing that Democrats imported "Latinos" from South America as "replacements for us" for "your voting rolls" and accused them of gentrifying Black neighborhoods. (Fox News Digital)

"What we're finding out coming from the left wing of the political spectrum is that they are conflating reparations with racial justice and social justice. All three are similar, but they are far from the same," Prince said. "So what happens is when people believe a rising tide lifts all boats … you're conflating repair for the badges and incidents of slavery with discrimination like not being able to catch a cab, or with the social justice of fair immigration policies."

Members of the U.S. Freedmen Project have become vocal fixtures at public hearings across the country. They maintain that true reparations must be lineage-based — strictly reserved for direct descendants of enslaved human beings in the United States.

Prince argued that for any reparations policy to survive inevitable legal challenges, it must be tied strictly to lineage rather than race.

"What the Democratic Party loves to do is push them all together to create 'people of color' coalitions. These policies are largely being pushed in blue states, which is also where these issues are happening," Prince said. "There is a responsibility for any political entity to address its constituents directly and, more importantly, specifically — because that's how true coalitions are built, not by cobbling people together and pretending they all have the same plight and political priorities."

New Jersey and New York are part of a broader wave of state and municipal governments exploring reparative frameworks. In Illinois, the Chicago suburb of Evanston made headlines as the first city to distribute government-funded reparations to Black residents to remedy historic housing discrimination.

However, Evanston’s program faces a high-profile class-action lawsuit filed by Judicial Watch, a conservative legal group, alleging the program’s race-based eligibility criteria violate the Equal Protection Clause of the Fourteenth Amendment.

The Trump administration wants to stop Illinois city's reparations effort for "simply handing out money based on race." (Associated Press)

"It either becomes something that is unconstitutional and will be challenged and shut down — like Evanston is on its way to being done — or you convert it into a universal program," he said.

"That is not reparations," Prince warned.

While Prince called broader social and racial justice initiatives "admirable," he reiterated that they should not hijack the legal definition of reparations.

"Reparations, in the context we're talking about, are only for those that were enslaved, emancipated, and then subject to the badges and incidents thereof," Prince said. "That is the American freedmen. Positioning it that way circumvents any legal challenge based on race."

The New Jersey lawmakers did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

articles.title: Indonesia suspends five officials over luxury apartments for inmates
articles.excerpt: A prison warden in Indonesia has been suspended, along with four other officials, after investigators discovered a compound of luxury apartment-style residences allegedly used by inmates at a penitent...
articles.body_text:
A prison warden in Indonesia has been suspended, along with four other officials, after investigators discovered a compound of luxury apartment-style residences allegedly used by inmates at a penitentiary near the capital, Jakarta.

The action was announced on Tuesday by Rudi Setiawan, the inspector general of the Ministry of Immigration and Corrections. “We have suspended five structural officials, including the Cibinong prison chief, who are suspected of being responsible for the incident uncovered by the Ombudsman,” he said.

Dozens of inmates and prison employees have been questioned, he said.

The units, more than 10 in all, stood apart from the regular cellblocks at Cibinong prison in Bogor, near Jakarta.

They were found on September 23 during a surprise inspection by Indonesia’s Ombudsman, the government’s public-service watchdog.

Investigators said the residences contained air-conditioners, big-screen televisions, refrigerators, sofas and dining areas. They also reported finding a gym, a golf simulator under construction, and luxury vehicles on the grounds.

“We found strong indications that certain inmates had access to special facilities unavailable to ordinary prisoners,” Syafrida Rachmawati Rasahan, an Ombudsman member, said at a news conference.

“We encountered inmates inside the residential compound and discovered facilities resembling homestays, apartments and villas rather than prison housing,” she said.

The buildings were originally intended as official housing for prison personnel, but investigators are examining whether they were converted into unauthorised accommodations for inmates.

The incident has drawn widespread public attention and renewed scrutiny of Indonesia’s prisons, which have long faced allegations that wealthy or well-connected inmates can obtain preferential treatment through bribery.

The Cibinong prison, which sits on 4 hectares (10 acres), holds a mix of inmates, including people convicted of corruption and other high-profile prisoners. The identities of those who lived in the compound have not been officially disclosed.

Lawmakers, anticorruption activists and watchdog groups have urged authorities to identify which prisoners occupied the facilities and whether prison officials accepted payments in exchange for the privileges.

The case is the latest embarrassment for the Indonesian corrections system, which has struggled for years with overcrowding, corruption and repeated allegations that affluent inmates can buy privileges unavailable to the broader prison population.

An investigation into Indonesia’s prisons in 2010 already found that some inmates live a life of luxury behind bars.

articles.title: Ukraine's prized steel industry left in ruins by Russian missile campaign
articles.excerpt:
After one attack on the Zaporizhzhia steelworks, a blast furnace was restarted only for the site to be hit again hours later

Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spe...
articles.body_text:
After one attack on the Zaporizhzhia steelworks, a blast furnace was restarted only for the site to be hit again hours later

Like thousands of other residents of Zaporizhzhia, Denys Maksyshko has spent years working for local steel factory Zaporizhstal. For generations, it has been the biggest and richest source of employment in this major Ukrainian city.

"Zaporizhstal is not just a big company, it's the heart of the city," he says.

Now, following a series of Russian missile strikes, this heart has stopped beating. The huge factory that employs 8,500 people shut down indefinitely after four waves of Russian attacks - two in August, and two in September.

"All the equipment has been almost completely destroyed. There are no windows left, and there are holes in the roofs. The blast furnaces have been almost completely ruined," Maksyshko complains.

Russia fired a total of 17 missiles at Zaporizhstal, according to Oleksandr Myronenko, chief operating officer of steelworks owner Metinvest. Eight workers were killed and 31 wounded.

"We're now clearing rubble and trying to plan recovery," Myronenko tells the BBC.

At the moment it is far from certain Zaporizhstal will ever start up again.

The Zaporizhstal works has been hit by four waves of Russian attacks

Russia's persistent campaign of air strikes against Ukrainian metallurgical plants started in August. By now, all of them have been hit, some several times.

This is a key sector of the Ukrainian economy, and naturally an attractive target for Russia.

Before the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022, metallurgy and mining accounted for roughly 10% of Ukraine's GDP and a third of its exports. It provided employment for more than half a million people, and every 13th job in Ukraine was linked to the industry one way or another.

Because of the recent Russian attacks, it has all but ground to a halt and its contribution to Ukraine's GDP now "is probably close to zero", says Myronenko.

Until recently his company was Ukraine's biggest producer of steel and iron, but all its steelworks are for now out of action.

"Clearly, they're trying to stop Ukraine's economy and stop Ukraine from getting [export] money from abroad, from paying taxes and wages, from ensuring that cities live and people have jobs," says Myronenko. "Their efforts have been very effective so far."

The damage to the metals industry could have devastating consequences for Ukraine's economy and society.

Ukraine had 12 metallurgical plants before losing parts of its industrial heartland in the east shortly after the start of hostilities with Russia in 2014.

By 2018, there were just nine, and three years into the full-scale war in 2025 that number had fallen to six. Among those lost were the Azovstal and Illich plants in Mariupol, Ukraine's south-eastern city captured after a months-long Russian siege.

Among the steel-making cities caught up in Russia's recent missile campaign is President Volodymyr Zelensky's home city of Kryvyi Rih.

On 25 September, Ukraine's biggest steelworks, Arcelor Mittal Kryvyi Rih, announced it was unable to reopen after repeated attacks over five weeks, praising the bravery of its workers, five of whom had died.

Russia targeting 'ordinary life' with attacks on Ukraine's data centres, Zelensky says

Eating garden weeds to survive in Russian-occupied city cut off from food and water

Cultural treasures are being destroyed worldwide - so why is no-one being punished?

Local Defence Council head Oleksandr Vilkul issued an emergency address to the city's residents, in which he spoke of a "very serious blow" that would affect more than just thousands of jobs.

The situation, he admitted, was very difficult.

"It is taxes feeding into our community's budget," he said. "They provided funds for keeping the city's infrastructure running, repairing heating plants and their pipes, funds for nursery schools, social services and many other things."

Taxes paid by metal-making companies have funded 30-70% of local government spending in their host cities, says Stanislav Zinchenko, head of Kyiv-based consultancy GMK Center.

"In other words, the physical survival of these cities depended on these companies," he told the BBC.

"This is a catastrophic problem for Ukraine's economy. Before the war, the mining and metallurgical industry was a key industry," he told the BBC. "It was always the biggest investor in the economy, investing $2bn-$3bn (£1.5bn-£2.3bn) a year on average."

Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual at Zaporizhstal any time soon

If the steelworks remain shut, hundreds of thousands of people may lose their jobs, and the resulting waves of migration will reach far beyond Ukraine, Zinchenko warned. "A humanitarian catastrophe is looming."

The end of steelmaking in Ukraine would also have severe consequences for its defence capabilities and reconstruction.

Steel is vital for producing military equipment, as well as for making shelters and repairing countless buildings damaged by Russia.

Russia has justified its attacks on the steel plants for that reason, alleging that the plants in Zaporizhzhia and Kryvyi Rih were all producing military hardware.

"We attempted relaunching Zaporizhstal. We restarted a furnace, and it worked for 10 hours before there was another air strike," Oleksandr Vodoviz of Metinvest told a conference in Kyiv.

There was no point yet on spending money on recovery as the situation was unclear, he added.

Even if production were to resume, it would not be business as usual for Ukrainian steelmakers any time soon.

Russian attacks on railways have made transporting their products within Ukraine difficult and dangerous, and strikes against ports have turned exports into a lethal lottery.

"Ports have essentially been blocked," said Oleksandr Myronenko. "Every ship is at risk of being attacked, and their chances are 50-50 - either you make it, or you don't."

EU quotas on steel imports introduced on 1 July may compound the problems faced by Ukraine.

But Denys Maksyshko, the Zaporizhstal worker, remains upbeat.

His colleagues are doing their bit to revive the factory, clearing away rubble and fixing whatever can be fixed.

"This is similar to what the military do in the trenches. Ordinary people are fighting to keep the factory alive like soldiers."

articles.title: Jack Smith defends investigations into Trump during tense US Senate hearing
articles.excerpt:
Former Special Counsel Jack Smith has defended his investigations of President Donald Trump in a United States Senate hearing, though Republican lawmakers accused him of abusing his authority.

On Tue...
articles.body_text:
Former Special Counsel Jack Smith has defended his investigations of President Donald Trump in a United States Senate hearing, though Republican lawmakers accused him of abusing his authority.

On Tuesday, Smith told the Senate Judiciary Committee that his investigations followed Justice Department policy and were based on evidence.

He rejected accusations that political considerations influenced his decision to bring criminal charges against Trump, the first US president ever to be indicted.

“Our investigation developed proof beyond a reasonable doubt that President Trump engaged in serious crimes against our nation,” Smith said.

A former war crimes prosecutor at The Hague, Smith was appointed special counsel in 2022 to independently investigate allegations about Trump’s behaviour after the end of his first term as president.

In 2023, Smith ultimately brought two criminal indictments against Trump: one for his alleged attempts to subvert the 2020 presidential election and a second for his handling of classified documents while out of office.

Separately, two further criminal indictments were brought against Trump. One, in New York, accused Trump of falsifying business records to conceal unflattering information during his 2016 presidential campaign.

A second, in Georgia, also concerned allegations that Trump and his allies sought to overturn the 2020 election results.

Only one case – the New York indictment – was brought to trial, resulting in felony convictions. The rest were dropped after Trump was re-elected in 2024.

Smith himself resigned shortly before Trump’s second inauguration in January 2025. The Justice Department has a policy of not prosecuting sitting presidents.

Trump has denied all the charges against him and has accused Smith and former President Joe Biden of orchestrating a political “witch-hunt” against him.

Republicans focused much of Tuesday’s hearing on Smith’s investigative methods, including subpoenas that obtained phone records associated with members of Congress and financial information from Republican donors and organisations.

Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley accused Smith’s team of using its investigations to “map out and target the entire Republican Party”.

Smith, however, maintained that his office had a duty to pursue evidence relevant to the investigation.

He also defended obtaining phone records from lawmakers. He said the records helped corroborate evidence that Trump and his allies contacted members of Congress as they sought to delay certification of the 2020 election results.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz, whose records were among those sought, pressed Smith about why lawmakers were not notified of the subpoenas. Smith said prosecutors feared Trump and his associates could destroy evidence or interfere with the investigation if the subpoenas were disclosed.

“Is it a crime to be a Republican?” Cruz asked.

Smith added that his office consulted the Justice Department’s Public Integrity Section before obtaining the records.

The information Smith sought reveals the time and duration of the telephone calls but not their content. Critics have pointed out that there was no law against seeking such records during the course of Smith’s investigation.

During his testimony, Smith not only defended his investigative decisions but also accused the Trump administration of retaliating against the prosecutors and agents who worked on the two cases.

He argued that members of his former team had been fired for “doing their jobs”. Those firings have prompted legal challenges.

In March, three former agents with the FBI who investigated Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election filed a class-action lawsuit alleging they were illegally terminated as part of a “retribution campaign”. The lawsuit seeks their reinstatement.

Smith, who said Trump has threatened him with jail, framed the scrutiny of his work as part of a broader challenge to the independence of the Justice Department.

“As I appear before you today, it is my belief that the rule of law faces challenges unlike any we have experienced in our lifetime,” Smith said. “I will not be silenced by continued threats of prosecution from the president or others.”

articles.title: Carville mocks Dem candidate staffers as 'weak' and 'soft' for complaining about treatment to New York Times
articles.excerpt:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville shredded a recent New York Times article for reporting complaints from former staffers about working under Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola.

articles.body_text:
Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville shredded a recent New York Times article for reporting complaints from former staffers about working under Alaska Senate candidate Mary Peltola.

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville blasted staffers who complained to The New York Times about working for former Alaska Rep. Mary Peltola as she runs for the Senate.

The Times article headlined, "Angry Outbursts, Slurs and Firings: Tumult Rocks a Key Senate Campaign," featured comments from former aides who described chaos in Peltola's congressional office and Senate campaign as the Democrat hopes to flip a Republican seat.

"I want to react to a story I read in the New York Times concerning the Democratic nominee for the United States Senate from the state of Alaska," Carville said in a brief video posted to the Politicon channel on Monday. "It would appear that we have some upset little staffers that she is not — when she's under pressure — not nice to ‘em."

"Of course, The New York Times didn't understand when you're in the middle of a political campaign, and you're a candidate, and you're under pressure, and you got everything coming in from everywhere, and you're trying to raise money, and you're trying to fend off attacks, and you're trying to do this, maybe you don't have time to be overly courteous to little pussified staffers that just — they — 'I want my name and my humanity,’" he continued.

GOP SENATOR, EX-HOUSE DEM EMERGE FROM ALASKA’S ‘JUNGLE PRIMARY’ DESPITE FAR-LEFT MEDDLING

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville blasted former staffers of a Democratic Senate candidate in Alaska for complaining about how they were treated. (Photo by Matt Winkelmeyer/Getty Images for Amazon Studios)

"I got news for you. When I ran campaigns, you didn't have a f---in’ name until you did something," Carville said. "'Hey, you, come over here! Do this! Do what the f--- you’re told and shut up!’ And you know what? Then, when you achieve something, or you do something, then you get a name. But until that, in politics, you don't have a name. Go do something else. Go be a social worker. They'll give you a name right away!"

"Now, if somebody does something obviously dehumanizing or overly rude, then that's one thing," Carville added, juxtaposing that with "Telling people to go get coffee for you or calling them by, ‘Hey, you.’ Everybody wants a pronoun. Well, I'll give you a pronoun. ‘You’ or ‘a--hole come over here.’"

He went on to mock various demands that employees might have, replying, "Well s--t, that’s why we lose."

He also suggested that female political candidates are scrutinized more heavily when accused of lashing out at staffers.

BAD BOSSES ON CAPITOL HILL COULD FACE RECKONING UNDER NEW ANONYMOUS STAFFER REVIEW PLATFORM

Alaska US Senate candidate Mary Peltola faced numerous allegations from former staffers in a New York Times piece. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu)

"Why don't we just call every female candidate for everything a goddamn b-----? You'd save time," he said.

"But let's stop this nonsense that everybody that works in politics is all equal and everybody's opinion needs to be respected, and it doesn't matter," he said, calling it "nonsense."

"But do me a favor. If you, if you're that f---in’ delicate, if you're that much of a some kind of a honeysuckle, whatever it is, go do something else with your life," he added. "You're too weak. You're too soft."

After predicting that he would be criticized by far-left media outlets, Carville emphasized his message was directed at the Democratic staffers listening.

"But all — every — to every staffer on every Democratic campaign, on every — anything: just put your head down, work your a-- off and save the country and f--- your feelings," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville argued that women do indeed face a double-standard for being tough in the workplace in the same way men are, and quipped, "Why don't we just call every female candidate for everything a goddamn b-----? You'd save time." (Cindy Ord/Getty Images for SCAD)

Democratic strategist and pollster Doug Schoen spoke to Fox News Digital about how working in politics absolutely requires a "thick skin," but said that the allegations against Peltola were troubling.

"He is absolutely right regarding the intensity of political campaigns," he said. "Working on a race is hard, and it is tense, and therefore a thick skin is definitely a plus. While it is absolutely inappropriate and wrong for a candidate to act as Peltola has been alleged to have acted, I don't believe the allegations, however serious, will affect the outcome of the Alaska Senate election. This is an election that is a referendum on Donald Trump and his governance first and foremost."

Former RNC national spokesperson Elizabeth Pipko agreed that the life of a campaign staffer is not for the faint of heart, and it becomes an absolute crucible as the election draws near.

"Criticisms of Peltola aside, I do agree with Carville when it comes to campaign life and intensity," she said. "He is 100% correct about how cut-throat campaigns can be, and I’m sure how cut-throat they were back when he was working on them and before our culture changed as dramatically as it has."

"Campaigns are full of surprises, usually bad ones, meaning you never know what you’re walking into," Pipko continued. "The closer you get to Election Day, the less you eat or sleep. And the high-stakes atmosphere usually gets the best of folks that aren’t able to compartmentalize their feelings and their thoughts, or who simply don’t have the stamina to keep up with how ruthless a campaign cycle can be. Campaign life is not for the faint of heart. In fact, I’d argue campaign life is not for most people, and that’s OK."

Fox News Digital contacted Peltola and The New York Times for comment but did not immediately receive responses.

Alexander Hall is an associate editor for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to Alexander.hall@fox.com.

articles.title: Australia news live: Shoebridge and Hodgins-May announce Greens leadership bid, saying Labor ‘can’t stop One Nation’

articles.body_text:

As we brought you earlier, senators David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May have now confirmed they will stand for leadership positions in the Greens’ party room ballot.

In a statement posted to Shoebridge’s Instagram, the pair said they would be a “fresh leadership team”.

double quotation markWe do not seek to reform Labor, but to replace them,” the statement reads, potentially signalling a bolder stance on how they would deal with the government and push for reform.

The answer to the rise of One Nation and the far right is giving people hope, and making people’s lives better with real economic and environmental security.

They cited “a meal before school” for children, “no new coal and gas”, and “holding back the wave of US billionaire tech bros and their vampire AI data centres” in the pitch.

This article includes content provided by Instagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content, click 'Allow and continue'.

Shoebridge and Hodgins-May also said the Greens needed to be “a bigger mass movement” and expressed support for the idea of former MP Max Chandler-Mather for ordinary party members – not just the parliamentary wing – to have a say in electing the leader. No details on how that would work, but the pair said they would “work with the party on this”.

‘Give and take’ relationship with AI giants, head of Australian Signals Directorate says

Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said Australia is beholden to AI companies that are willing to give the country access to sophisticated models, but added partnerships work “both ways”.

Bradshaw spoke to RN Breakfast this morning after the OpenAI breach of a Medicare website, saying Australia has “unique insights” to offer such companies that are valuable for technology giants. She said:

double quotation markIt’s a give and take here. And I think what’s important also is to look at the content of that apology. It’s not just the headline. The apology is important. We shouldn’t miss that moment.

But actually, look at the content of what OpenAI have set out there. That is not insignificant. They are agreeing actually to sharing, for example, preliminary findings. They have taken a really significant step in slowing down the release of the next model to ensure that guardrails and sufficient safeguards are put in place. They have given an offer of practical support.

And in fact, that is consistent with our experience, with our engagement with not just OpenAI, but the other labs, Anthropic and others, over the last six months. … And I think that’s a really important precedent for the way this relationship proceeds into the future.

Why are there so many bogong moths, and how can you safely remove them from your home?

Skies over parts of New South Wales have been aflutter in recent days as swarms of bogong moths begin their annual migration, travelling up to 1,000 km from their breeding grounds in different parts of the country to a small number of cool caves in the Australian Alps.

Sightings of the endangered moth have increased over the last two years, but reports to the citizen science program Moth Tracker this September alone have exceeded 2025’s total figures, according to Zoos Victoria, which runs the platform.

What do the burgeoning insect numbers mean for their recovery, and what should you do if you find bogongs inside your home?

Laneway festival just dropped its lineup for next year’s event, and there are some heavy hitters from both the international scene and Australian shores.

Irish rock darlings Fontaines D.C. are headlining alongside Paramore frontwoman Hayley Williams. In pop land, Slayyyter and Adéla join the deeply fun Kim Petras and Muna.

Australia’s own Ninajirachi, Ecca Vandal and Swapmeet are on the bill, too, as are many more acts bound to make a good time.

Shoebridge and Hodgins-May also said the Greens needed to be “a bigger mass movement” and expressed support for the idea of former MP Max Chandler-Mather for ordinary party members – not just the parliamentary wing – to have a say in electing the leader. No details on how that would work, but the pair said they would “work with the party on this”.

Hume says Reserve Bank had no choice but to raise rates after Chalmers ‘unable to control’ domestic factors

Jane Hume, the deputy opposition leader, said the Reserve Bank “of course” had no choice but to raise interest rates yesterday, laying blame on the Labor government’s spending.

Hume spoke to RN Breakfast this morning, touting the Coalition’s proposed petrol price “shield” to cut the fuel excise at a certain threshold. But she added:

double quotation markThe real issue here is whether your economy is resilient enough to be able to handle those international shocks. My concern here is that this particular rate rise, which we know has taken the cash rates to its highest level in 15 years, has demonstrated that Jim Chalmers has been found out as the emperor, he has no clothes. …

He has been unable to control the domestic factors using the fiscal levers. That means that Michelle Bullock, as the independent governor of the Reserve Bank, has had to pull the monetary policy levers that much harder.

Hume said there was “so much more” the government could do, claiming Labor had “frittered away” windfall gains and spent them, adding to inflation.

double quotation markThen we wonder why there’s domestic strains, domestic capacity issues. That’s what Michelle Bullock is referring to. She’s too polite to point the finger directly, but there is no way that she should take the blame for having to raise.

Who is potential Greens deputy leader candidate Steph Hodgins-May?

So who is the first-term senator expected to announce a leadership ticket tilt with David Shoebridge?

The 41-year-old Steph Hodgins-May was appointed to the Senate in May 2024 after Janet Rice called time on a decade in parliament the month before.

The party’s resources spokesperson, Hodgins-May in June accused fossil fuel companies of using the programs and sponsorships to “build social licence” with kids.

double quotation markGet your dirty hands off our kids, that is our message to the fossil fuel industry, who have no place in early-learning centres, in schools, or in our cultural institutions in this country.

Children should go to school to get evidence-based education, not to be brainwashed by fossil fuel corporations seeking to build social licence.

Born in Ballarat, Hodgins-May was head of the Pacific for Greenpeace Australia from 2020 to 2023, and also holds a law degree. She ran for the Victorian seat of Macnamara (and its predecessor, Melbourne Ports) at the 2016, 2019 and 2022 elections.

In a post on Instagram yesterday she wished Larissa Waters well, commending the outgoing leader on her “courage, wisdom and care”.
