The Greens are expected to hold a leadership vote today, and party sources yesterday and today said two new contenders are likely to enter the contest – David Shoebridge and Steph Hodgins-May.

A formal confirmation is expected shortly, which we’ll bring you. Shoebridge yesterday didn’t rule out running for the leadership role, and we’re told that he and Hodgins-May are looking at a joint ticket.

They would join Mehreen Faruqi and Nick McKim, who announced a run for leader and deputy respectively, and Sarah Hanson-Young who has also announced her candidacy.

Australian Signals Directorate chief says OpenAI’s ‘substantive’ steps key to future security after Medicare breach

Abigail Bradshaw, the director general of the Australian Signals Directorate, said yesterday’s apology by OpenAI after a hack of a Medicare website was important, but the “substantive” steps the tech company plans to better safeguard sensitive information is the bigger takeaway.

OpenAI apologised for the breach yesterday and said an executive will front parliament next week to speak about the episode and what will be done to prevent it from happening again.

double quotation markI think that the message out of this is – this is a demonstration, in fact, about how Australia can participate in developing new norms, new behaviours, and new protocols which are beneficial to Australians but, in fact, are shaping norms which will impact people around the world.

She added the signals directorate had been working to defend Australian data from emerging technology and “fortify” itself.

double quotation markThere has been work and engagement over the last six months utilising – including models that aren’t publicly available – to fortify the sensitive networks of, for example, financial institutions, health institutions, energy providers.

That process enabled us to – with great speed – identify vulnerabilities in code and patch those prior to the rollout of that really important national process.

Wife of Australian detained by Vietnam says she has concerns about his welfare

Chloe Dang, the wife of a missing Vietnamese Australian democracy campaigner, said she hasn’t slept for days after her husband went missing during a trip to Cambodia.

Tran Hiep, 50, was due to return to Bangkok, Thailand, earlier this month and reunite with his wife, but never returned. Dang said the government has since confirmed he has been detained by Vietnamese authorities on what have been described as “fabricated” charges.

Dang said she hasn’t heard anything from her husband, but found out yesterday from Vietnam that he was in the country. She said she does not know where he is being held, or the status of his wellbeing.

“My most concern is his wellbeing as well, because it’s been 12 days and we hadn’t heard anything,” she told ABC News Breakfast. “He’s an Australian citizen. He went into Cambodia legally. And now, the accusation is he tried to pass the border [into Vietnam] illegally.”

She’s asked the Australian government to do everything they can to secure his release, saying officials have been assisting her and her family.

Good morning, Nick Visser here once more to guide you through the day’s news. Let’s get to it.

Two men and a teenage boy have been charged in relation to the alleged mistaken identity shooting of Sydney student Marco Tapia – including the person who allegedly held the gun – police say.

Tapia, 23, was shot inside his family’s home in Glen Alpine early on 1 September. Police have alleged perpetrators had the wrong home and person.

The trio – aged 22, 23 and 16 – were arrested in Junee, near Wagga Wagga, yesterday and charged with a series of offences: murder, two counts of special aggravated break and enter and committing a serious indictable offence – weapon and possessing an unauthorised prohibited firearm.

Detectives will allege in court the three – one allegedly armed with a pistol – entered the home and confronted Tapia, before he was fatally shot.

All three will appear in court today – the teenager will appear in children’s court.

Two other teenage boys have been charged and remain before the courts.

Early works are beginning on the second stage of the long-awaited train line to Melbourne airport – a 7.6km stretch of the train line from Albion to Keilor East, where a new station will be built.

Anthony Albanese will be in Melbourne today with Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, to announce that site investigations, procurement and development work will begin in the coming weeks.

Built alongside the Jacana freight corridor, this stage of the project will feature a 500m rail bridge to carry trains over the Maribyrnong River.

Community engagement and early designs will follow next year, with major construction on the Keilor East station to begin in 2028 and finish in 2031.

The first stage of Melbourne Airport Rail, which involves the creation of the “Sunshine superhub” and the construction of new stations at Tottenham and Albion, is expected to be completed in 2030.

A man has been charged with murder after the deaths of two men at Gurranang, about 25km north of Grafton in northern New South Wales, police said.

About 3pm on Sunday 13 September, police were called to a house after reports the body of a 79-year-old man had been found.

Officers visited the house again on Monday when they found the body of a 59-year-old man in a shed on the property.

Detectives arrested a 32-year-old man at a hospital in Grafton yesterday afternoon.

He was taken to Grafton police station where he was charged with two counts of murder and stealing a motor vehicle.

He was refused bail to appear before court today.

OpenAI’s Medicare breach has prompted a government-wide assessment of cyber systems to bolster Australia’s public sector against further AI threats – deliberate or not.

Home affairs directed all government departments and agencies to undertake a “rapid” stocktake of legacy systems, to formulate risk management for legacy technology and to report their compliance back to the department.

The directive prioritises systems of government significance – the government’s critical systems – with a review due by the end of the year, while other systems will be assessed by March.

The acting home affairs minister, Richard Marles, said AI is “changing the environment in which we operate at extraordinary speed.”

double quotation markWe can’t wait for an old system to fail before replacing it. We need to identify vulnerabilities and deal with them before they can be exploited.

Good morning and welcome to our live news blog. I’m Martin Farrer with the top overnight stories and then it’ll be Nick Visser with the main action.

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, will be in Melbourne today with Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, to announce early works are beginning on the second stage of the long-awaited train line to Melbourne airport. More coming up.

A man has been charged with murder after the deaths of two men at Gurranang, about 25km north of Grafton in northern New South Wales, police said. More on that soon.

articles.title: Ex-NFL player Jack Brewer leads charge to end fines for players using religous, political eyeblack messaging
articles.excerpt: Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brewer met with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, pushing for change after a current player was fined for writing "GLORY BE 2 GOD" under his eyes durin...
articles.body_text:
Former Minnesota Vikings captain Jack Brewer met with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission, pushing for change after a current player was fined for writing "GLORY BE 2 GOD" under his eyes during a game.

Former NFL player Jack Brewer met with officials from the U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday as he seeks federal scrutiny of the league’s decision to fine Arizona Cardinals cornerback Kei’Trel Clark for displaying a religious message on his eye black.

Clark was fined $6,651 after wearing eye black bearing the message "Glory Be 2 God" during Arizona’s Week 1 victory over the Los Angeles Chargers.

Brewer, an ordained Christian minister and member of the federal Commission on the Social Status of Black Men and Boys, told OutKick that his meeting was intended to determine whether the NFL’s treatment of Clark could raise an employment-discrimination issue.

DOJ CRACKING DOWN ON MLB FOR POTENTIAL RELIGIOUS DISCRIMINATION AFTER PRIDE NIGHT CAPS CONTROVERSY

Kei'Trel Clark #13 of the Arizona Cardinals celebrates during the first half of an NFL game against the Tennessee Titans at State Farm Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Oct. 5, 2025. (Getty Images)

"When you start talking about freedom of speech in this country and you start talking about employees’ rights in this country, it’s a big deal," Brewer said. "As a Christian man, I’m not going to stand for that. And as a former NFL player, I’m not going to stand for that."

Brewer said the meeting was "very well received" and left him confident that further conversations with the agency would take place.

"The goal was to first understand: Do we have a potential case? What does that look like? What would the player’s rights be?" Brewer said. "My goal was just to establish some communication and talk about next steps, which we did. And so now we’ll start to work to gather information and get a deeper understanding of really what goes on in the minds of a league like the National Football League."

Brewer initially raised the issue in a Sept. 25 letter to EEOC Chair Andrea Lucas, requesting a meeting about the fine and the league’s policies governing religious expression.

"The NFL treated Clark’s gratitude to God, as expressed in four words, as a punishable personal message," Brewer wrote in the letter obtained by OutKick. "This fine represents an action that strikes at the heart of religious liberty and sends a chilling message to every person of faith in professional sports."

Brewer asked the EEOC to consider whether the NFL would be required to accommodate a player’s sincere religious expression when doing so would not impose an undue hardship on the league or its teams.

Title VII of the Civil Rights Act requires covered employers to reasonably accommodate employees’ sincerely held religious beliefs and practices unless an accommodation would impose an undue hardship on the employer’s business. In its 2023 decision in Groff v. DeJoy , the Supreme Court held that an employer must demonstrate that an accommodation would create "substantial increased costs" in relation to its particular business.

However, Brewer’s meeting does not mean the EEOC has opened an investigation or concluded that the NFL violated federal law. Any potential case would require a fact-specific examination that could include Clark’s employment relationship with the Cardinals and NFL, whether he requested a religious accommodation, and the effect an exception to the uniform rule would have on the league’s operations.

NFL TOLD AZEEZ AL-SHAAIR HE'D BE PULLED FROM TEXANS GAME OVER PRO-PALESTINIAN EYEBLACK MESSAGE

An individual or organization may file an EEOC charge on another person’s behalf, according to the agency, but Brewer did not say that a formal charge had been filed.

The NFL cited Rule 5, Section 4, Article 8 in its disciplinary letter to Clark. The rule prohibits players from displaying personal messages in writing or illustration on game day unless the message has received advance approval from the league's office.

Clark posted the fine notice on social media and wrote that he "needed answers."

"I got to report to God at the end of my days on the day of judgment," Clark wrote. "I’ll always give God the glory and out loud. All good."

Brewer argued that allowing four words on a player’s eye black would place little apparent burden on a multibillion-dollar sports league.

"If someone’s writing things across their uniform or putting it out there on top of their helmet, that’s a different story," Brewer said. "But the eye black — think back to Tim Tebow and many, many other athletes, myself. We would write stuff on our tapes, on our forearms. We would write stuff on our eye black.

"To think about fining someone for doing that, it’s unconscionable," he added. "It’s disgusting."

The NFL’s rule does not distinguish between religious and political messages. Houston Texans linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair, a practicing Muslim, was fined $11,492 this month after wearing eye black bearing the name "Hind Rajab," a Palestinian girl killed in Gaza in 2024. Al-Shaair was also fined $11,593 after displaying the message "Stop the genocide" during the previous postseason.

Azeez al-Shaair No. 0 of the Houston Texans warms up before a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at NRG Stadium on Sept. 20, 2026, in Houston, Texas. (Getty Images)

When asked whether Al-Shaair should receive the same protection he is seeking for Clark, Brewer initially distinguished between expressions of faith and political statements. But he ultimately said the NFL must apply its restrictions consistently, particularly while promoting league-approved social messages.

"I think he should be just as protected," Brewer said of Al-Shaair. "If you’re going to pull down the messaging, pull it all down, but don’t pick and choose."

The NFL has continued to display league-approved social justice messages in stadium end zones and on players’ helmets. Teams have been permitted to select from phrases including "End Racism," "Stop Hate," "Choose Love" and "Inspire Change," while the league has also promoted LGBTQ inclusion through team and league initiatives.

Brewer contended that the difference between league-selected messages and unauthorized player expression creates a double standard.

"You cannot treat people differently based upon whatever it is you want to promote," Brewer said. "If you are an organization like the National Football League, you cannot pick and choose the messaging that you want your players to play underneath."

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Brewer said his immediate objective is to build support among current and former players and ultimately force the NFL to address the treatment of religious expression.

"I want players across the National Football League, current and former, to take a stand, to show unity on something," he said. "As a National Football League player, you should be able to use your platform to profess the gospel, to profess your God and to write it on your eye black."

Brewer emphasized that he would support the right of players from other faiths to seek the same accommodation.

The Minnesota Vikings hosted a seminar for women at Winter Park.
IN THIS PHOTO: Eden Prairie, Mn., Sat. Oct. 12, 2002--Viking defensive back Jack Brewer (formerly a University of Minnesota defensive back) worked with a group of audience volunteers on kickoff mechanics. Brewer appeared with special teams coach Jay Hayes and the two took a team of women through a kickoff exercise. (From left to right are Katie Ruberto, Kristi Baer, Laurie Stark, Karolynn Olson and Brenda Palmer.) (Getty Images)

"I don’t care what religion you are," Brewer said. "If you want to have the Star of David on, or you want to say, ‘Thank you, Allah,’ you have every right to do that in this country. That’s what makes this country so great."

The NFL has not responded to request for comment.

Jackson Thompson is a sports reporter for Fox News Digital covering critical political and cultural issues in sports, with an investigative lens. Jackson's reporting has been cited in federal government actions related to the enforcement of Title IX, and in legacy media outlets including The New York Times, The Los Angeles Times, The Philadelphia Inquirer, The Associated Press and ESPN.com.

articles.title: Venezuelan man shot by ICE officer in Texas is charged with assault
articles.excerpt: A Venezuelan asylum seeker who was shot in the back by a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Texas is facing a federal assault charge, after prosecutors accused him of s...
articles.body_text:
A Venezuelan asylum seeker who was shot in the back by a United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officer in Texas is facing a federal assault charge, after prosecutors accused him of striking the officer with his car’s side-view mirror.

Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, appeared in federal court in Austin on Tuesday, where he was charged with assaulting, resisting and impeding a federal officer. He could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted.

The charge stems from a September 20 encounter that began while Garces Perez was making a DoorDash food delivery near a shopping centre in Austin, the Texas state capital.

A federal complaint filed on Monday says immigration officers noticed that Garces Perez’s car had its emergency lights flashing, and they ran a database check. They found it was registered to Garces Perez, who was subject to a final order of removal from the US.

When the officers approached, Garces Perez handed over his driver’s license through a partially opened window but did not get out of the car, the complaint says. He asked the officers to wait until his wife could arrive to retrieve the vehicle.

Court documents describe the exchange up to that point as “pleasant and not aggressive”.

About a minute later, however, court documents say Garces Perez “abruptly” closed his window and drove off, striking one of the officers in the torso with his driver’s side mirror.

That officer chased Garces Perez in his own vehicle and caught up with him a short time later. In the complaint, the officer alleges that Garces Perez then tried to drive into him, prompting him to open fire.

There is no publicly available footage showing the events described in the complaint, including the shooting.

Videos, however, have circulated online showing the shooting’s aftermath, with Garces Perez injured in his car.

The complaint relies on unreleased body-camera footage from one of the two ICE officers who stopped Garces Perez.

The second officer was not wearing a body camera, according to the affidavit. That officer says he was struck by Garces Perez’s side mirror and later shot him.

Garces Perez, however, gave federal investigators a different account of the moments immediately before he was shot.

He told investigators that, after a brief chase, a law enforcement SUV struck his car, causing it to spin around, according to the affidavit. He said the officer then opened fire, shooting him in the back.

Garces Perez has been held in a detention facility in south Texas since the shooting.

His lawyer, Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch, said on Sunday the bullet was still lodged in his body and that he has a fractured clavicle. In a social media post, Lincoln-Goldfinch explained that his supporters were worried he could develop sepsis or suffer permanent damage if he didn’t undergo surgery soon.

The Department of Homeland Security has argued, however, that Garces Perez is receiving adequate medical care.

Garces Perez’s legal team is also seeking to stop his removal from the US.

The Venezuelan national entered the US in 2024 through CBP One, an online programme expanded under former President Joe Biden to allow asylum seekers to make appointments with immigration authorities at the US-Mexico border.

Trump ended the programme on his first day back in office, accusing the app of contributing to an immigration crisis in the US. His administration has since relaunched CBP One as CBP Home, a self-deportation portal.

Lincoln-Goldfinch has said Garces Perez was legally seeking asylum in the US and had a valid work permit. She has asserted that he was ordered to be deported after missing an immigration court hearing because the notice had been sent to an old address.

Garces Perez is due back before a federal immigration judge on Wednesday for a separate hearing on whether he can remain in the country.

The case comes amid a surge in immigration enforcement during Trump’s second term, with ICE reporting more than 50,000 arrests in both July and August.

Landen Chambers ran for a 1-yard TD to extend the UCF Knights' lead over the TCU Horned Frogs.

Thanks to the modern Artemis Missions, mankind is headed back to the Moon in the next few years, but for their annual Space Game uniforms, the UCF Knights are throwing it back to the pioneers who got us there in the first place.

The Knights have been throwing on special space-themed getups for a decade now, and they're pretty much always a feast for the eyes with unique designs, nods to the space program, and of course, the Citronaut.

However, I think this year's batch, which pays homage to the Mercury, Gemini, and Apollo programs of the 1960s, is tough to top.

This is the school's tenth Space Game, which they've dubbed "Mission X," and there is so much cool symbolism in everything.

UCF opened its doors in 1963 — right around the time the Space Race was heating up — as Florida Technological University, and ever since, it has long served as a pipeline to the nearby Kennedy Space Center.

ANCIENT ARTIFACTS FOUND BENEATH CAPE CANAVERAL SPACE FORCE STATION AS ONE MYSTERY STILL STUMPS RESEARCHERS

That's why this year, the team is celebrating that particular era and, man, are there some cool details.

The UCF Knights' latest Space Game jerseys honor the 1960s era of space exploration. (Credit: UCF Athletics)

The black stitching that criss-crosses the jersey is a nod to the Mercury program's space suits, which featured black stitching and prominent zippers.

NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND—OR CHINA WILL

If you look at the cuffs, one is "Canaveral blue" — which has become the go-to Space Game color for UCF — and the other is red, just like the cuffs were on the Gemini program's space suits.

The collar is Canaveral blue, just like the inside of the suits worn throughout the 1960s.

On the shoulders, the patches mimic those worn during the Gemini missions, while this year's Space Game patch is modeled after the patch from the Gemini X mission.

The Knights Space Game Mission X helmets feature a red stripe like those worn by Apollo mission commanders, while this year's patch is an homage to the one used for Gemini X. (Credit: UCF Athletics)

The pants feature the school's old Citronaut mascot (which, as a UCF alum, I wouldn't hate seeing back full-time; I love it), and a striping pattern like the one that appeared on Apollo program rockets and space suits.

Finally, the helmets have a bold red stripe on them, which is a reference to the similar stripe worn on the helmets of Apollo mission commanders.

Alright, I've seen enough: ten out of ten. No notes.

What an absolute home run on all fronts. There are Easter eggs everywhere you look, but the entire uniform still looks killer in its own right.

These beauties will debut at the Acrisure Bounce House on October 30 when the Knights host the Baylor Bears.

articles.title: Iraq begins high-stakes security balancing act as US troops withdraw
articles.excerpt: Iraq is set to hold four “Sovereignty Days”, a national holiday marking the complete withdrawal of US troops from the country and underscoring the deep symbolism of the exit after more than two decade...
articles.body_text:
Iraq is set to hold four “Sovereignty Days”, a national holiday marking the complete withdrawal of US troops from the country and underscoring the deep symbolism of the exit after more than two decades of foreign intervention.

Wednesday’s withdrawal deadline affirmed the exodus of a few hundred remaining US soldiers in the country, who have served in advisory roles in a coalition operation against ISIL (ISIS) first launched in 2015.

While the exit plan predates Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, it fits into his wider vision of reasserting Iraqi state authority. That encompasses accelerating efforts to disarm all militias in the country by June 2027, including several powerful pro-Iran groups who have launched attacks throughout the region amid the US-Israeli war with Iran.

Speaking at the United Nations General Assembly (UNGA) last week, al-Zaidi said his government was “striving to ensure that the state is the ultimate decision-maker in matters of peace and war, and that weapons and tools of power remain in the hands of its constitutional institutions”.

He added, “With the end of the international coalition’s mission in Iraq, we are moving our relationship with our strategic partners to a new phase, moving from military cooperation to economic and development cooperation in service of our common interests.”

Indeed, the US withdrawal appears to be part of a strategy by al-Zaidi to “politically weaken” influential militias, including those linked to Iran, according to Douglas Silliman, the former US ambassador to Iraq and Kuwait.

Those militias have long pointed to the presence of the US military, and other foreign actors like Turkiye, as a pillar justification for maintaining their own weapons stores and chains of command. Some have already indicated they will refuse to hand over their arms.

“The prime minister is clearly trying to build a political case to Iraqis that these forces that are more beholden to Iran, and have used weapons without government authorisation, no longer have a political reason to have those weapons,” said Silliman, who serves as president of the Arab Gulf States Institute.

It is a high-stakes gambit, leaving room for Iran to assert greater influence in the country and opening the door to a potentially catastrophic domestic standoff down the line.

It also creates the potential for increased pressure from the US if Iraq-based groups continue to target Washington’s assets.

“It’s going to be a very difficult series of decisions,” Silliman said. “Both for the militias and for Prime Minister al-Zaidi and his defence team.”

How the Iraqi government navigates the end of the US-led coalition’s deployment, dubbed “Operation Inherent Resolve”, will have wide-ranging implications for the future security of Iraq.

The country has remained relatively stable in recent years following the 2017 territorial defeat of ISIL, despite being enveloped by conflict and insecurity on its borders. That stability has generally persisted since the US began its troop withdrawal in 2020 under US President Donald Trump, with the remaining military personnel consolidating at an airbase in Erbil, in northern Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region, at the end of 2025.

To be sure, al-Zaidi has already sought to build in some safeguards amid the wider effort to disarm and integrate militias into Iraqi government forces, pushing back on an initial September 30, 2026 deadline to June 2027 to bring all weapons under state control.

Al-Zaidi told The New York Times earlier this month that both the US and Iran-aligned militias have given assurances that they will refrain from any attacks for 90 days following the US withdrawal, in an effort to prevent the situation from devolving in the short term.

Still, Renad Mansour, director of the Iraq Initiative at Chatham House, said militias aligned with Iran’s “axis of resistance” in the region ultimately remain “in full-on war mode, working with the IRGC [Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] in the region. And so they will continue to target US and US interests.”

While al-Zaidi has promised continued integration and cooperation with the US and other Western allies, there is likely disquiet behind the rhetoric, Mansour assessed, with some seeing the US’s erstwhile presence in the country as having served as a bulwark against a wider policy pivot.

“The anxiety from the Iraqi government now is that the US might not need Iraq any more, or might, in the worst case, view Iraq as a pariah state, too close to Iran, and therefore another target,” he said.

The targeting could eventually come in the form of sanctions or in an escalation of US and Israeli strikes on Iraqi territory, Mansour said.

Mohammad Salih, a non-resident senior fellow at the Foreign Policy Research Institute and an expert on Iraq, also agreed that enthusiasm for the US troop withdrawal was likely more subdued within some segments of the Iraqi government than public statements – and national holidays – suggest.

Salih assessed an underlying wariness to change the security status quo at a time of regional upheaval, pointing to the continued threat from ISIL sleeper cells, shifting cross-border dynamics in a post-Assad Syria, as well as the US-Israel war with Iran.

“The official rhetoric tries to signal that Iraq is more or less fine, that it can take care of itself, and that it seeks stronger commercial and diplomatic ties with the US – that there is no need for the US military presence,” he said.

“But in reality, there is a great deal of concern that Iraq could be the next theatre of some major regional development,” he told Al Jazeera.

The operational implications of the end to the US-led anti-ISIL mission remain difficult to assess.

In the wake of the withdrawal, the two countries appear to be reverting to a 2008 Strategic Framework and Security Agreement, signed under the administration of US President George W Bush, Salih said. The deal pledges continued, if non-binding, US security support for Iraq.

Neither the Iraqi government nor the Pentagon have given a clear picture of what shape security cooperation could take going forward, particularly when it comes to the intelligence and logistical support that buoyed ISIL’s territorial defeat.

However, a regional source with knowledge of the situation told Al Jazeera the relationship is “likely to become less centred on a visible military footprint and more focused on intelligence, training, technical support, capacity-building and institutional cooperation”.

The source called the change a “test of whether a relationship built for a period of military intervention can evolve into a more conventional partnership between sovereign states”.

Several experts noted that Iraqi security forces – including its military, police, counterterrorism forces, and militias who fought as part of the Popular Mobilisation Forces – have taken major strides in responding to ISIL. That may potentially minimise any operational fallout from the physical exit of US personnel.

“There are real capabilities and real experience in the Iraqi security forces. People I talk to in the military are quite confident that they can take on most threats against the sovereignty of Iraq,” former Ambassador Silliman said.

But while the Iraqi parliament approved a partial cabinet in May, several key security roles, including minister of defence, remain unfilled.

The Iraqi government also continues to lack a substantial air defence capability of its own, which could prove a major weakness if the domestic security situation were to spiral, Silliman said.

“This is one area where there will be vulnerabilities because it is clear that the pro-Iran militias have been willing to use drones and rockets and missiles against Iraqi targets inside Iraq, and as of right now, the Iraqi military doesn’t really have a way to defend against that,” he said.

Kurdish officials have been among the most vocal critics of the US withdrawal, pointing to a barrage of attacks on Iraq’s semi-autonomous Kurdish region by Iran and Iran-aligned militias thwarted by US anti-missile and anti-drone weapons this year.

While experts say the US may maintain limited air-defence capabilities in Iraq to protect its diplomatic assets, the military has reportedly removed its Erbil-based Patriot and C-RAM defensive systems from the country as part of the withdrawal.

“The threat is real – we are vulnerable, we are being attacked,” Masrour Barzani, the prime minister of the Kurdistan Regional Government, told the Financial Times this week.

“Now, to be left alone without any, let’s say, appropriate defensive system,” he added, “it’s shameful.”

To be sure, the withdrawal of the remaining US troops is only one step in a larger, years-long effort to transform the US-Iraqi relationship from military to economic. Following the 2003 invasion as part of the US-led “global war on terror”, the US had initially withdrawn troops in 2011, only to redeploy them amid the rise of ISIL.

Speaking at the UNGA, al-Zaidi promised an economic “renaissance”, pledging to boost Iraq’s petrochemical industry and build new fossil fuel delivery routes beyond the Strait of Hormuz. The constriction of traffic in the strait amid the US-Israel war with Iran has had an outsized impact on Iraq, with its oil output dropping by as much as 60 percent in March.

For his part, during a meeting at the White House in July, US PresidentTrump pledged “a lot of deals” to come with Iraq, pointing to the country’s vast oil reserves.

Hamzeh Hadad, an adjunct fellow with the Middle East Security Program at the Centre for a New American Security, said there were no immediate signs the US planned a wholesale shift in its approach towards Iraq, which still houses the largest US embassy in the world in Baghdad and the largest consulate in Erbil.

But deeper economic integration may be stalled in the short term.

“It is important to note, for this to happen successfully, the situation in the region needs to improve,” Hadad said.

“Conflict around Iraq will always make economic cooperation more difficult. Not to mention, conflict gives armed groups an excuse to continue to exist.”

Lahib Higel, the deputy director of the MENA programme at the International Crisis Group, called on Washington to focus on cooperation, while avoiding “pressuring al-Zaidi into a military confrontation against pro-Iran groups that he is unlikely to win”.

“A better approach would be for the US to preserve bilateral security cooperation and support his efforts to strengthen state institutions over time,” Higel said in a social media post.

“Washington cannot dictate Baghdad’s relationship with Tehran, nor can Tehran dictate Iraq’s relationship with Washington,” she said. “What Iraq instead needs is the space to find its own balance.”

articles.title: Unearthed audit exposes vulnerable Dem's handling of COVID relief funds: 'Gross oversight'
articles.excerpt:
Scott Singer blasts Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., for a lack of oversight as director for the Florida Division of Emergency Management.

During his time as director for the Florida Division of Emergen...
articles.body_text:
Scott Singer blasts Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., for a lack of oversight as director for the Florida Division of Emergency Management.

During his time as director for the Florida Division of Emergency Management (FDEM), Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., allowed over $1 billion in COVID-19 relief funding to go out the door without required monitoring, records reveal.

The 2022 State of Florida Compliance and Internal Controls over Financial Reporting and Federal Awards flagged the weakness in its annual audit, stating, "FDEM did not monitor the activities of any subrecipients."

While Fox News Digital is not aware of fraud that may have been committed with those funds, the resurfaced audit casts an unflattering light on Moskowitz as he pursues re-election in one of the country’s most competitive districts.

It also raises questions about oversight efforts for state-level allocations for government funds, an issue Republicans have signaled merits more attention.

COVID CASH MEANT TO GET KIDS BACK ON TRACK TOOK SURPRISING DETOUR IN BLUE-STATE SCHOOL DISTRICT

Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., speaks to members of the media after a vote at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., June 23, 2025. (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Moskowitz’s FDEM approved $210,562,500 in funding to 39 local government recipients in the 2020-2021 fiscal year from the Coronavirus Relief Fund (CRF), according to the audit. The next year, it distributed $1,026,225,200 to 55 locations.

Taken together, the grants add up to $1.23 billion.

"Contrary to Federal regulations, the FDEM did not monitor the activities of CRF subrecipients," the audit states. "Such monitoring is to include, for example, reviewing subrecipient audit reports and determining whether management decisions are required for any audit findings related to the federal award."

According to the report, an acceptable level of oversight would normally include inquiries of the recipients as well as checks like onsite evaluations.

"Monitoring of the subrecipient must include reviewing financial and performance reports, following up and ensuring that the subrecipient takes timely and appropriate action on all deficiencies pertaining to the federal award detected through audits, on-site reviews and other means," the audit states.

MOSKOWITZ REJECTS RICK SCOTT'S CLAIMS HE'S 'SCARED TO DEATH' OF SOCIALISTS, BEHOLDEN TO HASAN PIKER

Rep. Jared Moskowitz, D-Fla., speaks during a news conference to address MAGA Republicans' decision to prioritize the impeachment of President Joe Biden over other domestic issues in the United States Dec. 13, 2023, in Washington, D.C. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for Congressional Integrity Project)

Notably, Moskowitz wasn’t head of FDEM for the entire 2020-2021 fiscal year. He resigned from the post at the end of April, two months before the end of the fiscal year in June, making him the head of the FDEM for the vast majority of the 2020-2021 audit cycle but not the complete window.

Even so, his congressional opponent, Republican candidate Scott Singer, believes the responsibility lies squarely on Moskowitz’s shoulders.

"When Jared Moskowitz ran a state agency, federal regulators and state auditors found that there was a gross lack of oversight of billions of dollars of taxpayer funds, a lack of reporting, a lack of review of where the funds were going," Singer said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"And that's unacceptable, especially with public tax dollars. But it's not surprising."

Singer argued the audit echoed earlier questions about Moskowitz's work involving disaster recovery funds.

He pointed to an incident in 2017, when Moskowitz, as an attorney for AshBritt, a disaster-cleanup company, had renegotiated compensation from the City of Parkland after Hurricane Irma. Disclosure reports showed that he was being paid over $400,000 by the company while also serving as a state legislator.

"When Jared was a state representative, he went to his own city and demanded that they pay more for hurricane cleanup that went to a disaster recovery company that paid him millions," Singer said.

"We can't afford people who are continuing to do the same thing. A gross oversight of funds and self-dealing."

When asked about Singer's criticisms, Moskowitz's campaign fired back, stating that the congressman was proud of the work that he did, noting that he had been reappointed to the role by a Republican governor.

"As Director of FDEM, I worked directly for Governor DeSantis and his administration. Florida had one of the best COVID responses in the country," Moskowitz told Fox News Digital.

TRUMP ANTI-FRAUD DIVISION'S FUTURE RESTS WITH SENATE DEMS AFTER BIPARTISAN HOUSE WIN

Democratic Rep. Jared Moskowitz said that eliminating the penny "might be the best thing" Trump has done since taking office. (Fox News Digital)

"I left almost a year before this report was issued as I had to leave the agency to be with my dad, who was battling cancer. Governor DeSantis appointed me again to the Broward County commission. To my knowledge, Florida COVID spending has passed the FEMA audit for reimbursements," he added.

Moskowitz also pointed out that he had received praise from even Republicans for his disaster-related work, including from Singer himself. Moskowitz shared communications between them in which Singer said the state was "in a much better place because of what you've done."

Having cleared their parties’ respective primaries, Moskowitz and Singer will face off in the Florida general election Nov. 3.

Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

articles.title: Ella Langley addresses criticism in emotional concert speech as 'Choosin' Texas' dominates charts
articles.excerpt: Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path during an interview tied to the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards held March 26, 2026, in Los A...
articles.body_text:
Ella Langley speaks about her deep appreciation for supporters and how their connection transformed her path during an interview tied to the 2026 iHeartRadio Music Awards held March 26, 2026, in Los Angeles.

Ella Langley shared an inspiring message with her fans during her latest concert.

During one of her recent performances in Columbus, Ohio, the 27-year-old singer opened up about the amount of criticism she's received since her breakthrough in the industry, saying, "I don’t think I’ve ever had more opinions on myself in my life than I have in this last year."

"The way I look. The way I speak. The way I dress. The way I move. The way I sing. The way I write," she explained per a TikTok video. "At first it bothered me. I won’t even lie. At first I was like, what am I going to do about this? I don’t know, if this is what I’m signing up to do, I don’t know about this."

She went on to say that what she "signed up" for was to make music, but if this was going to continue for her entire career, she thought, "I don’t know if I’m strong enough for this, Lord."

Langley shared how she is able to handle the criticism that comes with being in the public eye. (Jason Kempin/Getty Images)

ELLA LANGLEY TELLS FANS TO STOP MEASURING THEMSELVES AGAINST SOCIAL MEDIA IN VIRAL CONCERT VIDEO

While it bothered her at first, Langley explained she began imagining that the critiques were being aimed at her younger self who put in the hard work to get her to where she is today, which put into perspective how strong she actually has had to be.

"That’s the girl that rode in the 15-passenger van night after night after night. She rode in a Honda Accord night after night after night, chasing her dream, living on bar food, living on tip jar money. She didn’t have anything but a dream and the ability to get up and do it every single day. So I’m going to tell you right now, I am proud of that girl that everybody seems to be picking on a little bit," she said.

The singer recently went viral when a video of her turning down a fan who asked her out on a date following her concert in Knoxville, Tennessee.

In the video, TikTok user Tiki is heard taking his chance to ask the singer out on a date, shouting through a fence in the parking lot, "Ella, how many likes to take you on a date?" She replied, "Not enough in the world," as she frowned and looked away.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Langley received criticism recently for her reaction to a fan asking her on a date. (Rich Polk/Billboard via Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Some fans in the comments section were not pleased with Langley's reaction to the fan. "This rubbed me the wrong way. And I like her," one fan wrote. Another asked, "Literally what is her problem?"

Another added, "She could have laughed and said no in a whole different way."

Along with the online criticism comes career highs and record-breaking songs, as Langley's hit song, "Choosin' Texas," has stayed at the top of the Billboard Hot 100 list for a historical 24 consecutive weeks.

The previous record was held by Mariah Carey for her hit, "All I Want for Christmas Is You," which spent topped the list for 22 cumulative weeks between 2019 and 2026.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Langley made history with her song "Choosin' Texas." (Ethan Miller/Reuters)

"I’m genuinely trying to find the words to help explain what’s going on in my brain today," she said on Instagram last week. "What? I don’t know. Thank you so much. Thank you for loving this song, for listening to it. I feel like… I just don't even know what to say at this point. I'm running out of hyperboles to describe how I feel, so I will just let my dog in the background show you his excitement," she continued as her dog barked.

Adding: "Just thank you. Thank you so much. It's changing my life. It's changing the lives of the writers of this song. It's changing the lives of my family, and it is truly growing an atmosphere for something I'm gonna be able to do the rest of my life and I just… today doesn't feel like a real thing," Langley said. "It feels fake and somebody's going to come in and be like 'haha we're kidding the whole time just kidding.'"

"I'm really excited to just experience a moment like this in my life," she said.

The country music star told her fans that she was going to celebrate tonight before ending with, "Choosin' T… that's the one huh?"

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Arizona lawmakers demand independent investigation into ASU hockey workout that left player in coma
articles.excerpt: Arizona State University launches an investigation into a demanding team workout that left one hockey player, Matthew Mayich, incapacitated. Family attorney Rob Carey joins 'Fox & Friends First' to sh...
articles.body_text:
Arizona State University launches an investigation into a demanding team workout that left one hockey player, Matthew Mayich, incapacitated. Family attorney Rob Carey joins 'Fox & Friends First' to share details about the incident and demand accountability from athletic officials.

As seven anonymous Arizona State Sun Devils hockey players called for their coaching staff to be placed on administrative leave, the House and Senate education chairs have also called for an independent investigation into the team’s workout that left a player hospitalized, still fighting for his life in a coma.

Matthew Mayich remains on life support after an Aug. 20 workout in the blazing Arizona heat left him unconscious, and far worse than the players who wrote a 26-page letter that said they were initially told by head coach Greg Powers and the staff.

On Monday, House Education Committee Chairman Matt Gress and Senate Education Committee Chairman Hildy Angius called on the Arizona Board of Regents to retain an independent investigator to examine the workout.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Matthew Mayich poses for a portrait after being selected 170th overall by the St. Louis Blues during the 2023 Upper Deck NHL Draft at Bridgestone Arena on June 29, 2023, in Nashville, Tenn. (NHLI via Getty Images)

In a letter sent on Monday to Board Chairman Doug Goodyear, Gress and Angius cited unresolved questions about whether the school followed its own policies and allegations from the anonymous players, who all fear retaliation by the current staff for speaking up about their account of the incident.

Arizona State conducted an initial review, which acknowledged the hockey team’s staff didn’t submit a plan of training activities as part of the investigation. Also, the review’s findings were that Mayich didn’t receive proper hydration and had inadequate medical care after collapsing.

ARIZONA STATE HOCKEY PLAYER, BLUES DRAFT PICK HOSPITALIZED AFTER COLLAPSING DURING TRAINING

"Seven players who were on that field have raised serious questions that ASU’s own review does not answer," Gress said in a press release. "We need an independent investigation to determine whether ASU followed its own rules, who was responsible for protecting these athletes, and what happened when Matthew Mayich showed signs of distress. ASU should not be left to investigate its own conduct and decide whether anyone should be held accountable."

The lawmakers are asking the Board of Regents to figure out who authorized the workout, which the players said was led by an ex-U.S. Army Green Beret, as well as "whether required vetting and heat-safety procedures were followed, why ASU’s strength and conditioning professionals did not review the workout, and why the final exercise proceeded after the outside consultant left."

They also wish to have protection against retaliation for student-athletes and witnesses in this case.

"Student-athletes should never have to choose between telling the truth and protecting their scholarship, roster spot, or playing time," Angius said. "If players fear retaliation for speaking about what happened to a teammate, the Regents need to act. They should protect these students and appoint an investigator who answers to the Board, not ASU."

A response by Gress and Angius was requested from the Board of Regents by Oct. 9.

Matthew Mayich spent last season with the Clarkson University Golden Knights before transferring to Arizona State. (Photo by Dan Squicciarini/NurPhoto)

In the 26-page letter from the players, which was obtained by The Athletic, the players said they were put through a "grueling" workout by the Green Beret that day, but while the ASU review said players were given a water break about 20 minutes into the workout, that wasn’t the case, they claimed.

They said that the water break was around 40 minutes into the 75-minute activity, but it was just a few seconds. The players added that only about eight players actually drank water because they were the first to finish a bear crawl drill beforehand.

"The first of us to finish had a few seconds at the bottles before being ordered back while others, including Matthew, were still crawling," the players’ letter read. "This was the only water break."

The players also wrote that the ex-Green Beret admitted forgetting they needed a water break, but added he didn’t drink water during combat missions.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

As for Mayich, a draft pick of the NHL’s St. Louis Blues, the players wrote that their teammate showed signs of distress early on in the workout, saying he started to become disoriented during the bear crawl. Also, he was unable to carry a teammate during a buddy carry exercise.

"No one at ASU properly monitored him during the workout and no one intervened," the letter read.

When Mayich eventually collapsed, the players claim he remained in direct sunlight for several minutes, which contradicts Arizona State’s report stating he sat upright twice. The players say that Mayich needed to be carried into the shade by his teammates.

As for cooling him down, the players said the only things available were towels from a cooler, water from the bottles and a garden hose. This was in Arizona heat, which in August regularly sits somewhere in triple digits.

"Matthew spent most of his ‘off’ time in his air-conditioned apartment because the heat was too oppressive for him," the players wrote about the Ontario native. The players also noted that outdoor workouts prior to Aug. 20 last around 15 minutes before going back inside.

Matthew Mayich poses for a portrait after being selected 170th overall by the St. Louis Blues during the 2023 Upper Deck NHL Draft at Bridgestone Arena on June 29, 2023, in Nashville, Tenn. (NHLI via Getty Images)

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Powers was asked earlier this month about the incident, but he didn’t speak due to the "difficult time" it has been for the program. Players, though, said their head coach downplayed Mayich’s condition when initially speaking to them about it. They said that he simply suffered a "little heat stroke," while adding they were "closer to making the Frozen Four because of the workout…"

"From what we could tell, at no point did Coach Powers seem to appreciate the severity of the situation," the players’ letter added.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.body_text:
Curtis Wilkie Beasley was executed for the 1995 killing of Carolyn Monfort, after supreme court declined to intervene

A 77-year-old Florida man was put to death on Tuesday for his conviction in a deadly hammer attack on a woman decades ago, becoming the 16th person executed to date this year in the nation’s busiest death chamber.

Curtis Wilkie Beasley was pronounced dead at 6.12pm following a lethal injection at the Florida state prison near Starke, authorities said. He was convicted of first-degree murder, robbery and grand theft auto in the 1995 hammer attack on Carolyn Monfort at her home south of Orlando.

The Florida supreme court recently rejected arguments that executing a man Beasley’s age who is suffering from cognitive decline would amount to cruel and unusual punishment, and the US supreme court declined to intervene on Tuesday. Beasley is Florida’s seventh prisoner over 70 to be executed this year.

Beasley also was the 29th person, all men, who have been executed around the US this year. On Wednesday, Tennessee plans to execute a woman for the first time in 200 years by giving a lethal injection to Christa Pike, 50, for killing a classmate in a jealous rage when both were teens.

Court records show that Beasley had been staying at Monfort’s home in Dundee in August 1995 while he was pressure-washing and painting nearby apartments owned by her son-in-law. Monfort’s daughter went to her home after being unable to reach her for two days and found her body in a blood-splattered laundry room.

Monfort had suffered multiple blunt-force trauma injuries to the head, and a bloody hammer head was found wrapped in a towel nearby, according to investigators.

Authorities began searching for Beasley after a witness reported seeing him driving what turned out to be Monfort’s car. Investigators determined Beasley had traveled to Miami and later relocated to Alabama, where he was arrested while working under a false name for an electrical company, officials said. He was convicted and sentenced to death in 1998.

The state is getting closer to last year’s total of 19 executions, which was a record in Florida since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida executed two prisoners in one day, the first state in nearly a decade to do so.

Two more executions are scheduled for this year, but the Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, who leaves office in January, has temporarily paused the next one.

William Lee Thompson, 74, is scheduled to be executed 13 October for raping and fatally beating a woman at a Florida motel in 1976. After a doctor this month determined Thompson might be suffering from dementia, DeSantis ordered a panel of three psychiatrists to examine him to determine if he is competent to be executed.

DeSantis issued similar stays in 2023 and 2025 but both executions proceeded after evaluations.

William Reaves, 77, has a 20 October execution date. He was convicted of fatally shooting a deputy outside a convenience store in 1986.

All Florida executions are carried out via injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the state’s department of corrections.

articles.title: US supreme court allows Trump officials to resume deportations to third countries

Conservative majority temporarily lifts lower-court decision as liberal justices dissent from ruling

The Trump administration may deport immigrants to a “third country”, or a country other than their...
articles.body_text:
Conservative majority temporarily lifts lower-court decision as liberal justices dissent from ruling

The Trump administration may deport immigrants to a “third country”, or a country other than their homeland, without providing them an opportunity to dispute due to humanitarian concerns, the supreme court said in a brief order on Tuesday.

The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a lower court decision that determined immigrants being deported to a third country needed notice to argue they are at risk of persecution.

As is typical in emergency orders, the justices did not explain why it granted the administration’s request.

The three liberal justices of the court, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the ruling.

Tuesday’s ruling will take effect while the supreme court considers the larger question in the case. Justices said they would hear oral arguments in December.

articles.title: Stephen A Smith and ESPN should consider a full-time reunion with Skip Bayless
articles.excerpt: The latest ratings are in and they prove Stephen A. Smith is nothing without Skip Bayless on First Take. Dan Dakich breaks down the data behind the massive ratings spike and explains why the "Face of ...
articles.body_text:
The latest ratings are in and they prove Stephen A. Smith is nothing without Skip Bayless on First Take. Dan Dakich breaks down the data behind the massive ratings spike and explains why the "Face of ESPN" is officially in a state of desperation.

Last week, Skip Bayless returned to ESPN to reunite with his former debate partner, Stephen A. Smith, on "First Take." Under a new agreement, Bayless will appear on the program on the final Friday of every month.

The history between Bayless and the show is significant.

ESPN built "First Take," its daily debate program, around Bayless in 2007. Like Smith today, Bayless initially debated a rotating cast of analysts. He pushed the network to give Smith a recurring role, but executives initially resisted after Smith's previous, unsuccessful stint at ESPN.

SKIP BAYLESS BOOSTS STEPHEN A'S SLUGGISH "FIRST TAKE" RATINGS BY 24% ON THEIR REUNION SHOW

Smith eventually joined the show on a weekly basis and became Bayless' full-time debate partner in 2012.

Together, Bayless and Smith drew an average audience that well exceeded ESPN2's typical viewership, often outperforming the main ESPN channel during the same time slot.

Bayless left ESPN for FS1 in 2016 to launch "Undisputed," a similarly formatted debate program designed to compete directly with "First Take." Bayless partnered with Shannon Sharpe at FS1, while Max Kellerman replaced him at ESPN.

Comparing the success of the two programs warrants context. ESPN reached three to five times as many morning viewers as FS1 at the time. Even so, "First Take" lost more than 20% of its audience after Bayless departed. ESPN responded by moving the program from ESPN2 to ESPN. After the move, "First Take" attracted roughly twice the audience of "Undisputed."

The gap widened after Kellerman left "First Take" and Sharpe exited "Undisputed." By 2023, "First Take" regularly drew three to four times as many viewers as its FS1 rival. Bayless ultimately left the network in 2024.

Sports journalist and television personality Skip Bayless appears on television screens in the control room during the live filming of ESPN2's daily sports talk show First Take at ESPN Headquarters in Bristol, Conn., on Aug. 30, 2013. (Christopher Capozziello/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Smith and Bayless are in different positions than they were in 2012.

At the time, Bayless was one of ESPN's most viral personalities. Smith had been relegated to local radio. Today, Smith is among the most influential figures in sports media, having recently signed a five-year, $100 million contract with ESPN. Until recently, Bayless was the one without a television platform.

Bayless' transition to digital media has been rocky. His weekly show with his wife averages about 1,000 views per episode on YouTube. He has not uploaded a new episode of his eponymous podcast in nearly a year. He has, however, recently gained traction through a venture with former NFL cornerback Aqib Talib called "Gridiron."

Although Bayless accepted an invitation to become a monthly contributor to "First Take," the arrangement is undoubtedly awkward. Returning to the program you built, alongside the co-host whose career you helped build, in a limited role cannot be easy.

It is also reasonable to wonder whether Bayless believes Smith owes him the same full-time opportunity that he extended in 2012. OutKick asked Bayless about that possibility following Friday's show. He did not respond.

The current version of "First Take" has grown stale. The format of pairing Smith with two rotating panelists produces inconsistent results. Michael Irvin, Dan Orlovsky, Chris "Mad Dog" Russo and Marcus Spears are strong contributors. Much of the remaining rotation, however, consists of interchangeable ESPN personalities, including Chris Canty, Kimberley Martin and Domonique Foxworth.

Perhaps a more effective approach would be to reduce the size of the rotation and feature only the program's strongest personalities alongside Smith and perhaps Bayless. On Friday, Spears joined Smith and Bayless for most of the show.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Stephen A. Smith attends Fanatics Fest NYC for a special editon of ESPN's 'First Take' at the Javits Center in New York City on July 17, 2026. (Getty Images/Fanatics)

"First Take" is still one of ESPN's highest-rated programs, but its growth lags behind the network's other studio shows. ESPN's monthly press releases routinely emphasize year-over-year gains for "Get Up," "The Pat McAfee Show," "NFL Live" and other programs, but not "First Take's."

Smith himself has acknowledged the importance of evolving the program. Explaining why he wanted Kellerman removed from the program, Smith said it was necessary "to keep things fresh and make changes every three years." It has now been five years since Kellerman's departure.

Bayless also brings out a different side of Smith, one that is generally more appealing to viewers.

The formula is simple but effective: Bayless makes a provocative claim, Smith responds with theatrical indignation, Bayless defends his position and the segment often ends in good fun.

While not the most intellectually rigorous form of television, it's better than the pandering, faux sophistication that has come to define too much of sports television.

Despite his branding, Smith rarely offers a profound opinion on sports. He believes the Cowboys underachieve, Stephen Curry is the greatest shooter in NBA history and LeBron James is the second-greatest player in basketball history. Those are conventional positions.

In fact, Smith tends to expose a lack of depth when he tries to offer a unique opinion. His recent commentary on LSU, Shedeur Sanders and Deshaun Watson suggested a limited familiarity with those subjects.

Smith performs best opposite a contrarian, like Bayless. The same dynamic explains why his appearances with Will Cain and Sean Hannity on Fox News often generate more interest than his solo political monologues.

Smith, who has frequently responded to criticism from OutKick, may view that comparison as a slight. It is not. Michael Wilbon and Tony Kornheiser remain the gold standard of sports television because their partnership is stronger than either host individually. The same principle applies to Smith and Bayless.

Stephen A. Smith and Skip Bayless attend The Paley Center for Media 2014 Spring Benefit Dinner at 583 Park Avenue in New York City on May 28, 2014. (FilmMagic)

With Pat McAfee surpassing Smith as ESPN's most relevant personality, a full-time reunion with Bayless would represent an opportunity to regain momentum. Debating Chris Canty one day and Gerald McCoy the next does not.

ESPN may be reluctant to approve a broader reunion for Bayless. Our understanding is that there was pushback about bringing him back even in a limited role.

Executive Mike Foss, who oversees the network's daily studio programming, has emphasized a shift away from "embrace debate," the slogan that once defined "First Take," in favor of authenticity and conversation. Ratings trends suggest that approach has benefited much of ESPN's daytime lineup. But not "First Take."

"First Take" is a debate show. The program has never fully recaptured the cultural relevance and virality it reached with Bayless and Smith together.

If the plan is to keep Stephen A. in a prominent role as he approaches 60, ESPN should lean into what made him successful in sports-talk television.

It is also 2026. As Hollywood continues to demonstrate, nostalgia remains a more reliable commercial strategy than reinvention.

articles.title: Dumping stocks after Trump’s 2016 win was ‘stupid,’ NYU professor admits
articles.excerpt:
NYU professor Scott Galloway says selling stocks after Trump’s 2016 win cost him 40%

NYU professor Scott Galloway said Monday on "The Prof G Pod" that he sold all of his stocks in an emotional reacti...
articles.body_text:
NYU professor Scott Galloway says selling stocks after Trump’s 2016 win cost him 40%

NYU professor Scott Galloway said Monday on "The Prof G Pod" that he sold all of his stocks in an emotional reaction to President Donald Trump’s 2016 election victory, taking a major tax hit before buying back into a more expensive market months later, a decision he estimated cost him 40% of his liquid net worth in stocks.

Galloway, a professor of marketing at NYU Stern, called the move his "biggest investment mistake" during the "Office Hours" edition of the podcast as he warned listeners about allowing emotions to drive investment decisions.

"So when he was elected in 2016, I sold all my stocks," he said. "That was stupid. The market ripped for the next year. There was so much insecurity about him actually winning that the fear had been priced in. Stocks ripped up."

Scott Galloway said selling all his stocks after Trump’s 2016 election victory was his "biggest investment mistake" and estimated it cost him 40% of his liquid net worth in stocks. (Getty Images for Vox Media)

THE RICH HAVE ONE FINANCIAL HABIT MOST AMERICANS IGNORE AT THEIR PERIL

Galloway said the selloff also triggered taxes on significant capital gains while he was living in New York. He said he returned to the market about six months later after stocks had risen between 10% and 20%, compounding what he described as the cost of the decision.

"So you could argue, at least notionally, that decision cost me 40% of my liquid net worth in stocks," Galloway said.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle told Fox News Digital Tuesday that Galloway’s continued criticism of Trump reflected what he characterized as an obsession with the president.

"Scott Galloway should immediately seek psychiatric help to treat his severe case of Trump Derangement Syndrome that has completely rotted his peanut-sized brain," Ingle said.

Galloway said he triggered a major tax bill by selling his portfolio before buying back into the market months later at higher prices. (SXSW Conference & Festivals via)

GOVERNMENTS CAN TAKE YOUR STOCKS WITHOUT YOUR PERMISSION. IT HAPPENS ALL THE TIME

Galloway criticized Trump, saying he believed the president's economic and foreign policies could ultimately damage the U.S. economy.

"I think the president is a f---ing idiot and a stain on the American experience and that the grand sum of all of these head up your a-- economic and foreign policy decisions will eventually crash this economy or result in long-term structural damage that will take decades if not generations to repair," Galloway said.

The stock market rose substantially following Trump's 2016 presidential victory. According to the federal government's 2017 Economic Report of the President, the S&P 500 climbed 3.4% in November 2016 and reached a then-record high later that month. The 2018 report said the index went on to gain 19.4% in 2017, posting increases in 11 of the year's 12 months.

White House spokesman Davis Ingle blasted Galloway after the NYU professor renewed his criticism of Trump while recounting the costly investment decision. (REUTERS/Annabelle Gordon)

DAVID MARCUS: TRUMP DERANGEMENT SYNDROME ISN'T MENTAL ILLNESS, IT'S MASS HYSTERIA

Galloway said his experience reinforced his view that investors should remain in the market rather than attempt to anticipate political or economic turning points. While discussing current elevated valuations, he recommended diversification instead of trying to predict exactly when stocks will decline.

"Trying to guess when the top happens is dangerous," Galloway said. "Probably my biggest investment mistake was the emotional reaction I had to the 2016 election of Donald Trump."

"And what the government does matter, but the majority of the economy just grinds on regardless of who is tweeting what or not tweeting what," he continued.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Galloway predicted Trump would ultimately abandon his 2024 presidential campaign as part of a plea agreement that would keep him out of jail. Trump remained in the race and returned to the White House after winning the 2024 presidential election.

Fox News Digital reached out to Galloway for comment, but did not immediately receive a response.

CJ Womack is an associate editor at Fox News.

CJ joined Fox News Digital's team in 2026, which highlights the vital role journalism plays in shaping politics and culture. He has years of experience analyzing and reporting on the news media.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

You can send news tips to cj.womack@fox.com and follow CJ on Twitter.

articles.title: ‘You make me want to throw up’: Republicans attack ex-special counsel Jack Smith at Senate hearing
articles.excerpt:
GOP senators lash out on Smith, who led criminal cases against Trump, with invective and inaccurate information

Former special counsel Jack Smith, who led two criminal cases against Donald Trump in 2...
articles.body_text:
GOP senators lash out on Smith, who led criminal cases against Trump, with invective and inaccurate information

Former special counsel Jack Smith, who led two criminal cases against Donald Trump in 2023, faced attacks from Republicans in a wide-ranging hearing on Tuesday that included a basketball mix-up, a reference to the tooth fairy and accusations of perjury.

In the Senate judiciary committee hearing on Tuesday, the Republican senator Eric Schmitt, of Missouri, raised perjury allegations against Smith, seemingly over a mix-up about the Atlanta Hawks and University of Iowa Hawkeyes basketball teams.

Schmitt, who called Smith a “dirtbag”, claimed the prosecutor went to Atlanta to attend a Hawks game on 3 February 2024, and insinuated Smith may have met with Fani Willis, the former Fulton county district attorney who brought state charges against Trump.

But Smith denied ever attending an Atlanta Hawks game. He later clarified that he attended a University of Iowa Hawkeyes game in Maryland to watch Caitlin Clark play.

The Democratic senator Amy Klobuchar, of Minnesota, admonished Schmitt for presenting the claim as evidence and accusing Schmitt of lying.

“I would just say, for a US senator to have false information, and imply, based on a confusion about the name of a team … that you were in another city, that you were somehow involved, that day, in what was happening in Georgia, and then call you a ‘dirtbag’, is something that deserves an apology,” Klobuchar said.

The Guardian has asked Schmitt’s office for comment.

The unusual exchange between Schmitt and Smith became a highlight of the hearing on social media.

Smith also testified to the Senate judiciary committee to defend his handling of two federal investigations into Trump – one related to efforts to overturn the 2020 election and the other regarding Trump’s mishandling of classified documents.

Both cases were dismissed before going to trial.

Republicans have accused Smith of bringing the investigations to undermine Trump and targeting Republicans in the process – including by subpoenaing phone records from members of Congress.

Smith has defended his practices, saying the subpoenas were necessary to collect evidence that Trump called members of Congress to try to delay the certification of the 2020 presidential election.

But Tuesday’s hearing was also defined by other tense exchanges between Republican senators and Smith.

The Republican John Kennedy, of Louisiana, appeared frustrated after raising accusations that former president Joe Biden or his White House staff told the then attorney general Merrick Garland to prosecute Trump – an allegation with no public evidence.

Smith said he did not know about conversations between Biden and Garland regarding the subject.

“Do you believe in the Tooth Fairy?” Kennedy asked Smith. “How about the Easter Bunny?”

The question elicited a response from Smith: “I no longer believe in the Easter Bunny.”

At one point, Kennedy told Smith: “You make me want to throw up in my mouth.”

Ted Cruz, a Republican senator from Texas who became increasingly angry while talking about Smith subpoenaing congressional members’ phone records, told Smith: “Javert from Les Mis would look at you with astonishment.”

Cruz insinuated that Smith used his position as a special counsel to target Republicans by requesting records from the Republican National Committee and other conservative lawmakers.

Darline Graham, the senator from South Carolina, used her time during the hearing to accuse Smith of “trying to bully” her brother, the late senator Lindsey Graham, and causing him stress with subpoenas.

But Smith pushed back on Darline Graham’s assertion.

“I believe your brother was a patriotic public servant. He was not a target of our investigation, and in fact he likely would have been a witness in our case,” Smith replied, adding that Lindsey Graham did not believe the 2020 election was stolen.

Democrats, meanwhile, used Tuesday’s hearing to highlight the 6 January 2021 attack on the US Capitol and accused Trump of inciting the violent mob with false claims of election fraud during the 2020 presidential election.

Cory Booker, the senator from New Jersey, declared the hearing “a farce”.

Booker and Delaware’s Chris Coons highlighted that the current administration had fired justice department staffers who worked on Smith’s team.

Despite the partisan divide over Smith’s appointment and prosecutions, Smith said he maintained a nonpartisan approach to the investigations into Trump and that his team had compiled enough evidence to prosecute the president.

“If asked whether to prosecute a former president today, based on the same facts, I would do so regardless of whether that president was a Republican or a Democrat,” Smith said in his opening statement.
