articles.title: Iran denies link to attack on airbase as UK minister warns of ‘proxies’
articles.excerpt:
Iran has denied any involvement in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford Airbase in the United Kingdom.

Iran’s embassy in London condemned in a statement on Monday the “fabricated speculations” lin...
articles.body_text:
Iran has denied any involvement in a suspected plot targeting the Fairford Airbase in the United Kingdom.

Iran’s embassy in London condemned in a statement on Monday the “fabricated speculations” linking Tehran to the incident. Five British nationals were arrested in the vicinity of the base, which hosts United States military aircraft that have been used to bomb Iran amid the conflict between the two countries.

The suspects were detained on Sunday morning on suspicion of the “preparation of a terrorist act”. Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said on Monday that the UK must be prepared to “confront” all security threats facing Europe and the world, adding: “We will act against the proxies of Iran.”

Iran’s embassy in London said that it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets”, asserting that the accusations would fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” in Britain.

Iran reserves the right to “take appropriate legal measures”, it added.

British police have not thus far linked Iran to the arrests as Counter Terrorism Policing continues investigating.

British security officials are exploring “multiple lines of enquiry” on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and “preparation of a terrorist act”.

The UK government gave the US authorisation to use bombers based at the RAF Fairford to strike Iranian missile sites that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz.

On Sunday, a source familiar with the investigation said an Iranian-linked motive is considered the most likely, while a Russian sabotage operation or an Islamist plot were also being looked at.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) had said in July that the Fairford base was a legitimate target.

British police arrested the five men after receiving a tip that three suspicious vehicles appeared to be heading towards the base in southwest England.

In their statement on Monday, the counterterrorism police identified the men as British nationals aged 23 to 25 from London.

On Monday afternoon, the head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing said the five were being released on bail “following extensive interviews and inquiries”.

Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor added: “To be very clear, this does not mean that the investigation is over. They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others”.

US President Donald Trump said the suspects had been looking to ‌do “big damage” and had been under investigation by British and US authorities “for a long time, and we got them”.

⁠UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham ⁠was due on Monday to chair a meeting of the COBRA emergency ‌response team as British authorities continue to investigate the incident.

articles.title: SpaceX’s showpiece Starship rocket reaches orbit for first time
articles.excerpt:
The largest rocket developed by SpaceX has successfully reached orbit, marking an important milestone for the private aerospace company.

“Starship is orbital,” mission control announced to cheers on ...
articles.body_text:
The largest rocket developed by SpaceX has successfully reached orbit, marking an important milestone for the private aerospace company.

“Starship is orbital,” mission control announced to cheers on a livestream on Monday that showed the spacecraft’s launch from a base in Texas in the United States.

The uncrewed spacecraft almost didn’t achieve the long-desired goal after one of its engines shut down too soon. But with everything else working well and the bad engine no longer needed, flight controllers decided after several tense minutes to proceed as planned.

Founder Elon Musk’s showpiece rocket – the biggest and most powerful ever built – carried 26 of the latest and most advanced Starlink satellites to join the 11,000 older models already providing internet service. It was Starship’s 14th full-scale launch from Texas’s southern tip in three years. The earlier test flights ventured no farther than the Indian Ocean halfway around the world, often crashing in flames and briefly skimming space.

This time, SpaceX was intent on circling the globe from an altitude of 275km (170 miles) – not just once but six times over almost 10 hours, ending with a Pacific splashdown near Chile. The first-stage booster wasn’t meant to return to the Starbase launch site, either, instead dropping into the Gulf of Mexico within minutes of the morning liftoff.

SpaceX wants to ensure that everything works before flying Starship back to Starbase. If the spacecraft breaks apart over land and rains debris onto people, “our popularity would diminish very rapidly”, Musk said at a business summit earlier this month. “That’s why we’re being extremely cautious here.”

If all goes well with this orbital debut, the next Starship will return to the launch pad with giant mechanical arms grabbing the hovering spacecraft. If the catch works – Musk gives it even or slightly better odds – then SpaceX will re-fly the spacecraft by year’s end or early next.

The 124 metre (407-foot) rocket was designed from the start to be fully reusable – a key to lowering launch costs. SpaceX managed to salvage the last Starship from the Indian Ocean in July. Engineers modified the newly launched Starship’s heat shield based on hands-on inspections from the recovered spacecraft, which is being tugged back to Starbase.

SpaceX is pressing hard to certify Starship for orbital flight, a vital step towards moon and Mars travel.

NASA’s Artemis III mission is coming up as soon as next summer, and will feature a triple-launch docking exercise in orbit around Earth between an Orion capsule full of astronauts and competing lunar landers. Jeff Bezos’s Blue Moon will blast off first, then Orion – which will close in for a linkup – then Musk’s Starship for a docking with Orion once Blue Moon launches.

The next mission – Artemis IV, slated for no sooner than 2028 – would have astronauts landing on the moon in either Blue Moon or Starship, whichever is ready first. Subsequent moonshots will alternate between the two billionaires’ landers.

Musk originally developed Starship for Mars, intending to launch scores of them with the red planet’s first settlers. For now, he plans to focus on the moon and use Starship to haul satellites into orbit by the truckload, phasing out the company’s frailer Falcon 9 rocket within several years. A second Starship launch site is nearing completion at Florida’s Kennedy Space Center and a third is planned for the US state of Louisiana.

articles.title: RAF Fairford live updates: Five men arrested near base to be released on bail, police say
articles.excerpt:
Counter terror police say earlier that they arrested five men who were British national in their 20s from London

UK security forces aware of suspected bomb plot, hints defence secretary

RAF Fairford...
articles.body_text:
Counter terror police say earlier that they arrested five men who were British national in their 20s from London

UK security forces aware of suspected bomb plot, hints defence secretary

RAF Fairford suspected bomb plot: have you been affected?

Taylor goes on to say that the five men in custody are being released on police bail later today.

“To be very clear, this does not mean the investigation is over,” he says. “They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.”

The men remain under investigation, he adds.

A farmer who claims to have alerted the police to a suspected terrorist bomb plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire has said she has had “no follow-up at all” from the authorities.

The woman told reporters on Monday that she did not see herself as a hero for having reported vans blocking a road near the base while on her way back from a party.

Five men from London were arrested in the village of Whelford, near to RAF Fairford, on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.

The village remained shut off on Monday afternoon, with people evacuated from their homes dispersed to family, friends, hotels and a leisure centre.

The farmer, in her 50s, said she had been travelling home with her husband and a “young lad” who works for them when she spotted the vehicles parked in a “really strange formation”.

double quotation markYou couldn’t drive between them on the road, and you also couldn’t drive up the farm drive, and I think this has been one of the funny things that people are saying: ‘How could you notice?’ But when you live in Whelford, you notice everything. We all know what cars each other drive, we know who we are, we know the people that cycle through regularly.

She said one of the vans had some “strange sign writing on it” and she initially believed it belonged to undercover police.

double quotation markWe had a bit of a look at the vans, established there was no one in there, tried to phone the number on the side, just in case we could get it moved so we could drive down to the farmyard, and the number didn’t work.

The five men who were arrested and subsequently released on bail are all British citizens, home secretary Shabana Mahmood has just told the Labour party conference.

She adds that the scene is “now safe” and the residents living near to the RAF base are now able to return home.

“Let this be a reminder: you will never defeat us,” he says.

Police are considering whether the foiled attack may have involved “proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state”.

Taylor says rapid mobilisation was necessary. He says often these plots involve people seeking “quick financial gain”, rather than being motivated by terrorism.

The police works “hand in glove with MI5” to keep the public safe “from a myriad of threats” and urges people to report anything that does not “look right”.

And that ends the assistant commissioner for specialist operation’s statement on the steps of New Scotland Yard.

Taylor goes on to say that the five men in custody are being released on police bail later today.

“To be very clear, this does not mean the investigation is over,” he says. “They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.”

The men remain under investigation, he adds.

Head of counter-terrorism policing Laurence Taylor is providing an update outside New Scotland Yard in London.

He says Gloucestershire police received a report of suspicious vehicles in the vicinity of RAF Fairford and arrested five men on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and later preparation of a terrorist act, under section 5 of the Terrorism Act.

“The men had been travelling in three vehicles and, overnight, those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination,” he says.

Police remain at the scene and a cordon remains in place. He hopes residents will be able to return to their homes later today.

Andy Burnham has said he will chair an emergency Cobra meeting later today in response to the RAF Fairfod incident.

Such meetings are convened to handle matters of national emergency or major disruption, including natural disasters, terrorist attacks and major industrial accidents.

Speaking to LBC this afternoon, Burnham said:

double quotation markWhat I can say is that I will chair a meeting of Cobra later this afternoon. Just to make sure we have the full picture of the full situation, very clearly, in our sights. And so maybe I’ll say more about that later today.

Nato’s supreme allied commander Alexus G. Grynkewich has warned the global security environment is “unsettled,” “complex” and “likely to become even more so over the next several years”.

“We were reminded of this again this past weekend in the United Kingdom, where five men were arrested on suspicion of committing offences under the Explosives Act in preparation of a terrorist act near RAF Fairford,” he said.

Speaking to the European parliament’s Committee on Security and Defence, Grynkewich said that China, Russia, Iran and North Korea are “collaborating in ways directly counter to all of our global interests.”

He said the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East showed “not only a changing character of warfare, but also a sobering preview of how future simultaneous and potentially protracted conflicts might look: multi-theater conflicts, multi-domain conflicts, and highly autonomous conflicts.” You can read more in our Europe live blog here:

The Liberal Democrat MP for South Cotswolds, Roz Savage, whose constituency covers the military base, said she would be writing to the prime minister and the defence secretary with her concerns about the events over the weekend, adding that her constituent’s safety was a priority.

Speaking to reporters in the village of Kempsford, Gloucestershire, which is situated adjacent to RAF Fairford, Savage said:

double quotation markEver since it was first announced six months ago that RAF Fairford was going to be used as the base for US military airstrikes on Iran, I’ve been asking questions of the government about whether they can assure my residents, my constituents, of their safety.

They had given that assurance, however, I feel that the events of this weekend do cast that into doubt. It actually makes my blood run cold when I think how close we may have come to disaster this weekend.

But in the longer term, I have a lot of questions about what happened or so nearly happened this weekend.

Who knew what? When did they know it? Where was the ball dropped? What more could have been done to secure the safety and security of my constituents?

The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, has refused to comment on Donald Trump’s claim that the suspects arrested near RAF Fairford had been under surveillance for a long time. Speaking at a meeting on the fringe of the Labour Party conference in Liverpool, Milband, who took up the post in July, said:

double quotation markYou will understand there is an ongoing investigation and a limit to what I can say.

What I will say is, as I said in my conference speech, I think this emphasises the vigilance we need against the threats that our country faces, including on British soil.

I think that the counter-terrorism police, the intelligence services, the police themselves have done a really important job in arresting the suspects.

Beyond that, sorry to be disappointing, I’m not going to say anymore because it’s a live investigation.

The US air force said its personnel based at RAF Fairford “remain vigilant” but “for operational security reasons we will not discuss specific force protection measures”.

The US embassy in London, meanwhile, has warned Americans in Britain to be cautious and mindful of their personal security.

American B-1 and B-52 bombers have taken off from Fairford for operations during the ongoing US-Israel war on Iran.

Iran has previously said it considers any base used to attack its territory a legitimate target. But Iran’s embassy in London has this afternoon strongly rejected any speculation linking the country to the arrests of the five suspects near RAF Fairford.

The Reform leader, Nigel Farage, has told the BBC that the UK has to take national security a lot more seriously as he claims “we have allowed into Britain cells of people who intend to do us harm”.

In a separate interview with LBC, Farage said: “If a farmer coming home from a party at 1am is the person that discovered these people, it does raise questions.”

“Donald Trump is telling you more about the national security situation and about what I privately know, than we, as a country, are being told. We are in a very, serious situation. A very serious situation.”

Iran rejected ⁠the ⁠suggestion that ​it is ⁠linked to the ⁠five ​arrests ‌made ‌at ‌Britain’s Fairford airbase, according to ⁠a statement from ​the Iranian ​Embassy ​in ​London.

double quotation markThe Embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.

The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.

The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives.

Gloucestershire constabulary were initially alerted to three suspicious vans travelling towards RAF Fairford at 12.45am on Sunday and it is unclear what action was taken in the hour that followed.

The local farmer who spotted the vans and a group of masked men said she initially called the Ministry of Defence police but there was no answer, so called 999 at 1.36am and armed police arrived around 10 minutes later, PA reported.

She said the police had “dropped the ball”, telling journalists:

double quotation markWho knew that a farmer would have to roll their sleeves up and report the activity?

The counter terror police said the investigation has a “significant” number of resources dedicated to it, with military assets still deployed at the location.

The police confirmed that a cordon remains around the site and will be reviewed later today.

With roughly 85 properties located within the cordon, it is not clear when local residents, who were initially evacuated to Cirencester leisure centre before being relocated to Cotswold District Council’s chambers, will be allowed to return home.

The five men arrested over the suspected bomb plot near RAF Fairford are all British nationals in their 20s from London, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) has said.

In a statement, the counter terror police said they were detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act contrary to Section 5 of the Terrorism Act. They are a 24-year-old from Camden, north London; three men aged 23, 24 and 25 from Westminster, central London, and one aged 24 from Willesden, north-west London.

The police say the suspects, who were arrested in the village of Whelford on Sunday morning, are being held under the Police and Criminal Evidence Act and a custody extension has been approved until later today. The CTP are still working to establish a motive for the incident.

Counter Terrorism Policing senior national coordinator, deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, said in a statement:

double quotation markThis is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the MOD, and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community.

I know this has been incredibly disruptive for local people, but I’d like to reassure them that our activity is in the interest of national security, but most importantly in the interest of their own safety.

I’d also like to thank the emergency services for their response, including the armed officers who first attended the scene, not knowing what they may face.

I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident, and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time, Counter Terrorism Policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.

In an earlier post, we mentioned how the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, said the local farmer who contacted police after seeing a road blocked by “three white vans” near RAF Fairford only had a “partial picture” of events.

The farmer, from the village of Whelford, has now responded to those comments made by Streeting this morning. She told reporters:

double quotation markI know it’s been said by some of the higher ups today that I didn’t have the full picture, but the picture I had was three extremely unusual vehicles parked in the middle of our village and a group of unknown men running around. So, that’s my picture, I don’t know whether that’s the full picture or not.

double quotation markI don’t know how he knows what picture I’ve got, I’ve never met him. Literally nobody in any sort of official capacity has been in touch with me or anyone else in the village, no follow up at all, even now, from the police who had my number when I reported it to 999, so it’s just very odd.

Donald Trump suggested on Sunday that authorities already had the suspects under investigation. Asked about these comments, the farmer told reporters: “I think that’s wonderful, but perhaps they could have kept a closer tab on them.”

articles.title: Staff killed and wounded in Russian strike on Kyiv’s science academy
articles.excerpt:
Moscow’s jet-powered drones pummel Ukraine’s capital in switch to daytime attacks

Russia has hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv with a drone, killing at least one person in the late...
articles.body_text:
Moscow’s jet-powered drones pummel Ukraine’s capital in switch to daytime attacks

Russia has hit the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv with a drone, killing at least one person in the latest daytime attack on Ukraine’s capital.

Flames tore through the historic building on Monday as people clambered out of first- and second-floor windows to escape, in dramatic scenes increasingly familiar in the heavily bombarded city.

At least one person was killed and three others were wounded, according to Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, who said the injured had been taken to hospital.

The 19th-century building stands close to the German embassy, the National Opera, St Volodymyr’s Cathedral and several government buildings.

Anatoliy Zagorodny, the president of the national academy, said the blast struck while many staff members were inside. Standing outside the burning building, he said he did not know why Russia had targeted a leading centre of scientific research. “We are not connected with the military. This is an attack on science. It is terrorism,” he said.

He said he feared some of his colleagues could still be trapped inside the academy.

While the sciences building is a civilian scientific institution, it has longstanding ties to Ukraine’s defence sector. Among those injured in Monday’s strike was Volodymyr Horbulin, the academy’s first vice-president and a former high-ranking security official.

Another Russian drone struck a nearby private medical centre, killing at least one person.

Russian strikes over the past week involving missiles and increasingly sophisticated jet-powered drones have hit apartment blocks, offices, warehouses and datacentres across the capital, killing and wounding civilians almost daily and giving Kyiv an increasingly frontline feel as it faces some of its most sustained bombardment since the early stages of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022.

The drone and missile campaign is designed to grind down public resilience and damage the economy. Monday’s double strike is likely to raise fresh concerns over Ukraine’s ability to protect even the most heavily guarded parts of the capital.

The newer jet-powered drones fly faster and are harder to intercept than the older Shahed or Geran-2 models that were the backbone of Moscow’s air campaign. Ukraine is racing to develop and manufacture interceptors capable of bringing them down.

Moscow has also changed its tactics, launching more attacks in daylight hours so that residents in major cities have to spend more of the day under air raid alerts.

Buildings hit during daytime strikes are often occupied because many Ukrainians work through drone alerts rather than spend hours in shelters.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, called on western countries to intensify their pressure on Russia.

“Every Russian terrorist attack is a loss of life that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total,” he wrote on X on Monday. “The world must understand that terrorists will go further if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine. And we cannot turn a blind eye to such brutal strikes.”

Russia has signalled that its attacks on Ukraine could intensify and US-brokered efforts to end the war show little sign of progress.

“Ukraine will have to pay a price for the actions that have taken place in recent months,” the Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, told reporters on Monday, referring to Ukrainian strikes deep inside Russian territory. “That is happening right now.”

articles.title: Republicans zero in on key player accused of helping Democrat fundraising giant hide foreign cash
articles.excerpt:
Rep. James Comer, R-KY, joins Fox Across America with guest host Paul Mauro to provide an update on the House Oversight Committee's investigation on alleged fraud by fundraising platform ActBlue.

FIR...
articles.body_text:
Rep. James Comer, R-KY, joins Fox Across America with guest host Paul Mauro to provide an update on the House Oversight Committee's investigation on alleged fraud by fundraising platform ActBlue.

FIRST ON FOX: House Republicans' investigation into Democrats' main fundraising platform is heating up on the heels of an explosive report that raised questions about whether left-wing candidates' campaigns were raking in foreign cash.

Top House GOP committee chairs are summoning ActBlue attorney Ronald Machen for a closed-door interview sometime before Oct. 9, Fox News Digital has learned. A letter sent to Machen Monday morning stated that information he previously disclosed to investigators appears to contradict other data that has been collected, specifically on ActBlue's verification standards for making sure a donor is a U.S. citizen.

"On September 11, 2026, you provided a briefing to the House Administration, Judiciary, and Oversight and Government Reform Committees regarding the accuracy of ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones’s prior statements to Congress about ActBlue’s donor and passport collection processes," the letter said.

"Your review appears to be nothing more than an after-the-fact sugarcoating of ActBlue’s misconduct and Ms. Wallace-Jones’s misrepresentations to the House Administration Committee."

ANOTHER ACTBLUE LEADER PLEADS FIFTH AS HOUSE INVESTIGATES ALLEGED FOREIGN DONATIONS

ActBlue CEO Regina Wallace-Jones prepares to testify before the House Administration Committee's hearing on "Preventing Fraudulent Donations: Transparency, Verification, and Accountability" in Washington, D.C., on June 10, 2026. Wallace-Jones invoked the Fifth Amendment during questioning. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images)

The letter was sent by House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Wis., Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, R-Wis., and House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., who lead the panels probing ActBlue.

ACTBLUE CO-FOUNDER PLEADS FIFTH AMENDMENT IN CLOSED-DOOR HOUSE GOP GRILLING

ActBlue is a massive platform for campaigns to raise money that's used by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate, among others.

Republican lawmakers have long accused the company of having lax verification standards for donors, something ActBlue has said it actively improved since the start of the GOP's probe. But a new report released earlier this month, first reported by Fox News Digital, appears to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from.

FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT

Chief among the GOP's concerns is ActBlue's passport number verification. According to the report, the field only requires the correct number of characters for a U.S. passport number rather than a valid code for a donation to be accepted.

The Monday letter also points to a 2024 "contemporaneous review by ActBlue’s then-outside counsel, former Biden White House Counsel Dana Remus" which allegedly found "'a substantial risk that some of the funds' raised for Democrat campaigns and causes by ActBlue 'were impermissible contributions from foreign nationals.'"

Committee on House Administration Chairman Bryan Steil, House Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, and House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer are investigating ActBlue. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images; Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

Remus' review further found that "passport checks did not always happen" and were "never conducted" when donations were made using third-party fiscal platforms like Apple Pay or PayPal, the letter said.

The Republican chairs said Machen's prior comments to Congress "conceded that your 'forensic' review found that ActBlue processed and accepted donations with foreign indicators even though ActBlue failed to identify a 'passport number' or 'other indicia of eligibility' for the donor.

HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE

"Nonetheless, you defended Ms. Wallace-Jones’s representations to Congress by arguing that ActBlue’s compliance and vetting policy was 'as close to 100 percent as it could be,'" the letter said.

"Documents produced to the Committees undercut your assertion. These documents demonstrate that if a donor did not have a U.S. passport or a U.S. address, an ActBlue employee retained the ability to determine an 'alternative method of verifying the [donor’s] citizenship.' This means an ActBlue employee could put 'a placeholder,' including 'ACTBLUEXX,' 'in the passport number field of [the donor’s] ActBlue account.' The placeholder allows ActBlue to accept all subsequent contributions from the donor without requiring a U.S. passport number."

ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES

The letter said Machen's review was also limited to 2023, arguing it left out potentially valuable information about 2024.

"As such, the review did not accurately represent the totality of ActBlue’s foreign donation vetting and donor outreach practices during the 2024 election cycle. In fact, documents produced to the Committees show that ActBlue relaxed its vetting practices twice in 2024—data that your narrow 'forensic' review did not capture," the letter said.

ACTBLUE SUES TEXAS AG KEN PAXTON, ALLEGING POLITICAL RETALIATION OVER DEMOCRATS' FUNDRAISING

It also charged that he disputed Remus' analysis without going into detail on how he established his own findings.

ActBlue has consistently denied any wrongdoing and dismissed Republicans' most recent findings in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"There’s nothing to see here. After we released findings of a third-party forensic analysis that completely undermined a central claim that they have made against ActBlue, Republicans are refusing to move on," ActBlue said. "Instead, they are orchestrating another political stunt before rushing out of town weeks early to go campaign. This coordinated campaign against ActBlue isn’t about the facts, or legislating, it’s about Republicans’ efforts to silence organizations they believe threaten their agenda."

A closed-door interview summons is not the same as a subpoena, which is a legally binding order.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Investigation of alleged gang-rape at Cornell University fraternity house reopened
articles.excerpt:
Outrage over treatment of alleged offenders, members of Chi Phi fraternity, has grown since lawsuit was made public

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Prosecutors in New York said on ...
articles.body_text:
Outrage over treatment of alleged offenders, members of Chi Phi fraternity, has grown since lawsuit was made public

Sign up for the Breaking News US newsletter email

Prosecutors in New York said on Monday that they have reopened an investigation into the alleged gang-rape of a student at Cornell University after an outcry over “leniency” shown to seven fraternity members named as the perpetrators.

According to lawyers for the student, who filed a civil lawsuit against the university and her alleged attackers earlier in September, only two members of the Chi Phi fraternity were expelled after the October 2024 incident, in which she said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours.

None of the seven were arrested, they said, and the others were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions.

On Monday, Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, said his office was looking again at the case, after the woman, who was 20 at the time of the alleged assault, presented allegations in her lawsuit that were “dramatically different” from the statement she gave to police two years ago.

“It’s our intention to present the case to the Tompkins county grand jury with Jane Doe’s cooperation,” Van Houten told ABC News, using the name from the lawsuit to identify the woman.

“We want to re-examine whether there’s additional evidence that we were not aware of in November of 2024, that exists now that would change our assessment of the case and would result in the grand jury finding that there was criminal conduct.”

Outrage over the treatment of the alleged offenders has grown since the lawsuit was made public. The woman, who quit the university afterwards, said she went to visit a friend at the Chi Phi frat house in an already intoxicated state – and was made to snort a drug they told her was ketamine.

While they sexually assaulted her, she alleges, a message was sent to a frat house Snapchat group called Chi Phi Actives that stated there was “free pussy upstairs”.

At least five other frat members showed up and joined in, she said, and her ordeal lasted until about 5.45am. She made a report to campus police about three weeks later.

Cornell’s vice-president for university relations, Kyle Kimball, issued a statement on 21 September calling the allegations “deeply disturbing”. Kimball’s statement claimed the Ivy League institution’s offices of civil rights, student conduct and community standards carried out a number of inquiries at the time.

“The Xi chapter of Chi Phi fraternity remains barred from our campus,” Kimball’s statement also said. “Federal privacy law prohibits Cornell from disclosing specific information regarding individual students and we therefore are unable to make a public statement on any other disciplinary response.

“Violations of university policies could lead to sanctions up to and including suspension or expulsion. We will respond in detail through the legal process.”

An attorney for the student told CBS News that none of the alleged perpetrators faced legal consequences for their conduct, and nobody in the frat house that saw the message did anything to stop the rapes from taking place.

“Not one of these guys was arrested,” said the lawyer, Thomas Giuffra. “Not one. That I can tell you for a fact.

“There were so many people that could have prevented it and they didn’t. I’ve never seen anything like it.”

Giuffra also countered the statement of Van Houten, the Tompkins district attorney, which lays out what he said the alleged victim stated in her original police complaint from November 2024.

“She never says that she was drugged without her knowledge,” Van Houten said.

“She admits to taking drugs and alcohol voluntarily and with knowledge. She does not allege that she was forced to engage in any acts. She does not say that she was physically helpless or unconscious or incapacitated at any point during the time at the fraternity house.”

Giuffra told ABC News that neither the district attorney or Cornell police ever followed up with his client.

“In my experience, speaking with an abuse survivor requires delicacy, understanding and specialized training,” he said.

“An average university police officer would not have these skills. It would be the role of a specially trained detective or district attorney. However, Ms Doe was never contacted by anybody with those skills.”

On Sunday, the Academy Award-nominated actor Florence Pugh posted a lengthy statement on Instagram about Giuffra’s client, praising the “unbelievably powerful” victim and her “strong will”.

“This is really the moment where we need our men to be as horrified and as sickened as us,” Pugh wrote. “You need to be leading conversations about how we change the allowance and complicity of this behaviour as much as we are.”

Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organizations. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: Five UK nationals arrested at RAF Fairford released on bail
articles.excerpt:
Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state

Five British nationals have been released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of te...
articles.body_text:
Police say alleged offences could have been committed ‘knowingly or unknowingly’ on behalf of a foreign state

Five British nationals have been released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of terror offences at RAF Fairford, police have said.

They added that the alleged offences under investigation could have been “actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state”. Police have been reported to be investigating whether Iran is behind the alleged offences.

The men were pictured on Sunday being apprehended, shirtless, near the RAF base in Gloucestershire, which is being used by the US air force in its operations against Iran. Police said three of them were 24, one was 25 and one 23, and three resided in Westminster, one in Camden and the other in Willesden.

The head of counter-terrorism policing, Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, said on Monday afternoon: “I can confirm that following extensive interviews, and inquiries, the five men who were arrested are being released on police bail this afternoon.

“To be very clear, this does not mean the investigation is over, they are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others. They absolutely remain under investigation as we explore multiple lines of inquiry. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day and we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.”

Taylor asked the public to remain vigilant and to report anything suspicious to police. He also noted the nature of threats to the UK often “becomes visible to us as criminal activity often at a small scale committed by individuals whose primary aim is not terrorism but a quick financial gain”.

The suspects were arrested in Whelford on Sunday morning after reports of three vehicles travelling towards the airbase at 12.45am. They were detained on suspicion of offences under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act contrary to section 5 of the Terrorism Act.

Counter-terrorism policing said investigators examined the scene overnight and had been carrying out a range of activity that had led to multiple new lines of inquiry.

Eighty-five households were evacuated from the village on Sunday and a large police and emergency services presence has been there since then.

Police said they were using “significant numbers of resources, including military assets” at the location. “We are working hard to minimise disruption to local communities, but ask for their patience, as our work continues at the scene,” they said.

A cordon remains in place at the location and police said they would be reviewing it later on Monday.

The deputy assistant commissioner Vicki Evans, counter-terrorism policing’s senior national coordinator, said: “This is a hugely complex and large-scale operation, involving local and national policing, the MoD [Ministry of Defence] and local agencies, who are working together to progress the investigation and support for the community.

“I know this has been incredibly disruptive for local people, but I’d like to reassure them that our activity is in the interest of national security, but most importantly in the interest of their own safety.

“I am very aware of the levels of speculation about the motivation behind this incident and the geopolitical questions that are being raised. However, I ask that at this time counter-terrorism policing are given the space to work carefully and clearly.”

Officers have been investigating whether Iran may be behind the suspected bomb plot. In July, Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps publicly noted RAF Fairford’s use by US bombers, warning the UK that “any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces”.

In a statement on social media on Monday, the Iranian embassy in the UK said: “The embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in London categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.

“The circulation of such fabricated speculations, particularly in the aftermath of the criminal acts of aggression committed by the United States and the Israeli regime against the Iranian people, will serve no purpose other than to fuel Iranophobia propaganda in the UK.

“The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives.”

articles.title: Trump administration to slash clean car rules aimed at cutting climate emissions
articles.excerpt:
Environmentalists decry move that relaxes requirements on automakers to control pollution from gas-powered cars

The Trump administration on Monday announced it was slashing clean car rules that had b...
articles.body_text:
Environmentalists decry move that relaxes requirements on automakers to control pollution from gas-powered cars

The Trump administration on Monday announced it was slashing clean car rules that had been aimed at reducing planet-heating emissions and boosting electric vehicles.

The move, which was criticized by environmentalists, relaxes requirements on automakers to control pollution from gasoline-powered cars and light trucks for model years 2022 through 2031.

The new rule, announced by the Department of Transportation, reverses a push by the Biden administration to accelerate the transition to EVs. Transportation is the largest source of climate emissions in the United States, accounting for about 28% of total US greenhouse gas emissions according to the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

Monday’s move follows the Trump administration’s rollback of the government’s ability to impose requirements to track, report and limit climate-heating pollution from cars and trucks.

Donald Trump said on Truth Social Saturday that the less stringent mileage requirements would “take the waste out of building cars in America” and save families “thousands on a new, beautiful and safe car”, while boosting auto production in the US.

Trump has repeatedly pledged to end what he falsely calls an EV “mandate”, referring incorrectly to Joe Biden’s target that half of all new vehicle sales be electric by 2030. No federal policy has mandated auto companies to sell EVs.

Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, hailed the new initiative – called Freedom Means Affordable Cars – which the agency said would reduce the average cost of new vehicles by $1,300, and save consumers $138bn over the next five years.

Duffy said: “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

Green groups condemned the new rules. Dan Becker, director of the Center for Biological Diversity’s safe climate transport campaign, said that the final rule “ignores the feasibility of clean technology and the millions of fuel-efficient cars already on the road”.

“Trump is tanking sensible mile per gallon standards at the worst possible time for consumers, who are getting hit with sky-high prices at the pump,” Becker said in a statement. “Consumers will pay the price for these reckless rollbacks while Trump’s Big Oil and Big Auto buddies reap the short-term profits.”

Katherine García, director of the Sierra Club’s Clean transportation for all campaign, vowed the environmental group would fight the rule and said that the loosening of fuel standards would “make driving more expensive too”.

Fuel economy requirements set out how far new vehicles need to travel on a gallon of gasoline. The Biden administration had increased required fuel efficiency for cars by ​8% annually for model years 2024 and 2025, 10% for 2026 and 2% annually from 2027 to 2031.

The Trump ‌administration ⁠in December proposed retroactively revising down the 2022 model year fuel economy standard and then raising it between 0.25% and 0.5% annually through 2031. It estimated its ​proposal would cut average ⁠new vehicle costs by $930 each.

But it would increase fuel consumption by about 100bn gallons through 2050, fuel spending by $185bn and carbon dioxide emissions ​by about 5%, the department said.

The American Lung Association’s president and CEO, Harold Wimmer, said the new rule will “create more air pollution, harm health and accelerate climate change”.

Wimmer added: “For decades, fuel economy standards have ensured that new cars, SUVs and pickup trucks are more efficient, which saves lives and money. There is no reason to weaken standards that are technologically feasible and have a direct benefit for the quality of the air people breathe.

“Children are particularly vulnerable to the effects of traffic pollution, which can impede lung growth, cause new cases of pediatric asthma, make asthma symptoms worse and increase kids’ risk of respiratory infection and diseases.”

Wimmer added that making new cars cleaner has widespread public support, citing a poll the group did that found a strong majority of voters supported stricter limits on vehicle emissions.

articles.title: Golders Green stabbings no longer being treated as suspected terrorism
articles.excerpt:
Police say attack on two Jewish men in north London in April now being treated as alleged hate crime

The stabbings of two Jewish men in Golders Green, north London, in April are being treated as an a...
articles.body_text:
Police say attack on two Jewish men in north London in April now being treated as alleged hate crime

The stabbings of two Jewish men in Golders Green, north London, in April are being treated as an alleged hate crime and not as a terrorist attack, police have said.

Essa Suleiman, 45, was arrested by the Metropolitan police on suspicion of attempted murder shortly after the stabbings on 29 April.

At the time, police said they were treating the attacks, in an area with a large Jewish population, as suspected terrorist offences.

Suleiman has also been charged with attempted murder over the unconnected stabbing of another man earlier that same day.

On Friday, Suleiman appeared in court for a pre-trial hearing where he denied all charges and the prosecution said the case was no longer being treated as a suspected terrorism case.

In an email message sent to communities across London on Monday, the Met said: “At the hearing, the Crown Prosecution Service advised the court that it will not be pursuing a terrorist connection as part of the criminal proceedings.” It said it would treat it instead as a suspected hate crime.

“We understand this announcement may cause concern, particularly within the Jewish community, given the impact this incident had locally and against the backdrop of recent incidents affecting Jewish communities across London. We would like to reassure residents that the seriousness with which this matter is being treated has not changed.”

Cmdr Helen Flanagan, the head of counter-terrorism policing for London, said: “I fully recognise the impact this incident has had on the three victims as well as the public, particularly the Jewish community.

“I’m also aware this news comes shortly after the arrests of two men in Manchester for a suspected plot to target the Jewish community during the High Holy Days period. Counter-terrorism policing continues to work closely with the Met police to provide as much visibility and security as we can to Jewish communities across London.”

The victims of the Golders Green attacks were Shloime Rand, 34, and Moshe Shine, 76. The victim of the other stabbing earlier the same day in south London was Ishmail Hussein.

The case continues and the full trial is scheduled for March 2027.

articles.title: Queensland anti-corruption commission investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints in a year
articles.excerpt:
Statistics showed there is ‘almost no chance’ a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently, expert says

Get our breaking news email, free app o...
articles.body_text:
Statistics showed there is ‘almost no chance’ a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently, expert says

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Queensland’s anti-corruption commission has investigated just 20 of more than 6,000 complaints of suspected corruption in the past year, as the state government comes under renewed pressure to implement a years-late recommendation to end the practice of police investigating police.

The statistic was revealed in Queensland’s Crime and Corruption Commission’s annual report, tabled in state parliament on Friday afternoon.

It revealed the CCC assessed 6,198 corruption complaints in 2025-26. It referred 4,244 back to the agency concerned, including the police, local government and public service departments.

University of the Sunshine Coast criminology professor Tim Prenzler said the statistics showed the state was still operating a “discredited” approach, “facilitating misconduct through impunity”.

Prenzler was one of the key experts who advised the landmark 2022 commission of inquiry into police responses to domestic violence.

The inquiry considered numerous cases of conflicts of interest and lack of independence in police investigations of its officers. In one case, a police officer was even tasked with investigating their own actions.

Subsequent reporting by the Guardian has also revealed allegations by former police officers that the QPS covered up its own failures prior to domestic and family violence deaths and that in other cases policing failures were never properly investigated.

It recommended creating a new independent organisation – known as a police integrity unit – to investigate all complaints against police by May 2024, as one of its “four highest-priority recommendations”.

Both parties of government backed the recommendation, but progress has stalled.

Prenzler said the statistics showed that there was “almost no chance” a complaint made against a government department like the police would be investigated independently.

“From the outside, the CCC looks like a powerful independent agency that will thoroughly investigate all allegations and suspicions of public sector misconduct, protect parties, and provide justice,” he said.

“In reality, complainants and whistleblowers will have their expectations dashed as their matter is referred back to the agency involved and they will be doubly traumatised by the process.”

He said there was no rational justification for delaying the recommendation.

“Setting up the police integrity unit must be amongst the easiest things a government could do.”

The state’s police minister, Dan Purdie, said police “have got really robust systems when it comes to complaints about police”.

“All of those matters are overseen by the CCC. That’s been the case for a long time, and they review all of those matters,” he said.

The CCC assessed 6,198 complaints in 2025-26.

It retained 20 for its own investigation. It referred 4,244 to the “appropriate agency’”, with 46 referred subject to CCC monitoring, 375 with a requirement for advice on its outcome, and 3,823 referred without any oversight.

It also assessed 1,934 complaints as “requiring no further action”.

Asked if the unit would be established by the 2028 state election, Purdie referred the question to the attorney general.

Unlike New South Wales’ Icac, the CCC is also responsible for investigating crimes like murder and rape that don’t involve corruption.

The CCC held 16 days of corruption hearings in 2025-26 but more than 100 days of crime hearings, its annual report revealed.

The annual report revealed the number of corruption complaints has been steadily increasing, up about 47% in the last four years.

articles.title: Avanti West Coast to be renationalised in March
articles.excerpt:
Rail operator which linked London to Birmingham, the north-west and Glasgow had highest number of cancellations across network

Avanti West Coast will be renationalised in spring, as prime minister An...
articles.body_text:
Rail operator which linked London to Birmingham, the north-west and Glasgow had highest number of cancellations across network

Avanti West Coast will be renationalised in spring, as prime minister Andy Burnham declares “enough is enough” for passengers who have put up with a rail service “that has failed them time and time again”.

The rail operator, which is one of the worst in the country for train delays and cancellations, will come under public ownership from March when its contract ends.

The Labour government has been nationalising passenger rail services across the country as their contracts have expired, as the public body Great British Railways prepares to take full oversight in 2027.

Avanti had among the highest proportion of train cancellations in Britain, at 7.1% from April to June this year.

The company connects the north and south of England, with its service running from London to Manchester and Liverpool.

Burnham has previously complained about high prices on Avanti, with tickets for peak-time returns from Manchester to London as high as £300.

The prime minister wrote on social media that “for years, people have been expected to put up with Avanti’s cancellations, delays, overcrowding, and a service that has failed them time and time again”.

“So my Labour government is bringing Avanti West Coast into public ownership at the earliest opportunity in March next year. That means passengers, not shareholders, will come first.

“More investment, fewer delays, and a renewed focus on getting the basics right. We’re putting essential services back in public hands and building a railway that actually works for the people who use it.”

Avanti, which has the worst punctuality rating for any large rail company in the UK, has also cut multiple services in the past year, including the 7am train between Manchester and London.

The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, – who will formally announce the decision in her speech at Labour conference on Tuesday afternoon – added that “for years, we’ve heard stories of Avanti underperforming, with passengers left paying the price”.

She added that the Labour government “is committed to putting essential services back in public hands, connecting people to opportunity and delivering growth in every postcode and this move reflects that commitment”.

Andy Mellors, managing director at Avanti West Coast, said: “We’re proud of what we’ve achieved over the last six years – from refurbishing our Pendolino fleet and introducing our new Evero trains to running more services than ever before.”

He said the improvements had given “customers greater choice, more capacity and better connectivity, while we’ve continued to innovate to shape the future of the west coast and wider rail industry”.

articles.title: Children forced to give up school for work as fighting upends daily life in Yemen
articles.excerpt:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm

In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons ...
articles.body_text:
Renewed fighting between Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni forces has shattered four years of relative calm

In the mornings, 13-year-old Muneer Farie went to school, and in the afternoons he helped his father feed the livestock. He took his studies seriously, dreaming of becoming the first teacher in his family of farmers.

As fighting approached his village in al-Wazeyah district in Taiz, Yemen, two weeks ago, Muneer’s focus started to drift from his lessons. The classroom echoed with the distant sounds of explosions and gunfire. His home was suddenly on the frontline of renewed fighting between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government.

“We heard there was fighting in surrounding areas but we didn’t expect it would reach our village that fast,” Muneer said. “As soon as the sounds of clashes approached our village, we took our livestock and important belongings and fled home early in the morning.”

He and his family fled south-west, moving to a camp set up for displaced people in al-Shimayateen, Taiz. They arrived penniless and lacking even the most basic supplies.

Muneer and his family are some of the more than 130,000 people displaced by recent fighting in Yemen, which started in September when the Houthis launched a renewed military campaign and rapidly moved south-west, seizing control of towns along the Red Sea coast.

The Houthis’ campaign interrupted years of relative calm that had prevailed over Yemen, with frontlines remaining broadly static since a UN-mediated ceasefire came into force in 2022.

The Houthis are now battling government forces and a Saudi air campaign to seize strategic highlands and supply lines on the outskirts of Taiz. Civilians have been driven out of their homes by the fighting, fleeing airstrikes and missiles.

Muneer and his brother, instead of studying, now sell socks and other cheap products in the markets outside his displacement camp. His classroom has been replaced by a small tent where he and his five siblings and parents crowd together in the humid night air.

He joins the more than 3.2 million children whose studies were interrupted by Yemen’s civil war prior to this month’s escalation.

“Studying is important, but not in a situation like this where we are struggling to get enough food, water and other necessities,” he said. “For now, I will keep working until the war ends.”

His father, Ghaleb Farie, has been forced to ask his sons to work so that the family can scrape together enough to survive life in the displacement camp. Farie hopes the camp will be only a temporary home and that he can soon return to his village, but he is not optimistic as new displaced people arrive every day.

“What I was told by neighbours who have been displaced for longer is that the first few months are difficult and I will adapt,” Farie said.

Life has also grown harder for those who have remained in their homes. Abdulwasea Abdu, the principal of Musaab Ibn Umayr school in Taiz, tried to keep the doors of his school open for as long as possible to give children a sense of normality. But that normality was shattered two weeks ago when a missile fell nearby, exploding in sight of the students.

“On the day the missile struck, we witnessed severe panic among them, with crying and screaming due to the explosions. Some children showed psychological trauma as a result of the intensity of the blasts,” Abdu said.

The school was forced to close its doors, depriving the more than 600 pupils of their education. Abdu watches the battlefield developments closely, searching for a let-up that will let him resume classes, but so far the situation has been too chaotic.

“The area faces fighting from multiple fronts – south, west and north – which makes it difficult to take any steps toward resuming classes at the moment,” Abdu said. He fears that many of the children out of school and displaced will be forced into child labour.

The resumption of fighting has upended life for residents of south-west Yemen. Clashes severed the main road between the now Houthi-controlled port city of Mocha and government-controlled Taiz. The road is a vital artery for goods as it is one of the only in the area wide enough for large trucks and passenger buses.

Interrupted commerce has increased the price of basic goods, compounding the crisis, particularly for displaced people.

“It is civilians who bear the cost of military escalation, and it seems that we in Taiz are paying a particularly heavy price, as commodities no longer reach us easily,” said Essam Nabil, a 56-year-old carpenter in Taiz city. He added many people had begun giving up meat and resorting to cheaper foods.

The fighting has disrupted other, more mundane facets of daily life. Asaad, an expatriate who works in Saudi Arabia and asked to be identified only by his first name, can no longer take a direct trip back from Yemen.

“This reminds me of the early years of the war in Taiz, when the main roads were blocked and we had to travel through Aden before heading to Saudi Arabia,” Asaad said. “Now, we are repeating the same expensive and arduous journey.”

articles.title: Chancellor John Healey to promise ‘new age of industrialisation’ in speech to Labour conference – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Healey to announce new facilities to maintain nuclear submarines on the Clyde

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, has accused John Healey of offering the Labour conference “reheated announcements...
articles.body_text:
Healey to announce new facilities to maintain nuclear submarines on the Clyde

Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, has accused John Healey of offering the Labour conference “reheated announcements” in his speech later.

Referring to Labour briefing overnight that three new floating docks will go ahead on the Clyde (see 7.54am), Griffith said:

double quotation markThese are more reheated announcements without clarity on where the money is coming from. Additional docks were announced months ago in the defence investment plan, which still has a £4.7bn black hole.

John Healey resigned warning that Labour’s failure to fund defence was making Britain unsafe. Now that he is chancellor, he still won’t fund the 3% target he walked out over.

Labour are running scared of making the tough choices needed to pay for Britain’s defence. All they can offer is reannounced docks and more hot air from Healey.

Good morning. John Healey, the chancellor, is the main speaker at the Labour conference. He was a surprise appointment to replace Rachel Reeves, he is unveiling his budget four weeks on Wednesday, and some of the pre-briefing suggests when the budget does come, it will be a relatively low-key affair, with a lot of decisions postponed until the spending review next year. And so we are definitely not expecting huge announcements at lunchtime today.

But there will be some striking language. Healey is going to promise a “new age of industrialisation”.

According to the overnight briefing from Labour, he will explain that in these terms.

double quotation markMy politics were shaped by the industrial heartlands of South Yorkshire. Today, on the site of the Orgreave pit, is Rotherham’s Advanced Manufacturing Park. Our coal mines are not coming back. But this is how Britain’s industrial past is being remade now for the modern world. This is the new age of industrialisation. A new confidence in Britain.

And he will also announce that the government is commissioning “three new floating docks for the Royal Navy’s submarine service at HM Naval Base Clyde” to provide maintenance for nuclear submarines.

Known as Programme Euston, plans for the new docks were first set out in 2023 and are expected to upgrade Faslane’s facilities for the next generation of British submarines, the Press Association reports. The Ministry of Defence has previously said they are expected to come into service in the early 2030s, and the docks form part of a wider £15bn upgrade programme for the Royal Navy’s shipyards.

10am: The Labour conference opens. The first main speaker is Wes Streeting, the defence secretary.

10.30am: Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, addresses the conference.

11.10am: Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, speaks at the start of a debate on workers’ rights and reindustrialisation.

Noon: John Healey, the chancellor, gives his speech.

2pm: Heidi Alexander, the transport secretary, addresses the conference, in a debate covering transport and insourcing.

2.30pm: Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, speaks at an IPPR fringe event. Other cabinet ministers speaking at fringe events include Lisa Nandy, the culture secretary, at a Think Labour event; Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, at an IPPR event; Streeting at a BAE event; and Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, recording a What’s Left? podcast.

After 3.20pm: Alex Norris, the justice secretary, and Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, speak at the conference in a debate covering crime.
